p.seg: What Heaven and Earth value is humanity;
what sages esteem is righteousness;
what virtue and righteousness accomplish is wisdom;
what the wise and discerning seek is learning.
Even the most sagely
are not born with knowledge;
even the most talented
are not born with ability.
Thus, the Records say:
Huángdì took Fēnghòu as his teacher;
Zhuānxū took Lǎopéng as his teacher;
Dìkù took Zhùróng as his teacher;
Yáo took Wùchéng as his teacher;
Shùn took Jìhòu as his teacher;
Yǔ took Mòrú as his teacher;
Tāng took Yīyǐn as his teacher;
King Wén and King Wǔ took Jiāngshàng as their teacher;
the Duke of Zhōu took Shùxiù as his teacher;
Confucius took Lǎodān as his teacher.
If these words are trustworthy,
then one cannot but follow a teacher.
These eleven rulers
were all supreme sages,
yet they still relied on learning,
so their wisdom became broad,
and their virtue became great.
How much more so for ordinary people?
Therefore, "If a craftsman wishes to do his work well,
he must first sharpen his tools."
If a scholar wishes to proclaim his righteousness,
he must first read his books.
The Book of Changes says:
"The noble person, by remembering many words and deeds of the past, accumulates his virtue."
Thus, a person having learning
is like an object being crafted.
Thus, the jade disc of the Xià sovereign,
the jade disc of Chǔ Hé,
though possessing the raw material of Bìan Hé's uncut jade,
if not carved and polished,
would not differ from gravel.
The ritual vessels of hú and guǐ,
the court and sacrificial garments—
at their beginning,
they were merely trees from the mountains and wilds, silk from silkworm cocoons.
If the skillful Chuí applies the marking line and axe to shape them,
and the women workers apply the five colors and weave them on the loom,
then they all become vessels for the ancestral temple and embroidered patterns of fǔfú,
fit to be presented to ghosts and spirits,
fit to be worn by kings and lords.
How much more so for the noble person's solid and steadfast nature,
and keen and quick talent,
supported by good friends,
taught by enlightened teachers,
adorned with the Rites and Music,
guided with the Odes and Documents,
instructed with the Zhōuyì,
and enlightened with the Spring and Autumn Annals—
would he not succeed?
The Book of Odes says:
"Look at that wagtail,
flying and calling.
I daily advance,
and monthly journey.
Rising early and retiring late,
do not disgrace those who gave you birth."
Thus, "the noble person is diligent all day long,
advancing in virtue and cultivating his tasks"—
not merely to enrich himself,
but to think of transmitting the fine reputation of his ancestors,
and thereby bring glory to his parents.
Confucius said:
"I once spent a whole day without eating,
and a whole night without sleeping,
in order to think,
but it was of no benefit.
It is not as good as learning."
"In farming,
hunger lies within it;
in learning,
salary lies within it.
The noble person worries about the Way, not about poverty."
Jīzǐ enumerated the six extremes;
the "Airs of the States" sang the "North Gate";
thus it is said that one does not worry about poverty.
Is it that one loves poverty and does not worry about it?
It is because the will has something to focus on,
making clear what is important.
Therefore, when the noble person seeks abundance,
it is not for fine food, beautiful clothes, excessive pleasure, music, or beauty,
but to reach his Way and advance his virtue.
The Way is completed through learning and preserved in books;
learning advances through exertion and is abandoned through indolence.
Therefore, Dǒng Zhòngshū never concerned himself with family affairs throughout his life;
Jǐng Jūnmíng did not leave his courtyard for years;
they were able to sharpen their learning and make their achievements illustrious
because their families were wealthy.
Being as wealthy and at ease as they were,
yet able to be as diligent and focused as they were—
these are talented men.
Ní Kuān sold his labor in the city lanes;
Kuāng Héng sold himself as a servant—
because they themselves were poor.
Being as poor and distressed as they were,
yet able to advance in learning as they did—
these are outstanding scholars.
The scholars of the present age constantly number in the tens of thousands,
yet those who reach the end of the path are not even a few tens.
What is the reason for this?
The wealthy are defiled by bribes and lose their focus;
the poor change their plans due to lack;
some have their years cut short by chaos and mourning.
This is why they lose their initial efforts and remain in childish ignorance.
Therefore, without the talent of Dǒng and Jǐng,
or the determination of Ní and Kuāng,
and yet wishing to forcefully abandon oneself, leave home, and spend long days at a teacher's gate—
there will certainly be little success.
These four men
had keen ears and eyes,
were loyal, trustworthy, honest, and brave—
these qualities are not necessarily without peers.
Yet when it came to establishing their fame and achievements,
their virtuous reputations and fine names never ceasing—
there was a reason for this.
What was the reason?
Simply because they were able to base themselves on the canonical classics of the former sages,
and fix their hearts on the bequeathed teachings of the Master.
Therefore, Zàofǔ running swiftly
would be exhausted after a hundred paces;
but relying on a carriage,
he can sit and reach a thousand miles.
A sailor floating on a log
would drown if the rope is untied;
but relying on a boat,
he can sit and cross rivers.
Thus, the noble person
is not by nature surpassing the world,
but is good at relying on things.
Human nature and disposition
cannot differ a hundredfold,
yet their wisdom and discernment can differ ten thousandfold.
This is not due to the material of their true nature;
there must be something borrowed to achieve it.
The nature of the noble person
is not necessarily fully illuminating,
but through learning,
his hearing and sight have no obscurity,
his mind and intellect have no stagnation.
He looks back to record the emperors and kings,
looks forward to settle affairs for a hundred generations.
This is the clarity of the Way,
and the noble person is able to borrow it to make himself illustrious.
Therefore, the Way in relation to the mind
is like fire in relation to the human eye.
In a deep pit or a dark room,
it is pitch black and nothing can be seen;
but when a bright torch is set up,
then all things become clear.
This is the illumination of fire,
not the light of the eye;
yet the eye borrows it,
and it becomes its own clarity.
The Way of Heaven and Earth,
the workings of the spiritual and bright—
these cannot be seen.
But studying the sagely classics,
and thinking with the mind on the Way and its methods,
then they all come into view.
This is the material of the Way,
not the clarity of the mind;
yet man borrows it,
and it becomes his own knowledge.
Therefore, for seeking objects in a dark room,
nothing is better than fire;
for seeking the Way in the present age,
nothing is better than the classics.
The classics are the warp.
They were created by the former sages;
the former sages, having obtained the essence of the Way, practiced it in their own persons,
wishing worthy people to encourage themselves and enter the Way.
Thus, the sages created the classics to bequeath to later worthies,
just as the skillful Chuí made the compass, square, level, and marking line to bequeath to later craftsmen.
In ancient times, Chuí was so skillful that
he could discern circles and squares with his eyes,
determine level and straight lines with his mind,
and he also created compasses, marking cords, carpenter's squares, and ink markers to instruct later generations.
If we were to have Xī Zhòng and Gōng Bān and others
abandon these four measuring tools,
and try to imitate Chuí by making their own,
they would certainly be unable to do so.
However, any ordinary or even unskilled craftsman,
holding the compass and square,
setting the level and stretching the cord,
can achieve the same skill as Chuí.
Therefore, Chuí used his mind to create the compass and square,
and later craftsmen use the compass and square
to match Chuí's mind.
Thus, craftsmen who use these tools
come close to Chuí's skill.
The wisdom of the ancient sages,
whose minds reached divine clarity,
and whose natures were aligned with the Dào and virtue,
also created the classics to bequeath to later generations.
If we were to have worthy men and gentlemen
abandon learning and inquiry,
and rely solely on their innate qualities to act,
they would certainly not be fully equipped.
But if they follow teachers and pursue learning,
and act according to the classics,
then their intelligent understanding
and grasp of virtuous principles
will also be nearly sufficient.
Therefore, the sages used their minds to create the classics,
and [later learners] use the classics to match the sages' minds.
Thus, worthy men who study the classics
have virtue close to that of the sages.
The Book of Songs says:
"We look up to the high mountain;
we tread the great road."
"Day by day and month by month,
learning accumulates and leads to brightness."
Therefore, for all who wish to display meritorious achievements and spread glorious deeds,
there is nothing better than learning.
The general principle of governance
is that nothing is better than suppressing the trivial and focusing on the essential,
and nothing is worse than neglecting the essential and adorning the trivial.
For those who govern a state, enriching the people is the essential task,
and rectifying learning is the foundation.
Only when the people are prosperous can they be taught;
only when learning is rectified can righteousness be attained.
When the people are poor, they turn away from goodness;
when learning becomes excessive, deceit and falsehood arise.
Entering learning brings order,
attaining righteousness brings loyalty and filial piety.
Therefore, the method of an enlightened ruler
is to focus on these two things,
using them as the foundation for achieving great peace,
and bringing about auspicious signs of prosperity.
To enrich the people,
agriculture and sericulture are the essential tasks,
while itinerant occupations are trivial.
For the various artisans,
practical utility is essential,
while clever ornamentation is trivial.
For merchants,
facilitating the flow of goods is essential,
while selling rare curiosities is trivial.
If these three adhere to the essential and avoid the trivial, the people will be prosperous;
if they neglect the essential and cling to the trivial, the people will be poor.
Poverty leads to hardship and forgetfulness of goodness;
prosperity leads to contentment and the ability to be taught.
For teaching and instruction,
the Dào and righteousness are essential,
while clever argumentation is trivial.
For speech and language,
sincerity and compliance are essential,
while deceitful elegance is trivial.
For exemplary scholars,
filial piety and fraternal duty are essential,
while social networking is trivial.
For filial piety and fraternal duty,
providing support is essential,
while ostentatious display is trivial.
For ministers,
loyalty and integrity are essential,
while flattery and favoritism are trivial.
If these five adhere to the essential and avoid the trivial, benevolence and righteousness will flourish;
if they neglect the essential and cling to the trivial, the Dào and virtue will collapse.
Being cautious of the essential and slighting the trivial is still acceptable,
but abandoning the essential and pursuing the trivial is deplorable.
Utilizing the way of Heaven,
sharing the benefits of Earth,
the six domestic animals bred in season,
and all things gathered in the fields—
these are the foundation for enriching the state.
Itinerant occupations and trivial pursuits,
which gather the people's profits,
are the source of impoverishing the state.
Loyalty, trustworthiness, caution, and prudence—
these are the foundation of virtue and righteousness.
Emptiness, deceit, and trickery—
these are the root of disorderly ways.
Therefore, diligent farming is the means to enrich the state.
Now, if the people abandon agriculture and sericulture
to pursue itinerant occupations,
gathering various profits
and concentrating them in one household,
although that private household may become wealthy,
the public treasury will grow increasingly poor.
The various artisans are employed to prepare tools.
Tools are best when they facilitate tasks,
and superior when they are sturdy and durable.
Now, artisans prefer to create carved and polished tools,
cleverly and falsely adorning them
to deceive the people and obtain bribes.
Although this benefits deceitful artisans,
the state's economy becomes increasingly afflicted.
Merchants are meant to facilitate the flow of goods.
Goods should be valued for their usefulness,
and their worth lies in being sturdy and durable.
Now, merchants compete to sell useless goods and extravagant luxuries,
to delude the people and seize their property.
Although this brings gains to excessive merchants,
the state's economy suffers increasing losses.
These three groups,
although outwardly they may have the private reputation of diligent wealth-builders,
inwardly they cause the public reality of harming the people and impoverishing the state.
Therefore, those who govern should
clearly supervise artisans and merchants,
not allowing them to become excessive and deceitful;
restrict and disgrace itinerant occupations,
not allowing them to monopolize profits.
Be lenient and supportive toward fundamental agriculture,
and honor and promote scholars.
Then the people will be prosperous and the state peaceful.
Teaching and instruction
are meant to advance the Dào and arts and to honor virtue and righteousness.
Now, scholars of learning
enjoy discussing empty and虚无 matters,
competing to write ornate and华丽 texts,
seeking to appear extraordinary in the world.
Common people, lacking discernment,
praise them highly,
which harms the substance of the Dào and virtue,
and greatly deludes the masses.
Poetry and rhapsodies
are meant to praise virtuous and丑 conduct,
and express feelings of sorrow and joy.
Thus, they should be温和 and雅致 to broaden culture,
using兴喻 to fully convey meaning.
Now, those who compose rhapsodies and颂歌
carelessly create冗长, argumentative, and awkward phrases,
competing to present false and baseless matters,
seeking to appear bizarre in the world.
Foolish and simple-minded people
then marvel at them,
which perverts childish thinking
and promotes dishonest speech.
Fulfilling filial piety and fraternal duty toward parents,
and maintaining proper conduct within the household—
these are what make someone an exemplary person.
Now, many focus on social networking to form factions and seek help,
stealing reputation from the world to achieve success.
Those who夸耀 trivial pursuits
then esteem them,
which compromises the integrity of upright persons
and confuses the minds of世俗 society.
Nourishing life and顺从 one's parents' wishes—
these are what constitute filial piety.
Now, many violate their parents' wishes and practice frugal供养,
restricting life while awaiting death.
After their parents pass away,
they then extravagantly adorn丧纪 rituals and call it filial piety,
lavishly feasting guests to seek fame.
Those who falsely claim goodness
then praise them,
which distorts the true practice of filial piety and fraternal duty,
and misleads later generations, causing痛心.
Loyalty and integrity in serving the ruler,
trustworthiness and adherence to laws in governing subordinates—
these are what constitute holding office.
Now, many use deceit and flattery to gain favor,
bending the law to accommodate cunning.
Those who seek gain by any means
then consider them worthy,
which destroys the conduct of贞良 persons
and opens the source of disorder and danger.
These five groups,
although outwardly they may have the虚誉 of promoting talent,
inwardly they cause the utmost harm to the substance of the Dào and virtue.
All these eight matters
are the affairs of a declining age,
and what benighted rulers cling to.
Although they do not immediately lead to usurpation and regicide,
they are nonetheless the gradual approach of the way of disorder.
The struggle between the fundamental and the peripheral, between growth and decline,
all lies with the ruler;
it is not something the common people can shift.
For the people inherently follow the ruler's preferences,
pursuing profit to survive.
Therefore, the noble man says:
"Having insufficient wealth and goods,
inadequate clothing and food,
unrefined music and beauty,
and ineffective authority and power
are not the worries of a noble man.
Not performing many good deeds,
not making clear the extended Way,
not establishing moral integrity,
and not manifesting virtue and righteousness
—these are what a noble man feels ashamed of."
Therefore, when wise and worthy men deal with their descendants,
they discipline them with purpose,
not with cunning;
they encourage them with rectitude,
not with deceit;
they show them frugality,
not extravagance;
they bequeath them words,
not wealth.
Thus, Dǒng Zhòngshū never concerned himself with family affairs his whole life,
and Shū Guǎng did not leave behind the gold he was bestowed.
If descendants are worthy,
they do not require great wealth;
if they are unworthy,
then great wealth will only invite resentment.
Therefore it is said:
"To have no virtue yet abundant riches
is the embryo of calamity."
Formerly, Cáo Jī had a saying:
"To guard what Heaven has gathered,
one must bestow one's virtue and righteousness.
If virtue and righteousness are not bestowed,
the gathered wealth will surely be deficient."
Now, if a household relieves others and lends to the needy,
distributing relief to the poor,
showing compassion for the sick and suffering,
then it surely will not long remain wealthy.
The *Book of Changes* says:
"The Way of Heaven diminishes the full to supplement the modest."
Therefore, one who expends benevolence and righteousness for others over there
is rewarded by Heaven over here;
one who gains by wickedness in the former time
will decline in the later time.
Thus, the way to maintain fullness
is to draw from it and reduce it,
then one can also avoid the regret of the dragon at the zenith and the fault of Heaven and Earth.
Therefore, if one attends to the fundamental, then even hypocritical people will all return to the fundamental;
if one dwells on the peripheral, then even sincerely reverent people will all go to the peripheral.
Moreover, where there is freezing and starvation,
the people cannot but leave;
where there is warmth and satiety,
the people cannot but dwell.
Thus, in a declining, benighted age,
whether people are fundamental or peripheral
is not necessarily a matter of worthiness or unworthiness;
it is the place of fortune or misfortune
that inevitably makes it so.
Therefore, an enlightened ruler governing the state
must exalt the fundamental and suppress the peripheral,
to halt the sprouting of disorder and danger.
This truly is the gradual peril of governance,
and cannot but be examined.
In the discussions of worldly people,
none do not value integrity and deference and disdain wealth and profit;
yet when it comes to their actions,
most abandon integrity and relish profit at others' expense.
They only know that those things can benefit me,
but do not know that my obtaining those things
will also become a means for others to profit.
They know that fat and wax can brighten a lamp,
but do not know that too much of it will extinguish it.
They know that profit can please oneself,
but do not know that when it accumulates, calamity surely arrives.
Earlier people suffered from this,
later people contend for it—
such is the folly of the common people and the extreme of benighted decline.
Therefore I sigh and say:
Why do they not examine this?
I wish they would take warning from the Way,
not take warning from water.
The elephant is destroyed for its tusks,
the clam is cut open for its pearl;
a common man is innocent,
but harboring a jade becomes his crime.
Alas, how lamentable!
Those without virtue yet rich and noble
certainly can be mourned in advance.
Moreover, things that benefit creatures are all Heaven's wealth.
Heaven's regulation of this wealth
is like a ruler having a treasury.
Bestowing, rewarding, seizing, and giving
each have their measure, great or small;
how can the people forcibly take more?
Therefore, if a person is without virtue yet rich and noble,
they are a malign commoner stealing an official position and robbing the treasury;
they will surely be discovered in the end,
and upon discovery, surely executed.
A robber of people is surely executed;
how much more one who robs Heaven?
Can they avoid receiving calamity?
Dèng Tōng died without a hairpin for his burial;
Shèng and Guì brought destruction upon themselves.
Therefore, the Son of Heaven cannot defy Heaven by enriching the meritless;
the feudal lords cannot defy the Emperor by generously rewarding private persuasion.
It is not defying the Emperor,
nor defying Heaven.
The Emperor takes Heaven as the rule;
Heaven takes the people as its heart.
What the people desire,
Heaven surely follows.
Therefore, one who seeks fullness without having achieved merit or benefit for the people
has never not fallen mightily;
one who has merit and virtue for the people and is modest and self-diminishing
has never not been glorious.
From ancient times to the present,
from above with the Son of Heaven
down to the common people below,
none who loved profit did not perish,
and none who loved righteousness did not become illustrious.
Formerly, King Lì of Zhōu loved monopolizing profit;
Ruì Liángfū remonstrated but was not heeded,
so he retired and composed the poem "Sāng Róu" to admonish,
saying this great wind
will surely have its course;
these greedy people
will surely ruin their kind.
The king still did not awaken,
so he was eventually exiled and died at Zhì.
The Duke of Yú repeatedly sought [jade] and thereby lost his state;
Gōngshū Shù esteemed bribes and thereby incurred crime;
Huán Tuí did not moderate his food and drink and thereby was assassinated.
These all brought about their own destruction through goods,
using wealth to extinguish themselves.
Chǔ's Dòu Zǐwén served three times as Prime Minister,
yet had a hungry appearance;
his wife and children suffered cold and hunger,
barely making it from morning to night.
Jì Wénzǐ served as minister to four rulers,
yet his horses were not fed grain,
his concubines did not wear silk;
Zǐ Hǎn returned the jade;
Yànzǐ returned the residence.
These all were able to discard profit and restrain themselves,
therefore they incurred no resentment from others,
generations enjoyed Heaven's blessings,
and their good repute did not cease.
Bóyí and Shūqí starved at Shǒuyáng;
Báijū and Jiè Tuī fled and hid in the mountains and valleys;
Yán [Yuān], Yuán [Xiàn], and Gōngxī [Āi] suffered hardship and famine in the wilds;
they guarded their purpose steadfastly and firmly,
held fast to integrity without deficiency,
favor and emolument could not secure them,
authority and power could not move them.
Even if they had the dignity of facing south [as ruler] or the position of duke or marquis,
if virtue and righteousness were endangered,
ritual and righteousness not displayed,
bending their will like the zhǐ orchid,
bearing a heart like fragrance,
they certainly would not do it.
Therefore, even the lord of all within the four seas could not match their reputation,
the rulers of the various states could not equal their weight;
guarding their purpose within a single hut,
yet their righteousness overflowed beyond the Nine Provinces;
their trustworthiness established a thousand years above,
and their names transmitted through a hundred generations.
What are called worthy men and noble men
are not necessarily defined by high position, generous salary, wealth, honor, and glory;
these are what a noble man ought to have,
but they are not that by which he is a noble man.
What are called petty men
are not necessarily defined by poverty, low status, cold, hunger, hardship, disgrace, distress, and destitution;
these are what a petty man ought to be in,
but they are not that by which he is a petty man.
How can this be made clear?
Now, Jié and Zhòu,
were the rulers of the Xià and Yīn dynasties,
Chónghóu and Èlái
were the Three Dukes of the Son of Heaven,
yet they could not avoid being considered petty men,
because their hearts and actions were wicked.
Bóyí and Shūqí
were starving men;
Fù Yuè was a convict laborer,
and Jǐng Lěi was a captive,
yet the world still regards them as gentlemen,
because their aspirations and integrity were admirable.
Therefore, in evaluating a scholar, if one judges based on his aspirations and conduct,
and does not consider his fate,
then even possessing the world would not be enough to make him esteemed,
and having no position would not be enough to make him lowly;
being in servitude would not be enough to shame him,
and ruling the four seas would not be enough to bring him glory.
How much more so for those whose differences are not as extreme as this?
Thus it is said:
High position is not enough to make me noble,
and lowly status is not enough to make me base.
Good reputation arises from me,
while fate is bestowed by Heaven.
The Book of Songs says:
"Heaven indeed has done this;
what can I say about it!"
Thus, a gentleman is not necessarily wealthy or noble,
and a petty man is not necessarily poor or lowly.
Some are like hidden dragons not yet employed,
others are like soaring dragons in the sky;
this has been so since ancient times.
Now, observing the arguments of vulgar scholars,
they judge virtue based on clan,
and determine worthiness based on position.
This may be said to grasp one aspect of evaluation,
but it fails to attain the true essence of the highest judgment.
Yáo was a sage father,
yet Dān was wicked and arrogant;
Shùn was a sage son,
yet his father Gǔsǒu was stubborn and evil;
Shūxiàng was a worthy elder brother,
yet his younger brother Fù was greedy and cruel;
Jì Yǒu was a worthy younger brother,
yet his elder brother Qìngfǔ was licentious and disorderly.
If evaluation must be based on clan,
then Dān should have been given the throne and Shùn should have been executed,
Fù should have been rewarded and Jì Yǒu should have been exterminated.
That evaluation cannot be based solely on clan is clear from this.
In the past, Qí Xī said:
"Gǔn was executed, yet Yǔ rose;
Guǎn and Cái were punished,
yet Zhōu Gōng assisted the king."
Thus, the Book of Documents states: "Father and son, elder and younger brother do not implicate each other."
Yōu and Lì were noble,
as Sons of Heaven,
and moreover, they possessed the wealth of the four seas.
Yán Yuān and Yuán Xiàn were lowly,
as commoners,
and moreover, they suffered cold and hunger, often in want.
If evaluation must be based on position,
then these two kings should be considered outstanding scholars of their time,
and these two recluses should be considered foolish and vulgar.
That evaluation cannot be based solely on position
is also clear from this.
Thus it is said:
Benevolence is weighty, while power is light;
position is insignificant, while righteousness is glorious.
Modern evaluators
often do the opposite of this,
and further rely on the nine clans,
or on one's origins,
thus straying far from obtaining truly worthy men.
In the past, even Zhōu Gōng did not demand perfection from a single person;
how much more so, when one's virtue and righteousness are already evident,
should they be rejected for other reasons?
Yóu Yú was born among the Five Dī tribes,
Yuè Xiàng was produced among the Eight Mán tribes,
yet their achievements benefited Qí and Qín,
and their virtue was established among the various Xià states;
their fine reputations and good names
are recorded in books,
and remain undiminished to this day.
Zhāng Yí was a man of the Central States,
Wèi Yāng was a descendant of Kāng Shū,
yet both were slanderous, flattering, and treacherous,
spreading disorder throughout the four seas.
From this perspective,
whether a person is good or evil
does not necessarily depend on noble lineage;
whether one's nature is worthy or vulgar
does not necessarily depend on common customs.
In the central hall grow worthless plants,
while in the mountain wilds grow orchids and angelica.
The jade of Hé Shì
came from an uncut stone;
the pearl of Suí Hóu
was produced in a clam.
The Book of Songs says:
"When gathering mustard greens and turnips,
do not reject them because of their roots."
Therefore, if one possesses great excellence worthy of esteem in the world,
then how can minor flaws in conduct be enough to burden him?
Thus, in employing scholars, one should not worry that they are not men of the state,
but worry that they are not loyal;
the age should not worry about lacking ministers,
but worry that they are not worthy.
There is nothing to bind them.
Chén Píng and Hán Xìn were captives of Chǔ,
yet Gāozǔ made them his pillars,
and they truly pacified the four seas
and stabilized the Hàn house;
Wèi Qīng and Huò Qùbìng
were private retainers of Píngyáng,
yet Emperor Wǔ made them commanders,
and they truly repelled the Northern Dī
and established commanderies west of the river.
If they are capable for the task,
what does distance or lowliness matter?
However, the difficulty with those who are not men of this land,
or not of ministerial or general lineage,
is that they lack the ability for the position they hold,
lack the virtue for the nobility they possess,
and have no excellence to uphold and no power to wield.
The reason the world is not well-governed
is the difficulty with worthies.
What is called the difficulty with worthies
does not merely refer to the rarity of finding those with keen intelligence who adhere to virtue and righteousness.
That is the difficulty of seeking worthies,
not the difficulty faced by worthies themselves.
Thus, what is called the difficulty with worthies
refers to the fact that following goodness leads to envy,
practicing worthiness leads to jealousy,
and one is certain to encounter hardship and danger.
The reason Yú Shùn was exiled and killed,
and Wǔ Zǐxū was executed,
is that even the highest sages and greatest worthies could not avoid jealousy and envy;
how much more so for men of middling times?
This is why talented scholars, though possessing worthy material and fine substance,
still cannot follow the straight path
and fully realize their aspirations.
Recluses cannot act with integrity,
court ministers cannot speak with integrity;
this is why customs deteriorate,
and foolish rulers become isolated.
The Marquis of Qí lost his state because of this,
and the Duke of Lǔ was exiled because of this.
They were overwhelmed by defeat and ruin without respite—
how could they achieve order?
Thus, those with meager virtue hate to hear of fine conduct;
those with chaotic governance hate to hear of orderly speech.
This is why the fallen Qín executed those who spoke in pairs and buried the scholars alive.
Now, among vulgar people of the world,
there are many who neglect their own parents yet resent others for honoring them,
or who treat their own parents rudely yet resent others for loving them.
Is this only among the common masses?
Even among the worthy and talented, it occurs from time to time.
Dèng Tōng was favored by Emperor Wén,
devoted and obedient,
sucking pus without a grudging expression.
When the emperor was ill and unhappy,
he casually said:
"Who in the world loves me the most?"
Dèng Tōng, wishing to praise the crown prince's filial piety,
then replied:
"None loves Your Majesty more than the crown prince."
When the crown prince came to inquire about the illness,
the emperor ordered him to suck the pus,
but the crown prince showed a reluctant expression.
The emperor was displeased and sent the crown prince away.
Later, hearing that Dèng Tōng often sucked the pus,
he felt ashamed and resented him.
When he succeeded to the throne,
he brought charges against Dèng Tōng, causing him to starve to death.
Thus, Dèng Tōng's actions were devoted and harmless to others,
and his words praised the crown prince and illuminated filial piety and kindness.
The crown prince himself could not live up to the praise,
yet instead bore a grudge and blamed him.
To praise another's strengths,
wishing to highlight his filial piety,
was still considered a crime;
how much more so for those who expose others' faults to correct the world?
Moreover, the reason why scholars are considered worthy
lies precisely in their words and deeds.
Loyal and upright words
are not merely for praising others,
but inevitably provoke offense;
filial and virtuous conduct
is not merely about sucking pus from sores,
but inevitably invites criticism.
Thus, scholars who follow righteous conduct and engage in principled discourse,
who manage to avoid the reputation of being envious and jealous,
and escape the calamity of punishment and execution,
are indeed fortunate.
Bǐ Gān had his heart cut out,
Jīzǐ was enslaved,
Bó Zōng died for it,
Xì Wǎn perished because of it.
A state is never lacking in jealous men,
just as a household is never lacking in jealous women.
From recent antiquity to the present,
both externally and internally,
how rare are those who compete for merit and fame and envy those surpassing them?
Would one think that only two worthies should not harm each other?
Yet,
Fàn Jū demoted Bái Qǐ,
Gōngsūn Hóng suppressed Dǒng Zhòngshū—
was this due to rivalry for favor, rank, and emolument while serving the same ruler in the same court?
Would one think that only those of different states and divergent paths, with no conflict of interest, can avoid this?
Yet,
Sūn Bìn cultivated his talents in Chǔ,
Páng Juān, from Wèi, changed countenance,
lured him and had his feet amputated;
Hán Fēi illuminated governance in Hán,
Lǐ Sī, from Qín, harbored thoughts,
summoned him and had him killed.
Alas! How extreme is the mutual jealousy among scholars!
Is it because they failed to reach the ruler that they suffered calamity?
Would one think that only being recognized and understood can lead to trust?
Yet,
Jīng Fáng repeatedly debated and challenged Emperor Yuán,
causing him to institute the examination of merit and select governors;
Cháo Cuò was deeply known by Emperor Jǐng,
who had him systematize Hàn laws without disorder.
These two men, in relation to their rulers,
could be said to have been deeply recognized and exceptionally favored,
yet Jīng Fáng died unjustly without the emperor’s awareness,
and Cháo Cuò was beheaded before the emperor regretted it.
Is it because their talent and wisdom were insufficient to protect themselves, thus leading to disaster?
Would one think that only the great sages can remain unburdened?
Yet,
Dì Yǐ was imprisoned for righteousness,
King Wén was confined for benevolence.
Those who embody the highest conduct and practice benevolence and righteousness,
occupying the southern-facing position as mentors, ministers, and officers,
still cannot avoid calamity;
then how much more so for Confucius, whose traces were erased,
Shū Xiàng, who was bound in fetters,
Qū Yuán, who was exiled and drowned,
Jiǎ Yì, who was demoted and dismissed,
Zhōnglí, who was deposed and replaced,
Hé Chǎng, who was bound and restrained,
Wáng Zhāng, who was convicted of crimes,
Píng'ē, who was expelled and banished—
these are all cases of scholars being treated lightly.
The Book of Songs says:
"Guiltless and innocent,
yet slanderous mouths are clamorous."
"The heart of that man,
to what does it not extend?"
From this perspective,
the attacks of envy and flattery
are indeed skillful!
Worthies and sages living in the world
are indeed in peril!
Thus, what is called the difficulty with worthies
is not that worthies are difficult,
but that avoiding calamity is difficult.
Those great sages and multitudes of worthies,
having achieved merit and attained fame,
some enfeoffed as marquises or earls,
some positioned as dukes or ministers,
administering heavenly offices,
selected in the emperor’s heart,
serving day and night and attending feasts,
renowned and prominent, yet still faced such things—
how much more then for those retired commoners in the fields,
hermits in mountain valleys,
who rely on others to advance,
and whose reputations depend on contemporary judgment?
This is why wise scholars seal their lips and tie their tongues,
closing their bags and remaining silent.
Moreover, ordinary folk in the alleys,
what do they truly discern?
They merely follow the dust and mimic sounds.
Observing their judgments,
they cannot base them on the conduct and traces within the inner chambers,
nor examine the truth or falsity of good and bad;
they simply regard those who praise them to their faces as wise,
those who flatter and fawn on them as benevolent,
those who engage in wicked profiteering as virtuous,
and those who steal ranks and positions as worthy.
How could they further understand the source of filial piety and fraternal duty,
the uprightness of loyalty and integrity,
the transformation of order and discipline,
and the return to the fundamental way?
This is why Bào Jiāo stood withering by the roadside,
and Xú Yǎn drowned himself in the vast sea.
A proverb says:
"One dog barks at a shadow,
a hundred dogs bark at the sound."
The world’s affliction with this has indeed been long!
I grieve that the world does not examine the truth of genuineness and falsity,
so I construct an imaginary parable to illustrate its mind:
Observing now how ministers in charge select scholars
is similar to how the Sīyuán hunted.
Once there was a man of the Sīyuán clan
who hunted with fire in the wilderness.
A deer fled eastward,
and Sīyuán shouted and chased it.
A crowd in the west was pursuing a pig,
and hearing Sīyuán’s shouts,
they all raised their voices and joined in.
Hearing the multitude of voices, Sīyuán
stopped his own pursuit and went to lie in wait,
encountering a vulgar, ugly pig.
Sīyuán was delighted,
thinking he had captured a white auspicious beast, a precious bird,
and exhausted his fodder, emptied his granaries to rear it.
The pig bowed and raised its head, grunting and squealing,
putting on an appealing voice,
and Sīyuán prized it even more.
Not long after,
a fierce wind arose and a heavy rain fell,
washing the huge pig so the foul mud sloughed off;
startled and afraid, it fled,
its true voice emerged,
and only then was it known to be an old boar of the household.
This is the error of following sounds and chasing echoes;
the crowd encountering it did not hasten to believe.
Now, the rulers of the age, regarding scholars,
see a worthy with their eyes but dare not employ him,
hear of a worthy with their ears but regret not reaching him.
Even if they themselves have knowledge,
they still cannot select him,
but must instead wait for the recommendations of various officials—
then they also fear losing the qílín deer and catching an old boar.
Why do they not distinguish?
It is because they have not encountered the change of wind and rain.
If one day both extraordinary governance and calamity converge,
then the treacherous and narrow-minded,
the lowly and inferior in substance,
will also be distinguished.
When many petty men form cliques to secure positions,
and slanderous, envious groups bark and bite at worthies,
how rare are the disasters and ruin they cause?
The three dynasties were overthrown,
the various states were destroyed,
yet later people still cannot reform—
this is why myriad offices repeatedly fail in their duties,
and the Mandate of Heaven frequently shifts without constancy.
The Book of Songs says:
"The state is already utterly cut down,
why do you not take warning!"
Alas!
The rulers of the time, the vulgar sovereigns, do not examine this.
The reason a state is well-governed is that the ruler is enlightened;
the reason it falls into disorder is that the ruler is benighted.
The reason a ruler is enlightened is that he listens broadly;
the reason he is benighted is that he believes partially.
Therefore, if a ruler communicates and must listen broadly,
his sageliness daily expands;
if he follows vulgar counsel and believes partially,
his folly daily deepens.
The Book of Songs says:
"The ancients had a saying:
Now, in the governance of Yáo and Shùn,
they opened the four gates,
illuminated the four directions,
and extended their hearing to the four quarters.
Thus, the world converged like spokes to a hub, and their sagely wisdom left nothing unilluminated.
Therefore, figures like Gòng and Gǔn could not block them,
and flattering words and deceitful actions could not delude them.
As for the Second Emperor of Qín,
he devoted himself to concealing himself,
and severed ties with his hundred officials,
alienating the distant and lowly while trusting Zhào Gāo.
Thus, his hearing was blocked by powerful ministers,
and his vision was obscured by arrogant and envious men.
Consequently, the empire crumbled and rebelled,
yet he remained unaware.
All who were killed by Zhào Gāo
dared not speak of it.
Only when Zhōu Zhāng reached Xì did he begin to panic,
and only after Yán Lè advanced with persuasion did he regret,
but was it not too late!
Therefore, if a ruler listens broadly and accepts advice from below,
then noble ministers cannot deceive him,
and distant people cannot cheat him.
If he neglects the lowly and trusts the noble,
then honest words will not reach the court,
and upright scholars will retire to the wilderness, bearing their guilt.
Court ministers are meant to govern,
but if many form cliques, chaos ensues.
Worthy men are meant to serve,
but if they hide and retreat to the wilderness, the ruler becomes isolated.
That such a ruler could survive
has never been heard of.
Therefore, an enlightened ruler, when overseeing the multitude,
strives to heed lower voices to illuminate external affairs,
and respectfully accepts the humble to attract the worthy.
Not rejecting advice
does not mean that all who speak are entirely useful,
but rather it is the fear that rejecting the useless may also dismiss the useful.
Not neglecting the lowly
does not mean that all such people are entirely worthy,
but rather it is the fear that neglecting the unworthy may cut off the hopes of the worthy.
Therefore, a sage king values the small to encourage the great,
rewards the humble to attract the worthy.
Only then will good scholars gather at court,
and the sentiments of the lower ranks reach the ruler.
Thus, the ruler will have no misguided policies,
and officials will have no ministers who disrupt the law.
This benefits both ruler and people,
and is what treacherous and flattering ministers fear.
In the past, a single audience with Zhāng Lù led to the dismissal of Ránghóu,
and Yuán Sī’s remonstrance caused Zhōu Bó to be removed.
Therefore, those in power
constantly envy upright and righteous scholars,
who, with a single word to the ruler, can correct their wickedness.
Thus, the powerful adorn false words to please the ruler’s mind,
and establish authority below to control scholars and people.
Zhào Gāo, in his disordered governance,
feared that his evils would reach the emperor,
so he preemptively urged the Second Emperor, saying:
“Frequently meeting with ministers to discuss governance is demeaning;
it demeans and reveals shortcomings.
It is better to conceal yourself and decide alone,
for then you will be divine and dignified.
The Son of Heaven calls himself ‘zhèn,’
and indeed should only be heard of, not seen.”
The Second Emperor then deeply secluded himself,
admitting only Zhào Gāo.
Zhào Gāo, when entering, spoke pleasing words to delight his lord;
when exiting, he relied on edicts to exalt himself.
The empire rotted like fish,
and all rebelled against Qín.
Zhào Gāo, in fear,
shifted the blame to the ruler,
and sent Yán Lè to accuse and kill him.
The emperor wished to see Zhào Gāo once but could not, and died.
Now, Tián Cháng imprisoned Jiǎngōng,
and Zhuō Chí hung Mǐnwáng.
The Second Emperor had also heard of these events.
Yet why did he still follow in their footsteps of failure?
The fault lay in not accepting the admonitions of his ministers,
not heeding the songs and rumors of the people,
believing himself more worthy than Jiǎn and Mǐn,
and Zhào Gāo more worthy than those two ministers.
Thus, the state was already in chaos, but the ruler did not know;
disaster had already struck, but those below did not rescue him.
This was not because the multitude abandoned the ruler,
but because the ruler tied the fate of the multitude to Zhào Gāo,
cutting himself off from the people.
How can later degenerate rulers recognize such dangers?
Shùn said:
“When I err,
you must correct me.
Do not flatter me to my face,
only to criticize behind my back.”
Therefore, the way to govern a state
is to encourage remonstrance,
to promote open speech,
so that the ruler’s vision becomes clear and governance flows smoothly.
Moreover, arrogant ministers who like to obscure the worthy
not only fear their righteous standards judging them,
but also feel ashamed to hold high positions while their wisdom does not surpass those below,
or to hold office while strategies do not originate from themselves.
Thus, Xì Wǎn gained popular support, but Zǐ Cháng killed him;
Qū Yuán gained the ruler’s favor, but Jiāo and Lán slandered him;
Gěng Shòu established the ever-normal granary, but Yán Yán妒 envied his advice;
Chén Tāng killed Zhìzhī, but Kuāng Héng disputed his merit.
From this, it is clear that
those in lowly positions who wish to serve the ruler well
must first become enemies of the favored.
Relying on old favor to obstruct them within,
while oneself, connected to the lowly, seeks to gain trust from without—
this is why rulers who desire goodness
and scholars who wish to be loyal,
though born in the same era,
with hearts full of mutual concern,
ultimately never meet.
Among the great duties of facing south as ruler,
none is more urgent than knowing the worthy;
and the nearest path to knowing the worthy
is none more urgent than examining achievements.
If achievements are truly examined, then order and chaos become starkly clear;
if good and evil are trusted, then the upright and worthy cannot be obscured,
and the cunning and deceitful cannot hide their wickedness.
If a sword is not tested, its sharpness or dullness remains obscure;
if a bow is not tested, its strength or weakness is misjudged;
if a hawk is not tested, its skill or clumsiness is confusing;
if a horse is not tested, its excellence or inferiority is doubtful.
The confusion about these four things
arises from the lack of examination.
Now, if ministers are not examined,
the harm is not limited to misjudgment, obscurity, doubt, and confusion alone,
but will inevitably lead to negligence and laziness.
Suppose a family has five sons and ten grandsons:
if the parents do not discern diligence and weakness,
then the hardworking will slacken,
and the lazy will persist in error.
This is the way to waste the estate and ruin the family.
Among fathers, sons, and brothers,
within a single household’s plans,
it is already like this—
how much more so for the multitude of ministers managing public affairs?
The *Zhuàn* says:
“If good and evil are not made clear,
how can discouragement and encouragement be applied?”
Therefore, if a great man does not examine achievements,
his descendants will become lazy and the family will fall into poverty;
if an official does not examine achievements,
his subordinates will become negligent and arrogant, and wickedness will flourish;
if an emperor does not examine achievements,
the upright and worthy will be suppressed, and deceit and falsehood will prevail.
Thus, the *Shū* says:
“Every three years, examine achievements,
demote the obscure and promote the enlightened.”
This is to clarify the worthy and foolish and encourage the capable and incapable.
When a sage king establishes the hundred offices,
it is to receive Heaven’s mandate, govern the earth,
and shepherd and nurture the myriad people.
Therefore, those with titles must correspond to the classics,
and those who govern by name must prove their reality.
Then offices will have no idle duties,
and positions will have no unfit persons.
Prefects, chancellors, magistrates, and chiefs—
their effectiveness lies in governing the people;
regional inspectors and provincial governors—
their duty is to be vigilant and discerning;
the nine ministers divide responsibilities
to assist the three dukes;
the three dukes oversee comprehensively,
harmonizing yīn and yáng.
All should be examined for their governance, proving their reality as the king’s blessing.
Palace attendants, grandees, erudites, and advisory courtiers—
their duty is speech,
their office is remonstrance;
as well as selecting the茂才, filial and incorrupt, worthy and upright, sincere and simple, virtuous,明经, broad and learned,武猛, and those skilled in handling difficult cases—
these all have names and titles self-determined,
and ministers should exhaust their thoughts and efforts to fulfill the ruler’s commands.
Nowadays, however, it is not so.
The magistrates, district chiefs, governors, and chancellors do not think of achieving merit.
Instead, they are greedy, cruel, arbitrary, and self-indulgent.
They do not uphold the laws and decrees,
but oppress and wrong the common people.
The provincial authorities do not address these matters,
forcing people to travel far to the capital to submit petitions and lodge complaints.
The Imperial Secretariat does not hold the Three Excellencies accountable,
the Three Excellencies do not reprimand the provinces and commanderies,
and the provinces and commanderies do not investigate the counties and towns.
Thus, the wicked and cunning easily wrong one another.
The officials serving as Palace Attendants, Erudites, and Remonstrance Counselors—
some of whom have held their positions for years—
never utter words about promoting the worthy, hating the wicked, remedying oversights, or correcting deficiencies,
nor do they worry about being demoted or dismissed.
Those among the officials who recommend scholars
sometimes put forward the stubborn and dull as "Outstanding Talents,"
the rebellious and defiant as "Paragons of Filial Piety,"
the greedy and rapacious as "Incorrupt Officials,"
the cunning and crafty as "Upright and Rectitude,"
the flattering and sycophantic as "Frank and Forthright,"
the frivolous and shallow as "Sincere and Honest,"
the empty and hollow as "Possessors of the Way,"
the deceitful and ignorant as "Masters of the Classics,"
the cruel and harsh as "Broad-minded and Tolerant,"
the timid and weak as "Martially Ferocious,"
and the foolish and obstinate as "Capable of Handling Difficult Affairs."
Names and realities do not correspond,
and recommendations do not match the qualities sought.
The wealthy rely on their resources and influence,
the noble exploit their power and connections.
Wealth is considered a mark of worthiness,
and forcefulness is esteemed as superior.
This is why so many in office are unfit for their positions,
and why governance is repeatedly thrown into chaos and disarray.
In ancient times, when the feudal lords recommended scholars,
one proper recommendation was called "fondness for virtue,"
two proper recommendations were called "esteem for the worthy,"
and three proper recommendations were called "having merit,"
for which they were rewarded.
If they failed to recommend scholars,
once, their noble rank was reduced;
twice, their territory was reduced;
three times, both rank and land were taken away entirely.
Those who colluded with subordinates to deceive superiors were put to death;
those who colluded with superiors to deceive subordinates were punished;
those who participated in state affairs but brought no benefit to the people were dismissed;
those in high positions who failed to promote the worthy were expelled.
They undertook their duties with great care in selecting and recommending,
and examined names and realities to determine rewards and punishments in this manner.
Thus, they could distinguish the worthy from the foolish and obtain many talented men,
accomplishing moral transformation and bringing peace to the people.
The Three Dynasties, in their time,
all achieved great peace.
Our sagely Hàn dynasty ascended the throne,
and now, after four hundred and eight years,
it has still not achieved this,
because instruction is not thorough and merit is not examined,
rewards and punishments are delayed, and pardons and redemptions are frequent.
As the proverb says:
"Crooked wood hates the straightening line;
those facing heavy punishment hate clear evidence."
This is why the officials delight in being numerous and disorderly and hate the examination of merit.
The sage is the mouth of Heaven,
and the worthy are the interpreters of the sage.
Therefore, the words of the sage
are the heart of Heaven.
What the worthy expound
is the meaning of the sage.
Our late teacher, Jīng Jūn,
established categories for investigation and examination of merit,
to bequeath to the worthy and outstanding.
The foundation of great peace
must begin from this;
the transformation of non-action
must come from this.
Therefore, if the rulers of the age do not follow the examination of merit yet hope for great peace,
it is like trying to create squares and circles without compass and square,
or wanting to cross a great river without boat or oar.
Even if some may let things go unchecked,
they do not realize how easy and swift it would be to follow the proper measures.
All the officials and ministers
have their prescribed duties;
each should remain in his post
and be held accountable for his performance.
The hundred commanderies and thousand counties
should each build on what came before
to plan for what comes after.
Words and responses
should each follow their proper form,
so that their substance may be verified.
Then, those in office will not neglect their duties,
and those who submit proposals will not be able to deceive.
The *Book of Documents* says:
"Collect and consider their words,
clearly test them by their achievements,
and reward them with chariots and robes according to their service."
"Who can avoid being humble?
Who can avoid responding with reverence?"
This is how Yáo and Shùn nurtured the people and brought about harmonious times.
What enables a state to survive is order;
what causes it to perish is chaos.
No ruler fails to love order and hate chaos,
to delight in survival and fear destruction.
Yet, looking at historical records,
from recent antiquity onward,
there have been three fallen dynasties,
and corrupt states are too many to count.
What is the reason for this?
Examining their downfall,
it is always because the ruler loved what leads to chaos
and hated what leads to order;
he detested what enables survival
and cherished what leads to destruction.
Therefore, even if separated by a hundred generations,
spanning years and epochs,
divided by the Nine Provinces,
and with customs differing for a thousand *lǐ*,
the signs of their destruction and traces of their downfall
are like repeated applications of compass and square,
matching as tally and tally-case.
Thus it is said:
Even with the virtues of Yáo and Shùn,
one must be examined against the "Zhōu Odes";
even with the wickedness of Jié and Zhòu,
one must be judged against the "Bǎn" and "Dàng" odes.
"The mirror of Yīn is not far off—
it is in the age of the Xià sovereigns."
He who shares the same illness as a dead man
cannot live;
he who follows the same path as a destroyed state
cannot survive.
How can this be empty words!
How do we know a person is about to fall ill?
By his lack of appetite.
How do we know a state is about to fall into chaos?
By its lack of appetite for the worthy.
Therefore, in the kitchen of a sick household,
it is not that there are no delicacies,
but that the person cannot eat them,
and so he proceeds to death.
In the bureaucracy of a chaotic state,
it is not that there are no worthy men,
but that the ruler cannot employ them,
and so it proceeds to destruction.
Fine rice and millet,
sweet wine and good ale,
are meant to nourish life,
yet the sick person detests them,
thinking them not as good as beans, wheat, chaff, or dregs—what he craves—
and this is a sign that he is about to die.
Honoring the worthy, employing the capable,
trusting the loyal, and accepting remonstrance
are what bring security,
yet the benighted ruler detests them,
thinking them not as good as the words of the treacherous, flattering, vile, and slanderous—
and this is a sign that he is about to perish.
Lǎozǐ said:
"It is only because one treats sickness as sickness
that one does not fall ill."
The *Yì* says: "If it perishes, if it perishes,
it will be tied to a clump of mulberry trees."
Therefore, those who nurture longevity
take medicine before falling ill;
rulers who nurture the age
employ the worthy before chaos arises.
Thus, their persons are ever secure and their states endure forever.
The highest physician heals the state;
the next heals illnesses.
Governing a state
is indeed analogous to governing one's body.
Illness is a disease of the body;
disorder is a disease of the state.
The body's disease awaits a physician for cure;
the state's disorder awaits the worthy for governance.
For governing the body, there are the methods of Huángdì;
for governing the world, there are the classics of Kǒngzǐ.
Yet if illness is not cured and disorder not governed,
it is not that the methods of acupuncture and moxibustion are wrong,
nor that the words of the Five Classics are false,
but rather that those who implement them are not the right persons.
If they are not the right persons,
then the compass will not draw circles nor the square draw right angles;
the marking line will not be straight nor the level be even;
drilling wood for fire will yield no flame;
smelting ore will yield no metal.
A metal horse cannot chase speed;
an earthen boat cannot cross water.
In all these eight cases,
which are the manifest ways of Heaven,
visible and tangible things,
if the person is not right,
they still achieve nothing.
How much more so for one who embraces the Way and its arts to comfort the people,
or rides the six dragons to master the heart of Heaven?
If, in governing the world, one does not obtain true worthies,
it is like treating an illness without obtaining a good physician.
To treat an illness, one should obtain genuine rénshēn,
but instead gets zhīluófú;
one should obtain màiméndōng,
but instead gets steamed kuàngmài.
If one does not recognize the genuine,
mixes and takes them,
the illness will worsen progressively,
and one will not realize having been deceived.
Instead, one will say the prescription is untrustworthy and the medicines are all useless for curing the illness,
thus discarding the later medicine and daring not to drink it,
and hastily seeking shamans and sorcerers;
then death is certain.
When a ruler seeks worthies,
those below respond with the base,
presenting the crooked instead of the upright.
If he does not attract the genuine,
but accepts and appoints the unworthy to office,
the state will decline into disorder,
and he will not realize being deceived by those below.
Instead, he will say the classics are untrustworthy and worthies are all useless for saving disorder,
thus abandoning true worthies and no longer seeking to advance them,
and further employing vulgar officials;
then ruin is certain.
Since the Three Dynasties,
all have used zhīluófú and steamed kuàngmài to compound medicines,
so illnesses grow daily like malaria and end in death.
The Shū says:
"If a man has ability,
let him follow his conduct;
then the state will prosper."
Therefore, the former kings, in selecting men for office,
necessarily obtained men of talent.
Their achievements benefited the people;
their virtue matched their positions.
Through human consultation and spiritual consultation,
the common people endorsed the capable.
Striving to accord with Heaven and Earth, they acted thus.
The Three Dynasties, in founding states and establishing lords,
were thus able to transmit their lines for a hundred generations,
spanning a thousand years and more.
Since the Spring and Autumn period,
under the institutions of the Warring States,
generals, ministers, and powerful officials
were necessarily from among relatives and in-laws.
Brothers of the empress,
sons-in-law and maternal grandsons of the ruler,
though their years were tender and youthful,
not yet free from swaddling clothes,
thereby occupied these offices and ranks.
Their achievements brought no benefit to the people;
their favor did not reach those below, yet they obtained marquisates,
receiving many fiefs of land.
Moreover, they did not govern the people or demonstrate efficacy to repay the common people,
but consumed heavy emoluments idly,
holding positions without merit,
and only engaged in excessive luxury,
acting with arrogance and extravagance.
Thus, they were destroyed and unable to transmit their positions for generations.
Zǐchǎn said:
"To give a knife to one who cannot wield it to cut,
the injuries will indeed be many."
Therefore, when rulers of the age deal with noble relatives,
loving their charming beauty,
they do not assess their talents but give them office.
They do not let them achieve merit to establish themselves among the people,
but hastily strive to raise their noble ranks,
increase their rewards and gifts,
causing them to incur resentment among the lower people,
and suspend crimes inviting evil.
When accumulated faults are fully formed,
how can there be no downfall?
This is what is called:
"In loving a person,
you merely harm him!"
According to the institutions of the former kings,
appointing officials among the people must involve assessing their talent.
After assessment is determined, then rank is conferred;
after position is determined, then emolument is granted.
If a ruler does not examine this,
but hastily puts relatives and those appointed for their looks in charge of offices,
it is like exchanging a beloved son for a carriage driver,
or exchanging a bright pearl for a tile fragment.
Although there may be feelings of love and fondness,
yet overturning the great carriage and killing the sick person is inevitable.
The Shū says, "Heaven's work, man should act in its place";
the Zhuàn says:
"Those who complete the power of Heaven and Earth
have never failed to flourish."
From this perspective,
if a ruler of the age desires to enrich by force those who have no merit,
then he is contending with Heaven.
To make those without virtue or favor contend with August Heaven,
and yet wish to long endure,
since ancient times,
this has never been.
In all governance by a ruler,
nothing is greater than harmonizing yīn and yáng.
Yīn and yáng take Heaven as their foundation.
If the heart of Heaven is accordant, then yīn and yáng are harmonious;
if the heart of Heaven is contrary, then yīn and yáng are discordant.
Heaven takes the people as its heart.
If the people are peaceful and joyful, then the heart of Heaven is accordant;
if the people are sorrowful and suffering, then the heart of Heaven is contrary.
The people take the ruler as their guiding principle.
If the ruler's governance is good, then the people are harmonious and well-governed;
if the ruler's governance is bad, then the people are wronged and disorderly.
The ruler takes caring for the people as fundamental.
If ministers are loyal and good, then the ruler's governance is good;
if ministers are treacherous and crooked, then the ruler's governance is bad.
This takes selection as fundamental.
If selection is genuine, then loyal and worthy men advance;
if selection is false and hypocritical, then factions of the wicked are presented.
Selection takes laws and ordinances as fundamental.
If laws and ordinances are correct, then selection is genuine;
if laws and ordinances are deceptive, then selection is false and hypocritical.
Laws take the ruler as master.
If the ruler trusts the laws, then laws are followed and implemented;
if the ruler deceives the laws, then laws are abandoned.
The achievements of ruler, ministers, laws, and ordinances
must be manifested among the people.
Therefore, if ruler, ministers, laws, and ordinances are good, then the people are peaceful and joyful.
If the people are peaceful and joyful, then the heart of Heaven is comforted.
If the heart of Heaven is comforted, then yīn and yáng are harmonious.
If yīn and yáng are harmonious, then the five grains are abundant.
If the five grains are abundant, then the people attain longevity.
If the people attain longevity, then righteousness flourishes.
If righteousness flourishes, then there are no treacherous deeds.
If there are no treacherous deeds, then the age is peaceful,
and the state is tranquil, the altars of soil and grain are secure,
and the ruler is honored and glorious.
Therefore, the heart of Heaven, yīn and yáng, ruler and ministers, the common people, good and evil complement each other and reciprocally manifest.
Heaven is the foundation of the state;
the ruler is the guiding principle of the people;
ministers are the material for governance.
"If a craftsman wishes to do his work well,
he must first sharpen his tools."
Therefore, one who wishes to bring about great peace
must first regulate yīn and yáng;
to regulate yīn and yáng,
one must first accord with the heart of Heaven;
to accord with the heart of Heaven,
one must first give peace to the people;
to give peace to the people,
one must first carefully select the right persons.
Therefore, the root of the state's survival or demise,
the pivot of order or disorder,
lies solely in making selection clear.
The sages understood this,
therefore they made it the foremost matter for promotion and demotion.
The Shū says:
"You give peace to the hundred surnames;
why select anyone but the right person?"
This is how the former kings brought about great peace and gave rise to sounds of praise.
The alternation of decline and prosperity,
the non-coexistence of yīn and yáng,
by observing what is gathered together,
the beginnings of flourishing and decay can be seen.
Jì, Xiè, and Gāoyáo gathered together and brought about harmony and prosperity;
Huángfù, Jué, and Jǔ gathered together and brought about calamities and anomalies.
Now the signs of good and evil,
correspond over a thousand lǐ,
accumulate traces over a hundred generations;
by nature they are close, but by habit they grow apart.
Therefore, wisdom and foolishness lie in the heart,
not in nobility or baseness;
trustworthiness and deceit lie in nature,
not in closeness or distance.
The reason why the Second Emperor [of Qín] lost the empire together [with others] was
the Chancellor and the Imperial Secretary.
The reason why Emperor Gāozǔ [of Hàn] took the empire together [with others] was
the silk merchant and the dog butcher;
the convicts from Líshān,
the bandits from Jùyě,
all became famous generals.
From this we see that,
if one obtains the right person,
one need not worry about poverty or low status;
if one obtains the right talent,
one need not dislike their reputation or past.
Looking back from Emperor Yuán of Hàn onward,
arrogant and noble ministers,
whenever they were punished and executed,
their factions in office,
and those who shared their guilt,
often amounted to two or three out of ten.
From this we see that,
honored and favored ministers,
have never failed to appoint their private followers and advance treacherous cliques.
Thus, Wáng Mǎng together with the Hàn dukes, ministers, governors, and prefects seized Hàn,
while Emperor Guāngwǔ together with Hàn's surviving people and abandoned scholars destroyed him.
If the noble were necessarily wise and loyal,
and the base necessarily foolish and deceitful,
then how could it be like this?
From Emperor Chéng onward,
down to Wáng Mǎng,
dukes, ministers, ranked marquises,
down to magistrates and commandants,
officials great and small,
amounted to nearly a hundred thousand,
all were what Hàn called wise, loyal, upright, honored, and favored men.
When Wáng Mǎng usurped the throne,
only Marquis Ānzhòng Liú Chóng and Dōngjùn Prefect Zhái Yì remembered the rites of serving their lord,
with righteous courage and vigorous spirit,
desired to destroy Wáng Mǎng.
Though their efforts did not succeed,
their will and integrity are worthy of record.
Out of a hundred thousand or so,
those able to repay kindness,
were only these two.
From this we see that,
in a declining age, the group of ministers truly has few worthies;
the greater their office, the heavier their crime;
the higher their rank, the deeper their guilt.
Therefore it is said:
The virtue of a well-governed age,
and the wickedness of a declining age,
often correspond exactly to rank and position.
Confucius said:
"When the state has the Way,
to be poor and lowly is a disgrace;
when the state is without the Way,
to be rich and noble is a disgrace."
The *Book of Songs* laments: "Bright, bright the white colt,
in that empty valley";
"With artful speech like a flowing stream,
he makes himself dwell in comfort."
This speaks of scholars in a declining age:
the purer their will, the lower their status;
the more artful their flattery, the higher their office.
"Things of like kind come together,
creatures form in groups";
those with the same clarity see each other,
those with the same hearing hear each other;
only the sage knows the sage,
only the worthy knows the worthy.
Now those in power,
not only fail to clearly distinguish the worthy from the base,
but also yield to the hints and gestures of the noble,
intimidated by the entreaties of power and influence;
requests crowd the gates,
gifts of ritual and tribute converge like spokes;
pressed by immediate urgency,
they give them priority.
This is what upright scholars alone are obscured by,
and what all the wicked advance in cliques.
When the Duke of Zhōu served as chief minister,
he humbled himself before scholars,
thus he could obtain true worthies.
When Qí Xī served as Grand Master,
he recommended his enemy and his son,
thus he could obtain upright men.
Those who attain position in the present age,
rely on the favor of sisters and daughters to be arrogant toward scholars,
borrow the power of the overreaching dragon to oppress the worthy;
and yet they wish to make men of purpose and integrity
crawl and bow to serve themselves,
ruin their faces with flattery to seek closeness;
only then do they protect and maintain them.
Thus, principled scholars gather ferns and suffer cold and hunger,
perish hidden in mountain caves—that is all.
How could there be any willing to tread their thresholds and associate with such men?
Generally, rulers who possess a state,
have never not desired good governance,
yet well-governed ages are not seen generation after generation—
it is because those appointed are not worthy.
The age has never been without worthies,
yet worthies do not get employed—
it is because the ministers are jealous.
The ruler has a mind to seek worthies,
but lacks the method to obtain them;
ministers have the name of advancing worthies,
but not the reality of advancing them.
This is why the ruler is isolated and endangered above,
and the Way is alone suppressed below.
The reason why a ruler brings about good governance is public-mindedness;
when public laws are practiced, disorder and rebellion are cut off.
The reason why flattering ministers benefit themselves is selfishness;
when selfish methods are used, public laws are usurped.
The reason why exemplary men establish integrity is righteousness;
when upright integrity is established, the vile kind is replaced.
These treacherous ministers, disorderly officials, lawless types—
this is why they are said to block day and night the interaction between worthy rulers and righteous scholars,
ensuring they cannot connect with each other.
Now when a worthy serves as minister,
he does not harm the ruler to please flatterers,
does not fawn upon the multitude to gain acceptance,
does not subvert public duty to heed private interests,
does not distort the law to swallow the hard;
his clarity can illuminate treachery,
and his righteousness does not form cliques.
Thus, when Fàn Wǔ returned to Jìn, the state's traitors fled;
when Huá Yuán returned to court, the Yú clan perished.
Therefore, upright and righteous scholars and wicked, crooked men cannot stand together.
Now when a ruler selects scholars,
if he cannot broadly listen to the common people,
and judge with intelligence,
but instead merely trusts the words of disorderly ministers,
solely employs the statements of corrupt officials—
this is what is called choosing envoys together with enemies,
letting prisoners select officials.
The *Book of Documents* says:
"Consult your own heart,
consult the common people."
Confucius said:
"If the multitude likes him,
you must examine him;
if the multitude hates him,
you must examine him."
Therefore, when the sage gives or withholds,
he does not necessarily follow the multitude,
nor does he necessarily rely solely on himself;
he must examine the actions of both others and himself,
and measure them with righteousness.
Sometimes he rejects others and chooses himself;
thus, no recommendations are missed and governance is not abandoned or destroyed.
Some rulers are not like this:
if they have personal favorites,
they then decide accordingly,
not checking with the multitude,
not consulting their own hearts;
blinded by favor,
they follow only what is said.
This is why governance fails and falls into disorder,
and why scholars are neglected and dispersed.
In ancient times, King Zhòu was fond of beautiful women.
Jiǔhóu heard of this
and offered his own daughter.
King Zhòu was greatly pleased,
believing that no beauty in the world could compare to her.
He asked Dájǐ about her,
but Dájǐ, fearing that the new consort would usurp his affection,
pretended to bow her head and weep, saying:
"Has Your Majesty reached old age?
Has your eyesight already declined?
How can someone so ugly be called beautiful?"
King Zhòu then changed his mind and considered her ugly.
Dájǐ, fearing that others would present even more beautiful women,
then declared,
"Jiǔhóu is acting without principle,
seeking to bewitch Your Majesty with this woman.
If Your Majesty does not punish him,
how will you prevent such acts in the future?"
King Zhòu flew into a rage,
had the woman minced and Jiǔhóu boiled alive.
From then on,
those in the world who had beautiful daughters
kept them locked indoors even during the day,
fearing that King Zhòu might hear of them.
When Zhào Gāo monopolized power in Qín
and intended to kill the Second Emperor,
he first demonstrated his authority to the court
by presenting a deer to the sovereign,
claiming it was a fine horse.
The Second Emperor examined it and said,
"It is a deer."
Zhào Gāo insisted,
"It is a horse."
The Second Emperor narrowed his eyes and stared intently, saying,
"Is the Chancellor mistaken?
This is a deer."
But Zhào Gāo maintained it was a horse.
When the court ministers were questioned,
some supported the Second Emperor and contradicted Zhào Gāo.
Zhào Gāo then reported to the Second Emperor:
"These men all flatter their lord and delude their sovereign—
there is no greater disloyalty."
He then had them all executed.
From then on,
no one dared to offer honest remonstrance,
and Zhào Gāo eventually killed the Second Emperor at Wàngyí Palace,
leading to the dynasty's collapse.
Now, beauty and ugliness are perceived by the eyes,
and deer and horses are distinguished by their form—
these are already fixed.
Yet when it comes to slander,
such as when courtiers and concubines embellish falsehoods and craft deceitful words,
then the ruler loses his own judgment,
and people and things lose their true nature.
Moreover, when encountering obscure prisoners
and awaiting verification of their credibility,
it is not as reliable as observing the intentions of a bewitching woman;
distinguishing the worthy from the unworthy
is not as certain as distinguishing a deer from a horse.
These two things
were both presented in the court hall,
exposing their substance before the ruler's own ministers.
Yet when it comes to the delusions caused by favoritism, flattery, cunning persuasion, and artful sophistry that confuse a ruler,
they dazzle the ruler's eyes,
alter and seize his heart,
so that he takes beauty for ugliness
and a deer for a horse.
How much more, then, for worthy men in the countryside
and scholars beyond the palace gates,
who have never had the chance to be seen?
Now, those in power who delight in obstructing the worthy and strive to advance their own factions
have been thus since ancient times.
In the past, Táng Yáo, a great sage,
was intelligent and illustrious;
Yú Shùn, a great sage,
had his virtuous reputation widely heard.
When Yáo was Son of Heaven,
he sought out worthy men
and inquired among the various lords.
The lords refused to recommend Shùn and instead praised the likes of Gòng and Gǔn.
Only due to Yáo's sagacity
was Shùn later elevated and those four men exiled.
Considering the substance of the ancient sages,
the clarity of Yáo's intelligence,
and the prominence of Shùn's virtue,
a ruler's clarity cannot be deceived,
and prominent virtue cannot be obscured.
Their nature was rarely given to flattery,
yet those in power then were straightforward to such an extent.
Now, the conduct of present-day scholars
falls far short of Yáo and Shùn,
while customs are absurd
and worldly methods increasingly conspicuous.
Thus, rulers who seek the worthy
and scholars who grieve for the people
coming together
is surely not to be expected.
When King Wén was hunting and touring,
he encountered Jiāng Shàng by the Wèi River.
Observing his speech and gauging his aspirations,
he perceived his heart,
without consulting his attendants
or deliberating with his ministers.
He then took him back in his carriage,
entrusted him with governance,
and thereby was able to establish Zhōu.
Thus, Yáo consulted the local community to obtain Shùn,
and King Wén consulted himself to obtain Lǚ Shàng.
How could they be like Yīn Xīn (King Zhòu) and Qín Zhèng (the First Emperor of Qín),
who, having obtained worthy men,
instead became mired in enmity,
executed the upright,
and advanced and appointed factions of treacherous ministers?
Therefore, enlightened and sagely rulers, in following the correct path,
do not solely be driven by the noble and favored,
nor deluded by fawning concubines.
They do not discard the distant and estranged,
nor disdain the young and lowly,
but consider and employ them all.
Thus, under the Zhōu system,
when the Son of Heaven heard governance,
he had the Three Dukes down to the ranked scholars present statutes,
good historians present writings,
masters presented admonitions,
blind musicians chanted,
blind reciters recited,
the hundred artisans remonstrated,
commoners conveyed messages,
close ministers exhaustively admonished,
relatives supplemented and scrutinized,
blind historians instructed,
elders cultivated him,
and only then did the king deliberate and decide.
Thus, affairs were carried out without failure.
In decadent ages, it is not so.
They merely trust the arrogant and jealous opinions of the noble,
and exclusively employ flattering and beguiling words.
Those who practice abundant courtesy incur blame and fault,
while those who discuss virtue and righteousness are seen as particularly odious.
Then, sycophantic ministers further employ methods of slander and defamation,
imposing punishments for criticizing superiors.
This is how worthy scholars first become trapped.
Now, methods of slander and defamation
are the axes that cut down the worthy,
and arrogance and jealousy
are the dogs that devour the worthy.
If a ruler internally wields axes that cut down the worthy
and controls dogs that devour the worthy,
yet externally invites the worthy,
hoping they will come—
is this not tragic?
