In the world, there is fortune unsurpassed in greatness,
and also misfortune unsurpassed in pain.
Those who occupy the highest positions
cannot be without the greatest achievements.
Those who usurp the extreme nobility of the soaring dragon
have never avoided destruction and ruin.
Those who accomplish great merits matching heaven and earth
have never failed to flourish and prosper.
What emperors and kings respect
and what Heaven dearly loves
is the people.
Now, when ministers receive weighty positions from their sovereign
and shepherd what Heaven dearly loves,
how can they not secure and benefit them, nurture and succor them?
Therefore, when a noble man holds office, he thinks of benefiting the people;
when reaching the sovereign, he thinks of advancing the worthy.
What achievement is greater than this?
Thus, when above, those below are not burdened;
when in front, those behind are not harmed.
The *Shū* says:
"Heaven's work—men must act in its stead."
Kings model themselves on Heaven to establish offices.
From the dukes and ministers down
to the minor officials,
are they not all Heaven's officers?
Therefore, enlightened rulers dare not act from private favor,
and loyal ministers dare not claim false ability.
To steal another's wealth
is still called theft;
how much more so stealing Heaven's office for private gain?
To offend against men with crime
must incur punishment;
In the Five Dynasties, when feudal lords were established,
states were founded and families prospered,
their lineages passed down for a hundred generations,
spanning thousands of years,
all because they were able to fulfill the duties of heaven's officials,
bringing merit to the common people.
When the Duke of Zhōu campaigned eastward,
he was remembered by later generations;
the sweet pear tree of Duke Shào
was spared from being cut down by the people,
so beloved was he.
Could it be that anyone wished to harm them out of selfishness?
After them, there were many enfeoffed lords,
some not lasting a lifetime,
some not even a full month,
yet none fell into ruin.
Those whose lineages did not endure
did not fill a hundred years.
Why is this so?
The ministers of the Five Dynasties
served their lords with the Way,
governed the world with benevolence,
their grace reaching even the grass and trees,
benefiting both internal and external affairs.
Across the heavens and throughout the land,
none were untouched by their virtue.
The safety and security they brought
was truly the work of heaven.
Thus, their blessings flowed abundantly,
and their main and branch lineages lasted for a hundred generations.
The ministers of later ages,
not thinking to follow heaven's will,
flattered the rulers of their time,
calling those who crushed enemies loyal,
and those who killed many worthy.
Bái Qǐ and Méng Tián
were seen as meritorious by Qín,
but heaven saw them as bandits.
Xīfū and Dǒng Xián
were seen as loyal by their lords,
but heaven saw them as thieves.
Such types,
though honored by the rulers of their time,
did not accord with heaven's will above,
nor did they gain the people's favor below.
Thus, they ended up weeping blood and wailing,
meeting a disgraceful end.
The *Yì Jīng* says:
"When virtue is meager yet position is exalted,
wisdom is small yet plans are grand,
strength is slight yet burdens are heavy,
few escape calamity."
Therefore, when virtue does not match one's responsibilities,
the disaster is sure to be severe;
when ability does not match one's position,
the calamity is sure to be great.
Moreover, those who usurp positions
are deprived of insight by heaven,
and their minds are deluded by spirits.
Thus, in times of poverty and lowliness,
though they possess the qualities of clear insight and the will for benevolence and righteousness,
once they attain wealth and honor,
they turn their backs on kin and abandon the old,
losing their original heart.
They all distance themselves from flesh and blood and draw close to flatterers,
treat friends lightly and lavish care on dogs and horses.
Wealth and goods fill the hands of servants and concubines,
salaries and rewards are exhausted on cunning slaves.
They would rather see strings of cash rot away by the millions
than reluctantly give a single coin to others;
they would rather let grain spoil in overflowing granaries
than reluctantly lend a single peck to others.
People become increasingly arrogant and unrestrained,
failing to repay debts,
with family members resentful at home,
and commoners cursing them on the roads.
When predecessors have thus fallen,
later ones vie to follow in their footsteps.
Truly, this is lamentable.
Observing the intentions of the noble figures of past ages,
they are like infants.
Infants have constant ailments,
noble ministers have constant disasters,
parents have constant failings,
rulers have constant faults.
The constant ailment of infants
is injury from overfeeding;
the constant disaster of noble ministers
is injury from excessive favor.
The constant failing of parents
lies in being unable to stop doting on beloved children;
the constant fault of rulers
lies in being unable to stop indulging arrogant ministers.
If nursing is too excessive,
the child will inevitably suffer convulsions and develop epilepsy;
if nobility and wealth are too abundant,
one will inevitably become arrogant and dissolute, giving rise to faults.
Thus, those beloved children who bring harm to their own bodies
are not confined to a single household;
those arrogant ministers who bring ruin to their families
are not confined to a single generation.
Some, through betrayal, violence, and unrighteousness,
or through meager virtue unworthy of their high status,
are judged by Wénchāng for their merits,
and Sīmìng notes their faults.
Observing the depth of their wickedness,
weighing their crimes and delivering punishment,
some are captured and beheaded,
some have their shoulders torn and chests ripped open,
beaten to death in deep pits,
with knives in their mouths in the city markets,
corpses stiffened, families broken,
ancestral temples overturned, clans exterminated—
all were those who brought no merit to the common people.
Yet later people greedily seek power and crave favor,
accumulating without limit,
thinking to climb the tower of collapse,
delighting to follow the tracks of overturned carts,
hoping to increase their blessings and status,
to fill positions and complete their strings of cash.
What age is without such people?
When the Lǚ clan was at the height of its power,
the Empress Dowager held the reins of government and monopolized authority,
Lǚ Lù and Lǚ Chǎn managed affairs and grasped power.
They arbitrarily established four kings,
enfeoffed many sons and brothers,
simultaneously occupying military and ministerial posts,
intertwining internal and external power like a solid rock.
They themselves thought that even if Tāng and Wǔ rose again,
or the Five Hegemons emerged,
they could not be endangered.
Thus, they abandoned benevolence and righteousness and exalted威虐,
discarded ritual and trust, pursuing deceit and cunning.
Throughout the land, there was resentment and pain,
and people wished for their downfall.
Thus, in one morning they were wiped out, and none mourned them.
When the Huò clan was at the height of its power,
they monopolized the role of chancellor to the young emperor,
exterminated their colleagues,
deposed and installed emperors,
with none daring to oppose.
Huò Yǔ succeeded his father's position,
Huò Shān and Huò Yún managed affairs behind the screen,
their sons-in-law exclusively commanded the imperial guard,
and marriages were confined to their own clan.
When the Wáng clan was at the height of its power,
there were nine marquises and five generals,
and twenty-three vermilion-wheeled carriages.
The Empress Dowager monopolized governance,
holding power for three generations.
Wáng Mǎng became Zǎihéng,
was enfeoffed as the Duke Ān Hàn,
acted as regent under a false title,
personally facing south as ruler,
and finally usurped the throne,
for more than ten years.
He himself thought he had held the position so long,
his authority established and grace implemented,
that he would never face disaster or downfall.
Thus, he gave free rein to his heart and followed his whims,
drawing close to favorites and forgetting those afar,
gathering crowds of petty men,
heavily taxing and exhausting the people,
to support the meritless.
His actions were deceitful and cunning,
cloaked in the meaning of the classics,
deluding and bewildering the common people,
deceiving and lying to heaven and earth.
He thought himself secretive,
and that none knew of it.
But the August Heaven above observed his treachery,
and the spirits in the unseen illuminated his conduct.
How could there be any mistake!
Birds think the mountains low and build nests atop them,
fish think the abyss shallow and bore holes within it.
What ultimately captures them is the bait.
Noble relatives fear their households are inauspicious and gather auspicious names,
fear their gates are not sturdy and forge iron pivots for them.
What ultimately leads to their downfall
is not due to few taboos or rotting gate pivots,
but often stems from amassing wealth and acting arrogantly and presumptuously,
oppressing the common people and losing the people's hearts.
Confucius said:
"Do not worry about lacking a position,
worry about not establishing yourself."
Therefore, if a minister does not uphold and follow ritual laws,
devote his utmost energy to his duties,
sincerely assist his ruler,
serve the people with merit,
below, attaching himself to the common folk,
above, complying with the will of Heaven,
but instead wishes to rely on his private knowledge,
usurp the ruler's authority and virtue,
to oppress the lower people,
go against Heaven and Earth,
deceive the spirits,
stealthily advance and seek improper gains,
to enrich himself;
while dwelling in peril as precarious as a pile of eggs,
yet scheming for security as firm as Mount Tài,
engaging in actions as fleeting as morning dew,
yet thinking of achievements that will last for generations,
it is like the First Emperor abandoning virtue and relying on punishment,
yet wanting to count from one to ten thousand.
Is this not deluded?!
A true king regards all within the Four Seas as one family,
and considers the millions of people as a whole.
If one man does not plow,
the world will inevitably suffer hunger;
if one woman does not weave,
the world will inevitably suffer cold.
Now the whole world abandons farming and sericulture,
and rushes to trade,
oxen, horses, carts, and carriages
fill the roads,
idle hands engaged in clever crafts,
overflow the cities and towns,
those who attend to the fundamentals are few,
while those who live off others are many.
"The capital of Shāng is grand and orderly,
it is the model for the four directions."
Now observe Luòyáng:
those engaged in superficial trades outnumber farmers tenfold,
and deceitful idlers outnumber those in superficial trades tenfold.
Thus, one man plows,
and a hundred people eat from it;
one woman tends mulberries,
and a hundred people are clothed from it.
With one supporting a hundred,
who can supply it?
Throughout the land, there are a hundred commanderies and a thousand counties,
tens of thousands of market towns,
all similar to this.
How can the fundamentals suffice to support the nonessentials?
Then how can the people avoid hunger and cold?
When hunger and cold come together,
how can they avoid wrongdoing?
Wrongdoing leads to villainy and disorder,
and when villainy and disorder abound,
how can officials avoid being harsh and cruel?
When harshness and cruelty are repeatedly applied,
how can the people below avoid sorrow and resentment?
When the sorrowful and resentful are many,
then calamitous omens appear together.
The lower people are left with no recourse,
and Heaven above sends down disasters,
then the state is endangered.
Poverty is born from wealth,
weakness is born from strength,
disorder is born from order,
danger is born from security.
Therefore, when an enlightened king nurtures the people,
he worries for them and labors for them,
instructs them and teaches them,
carefully guards against small beginnings to prevent sprouts,
to cut off their wickedness.
Thus, the Yì praises "regulating by measures,
not wasting wealth,
not harming the people";
the "Seventh Month" poem,
teaches great and small matters,
ending and beginning again.
From this perspective,
the people indeed cannot be allowed to indulge.
Now the people are extravagant in clothing,
luxurious in food and drink,
engaged in gossip and skilled in deception,
mutually cheating and deceiving,
this is everywhere.
Some make plotting wickedness and forming cliques their occupation,
others take wandering and gambling as their business;
some able-bodied men never pass down plows and hoes,
but carry pellets and hold slingshots,
strolling hand in hand.
Some take good soil to make pellets and sell them,
which externally cannot ward off bandits,
internally cannot keep out mice.
Duke Líng of Jìn delighted in them, increasing his wickedness;
never have we heard of righteous scholars enjoying carrying them to stroll.
Only the mindless,
crowds of young lads,
take and hold them,
recklessly shooting at birds and sparrows,
missing a hundred times without a single hit,
but instead hitting their own faces,
this is the most useless and harmful.
Some sit making bamboo flutes,
sharpening their heads,
which have the appearance of causing harm,
coating them with wax and honey,
which resemble sweet tongues,
all are not auspicious or good omens.
Some make clay carts, pottery dogs, horse riders, and puppet shows,
various playthings to amuse children with clever deceit.
The Shī criticizes "not spinning their hemp,
the women dance and sway."
Now many do not attend to household duties,
"abandon their silkworms and weaving,"
and instead learn shamanistic prayers,
drumming and dancing to serve spirits,
to deceive the common people,
bewitching womenfolk.
Families with weak and sick members,
filled with worry and distress,
are easily frightened,
so that they rush about at convenient times,
leaving their proper homes,
huddling by the roadside,
leaking above and damp below,
injured by wind and cold,
taken advantage of by wicked people,
attacked by thieves and robbers,
increasing misfortune and hauntings,
so that the severely afflicted are too many to count.
Some abandon medicine,
and turn to serving spirits instead,
thus leading to death,
unaware they have been deceived by shamans,
instead regretting that they served the spirits too late,
this is the extreme of bewitching the common people.
Some cut fine silk,
making it into loose headpieces,
having artisans paint them,
hiring people to write prayers,
falsely embellishing with clever words,
hoping to invite much fortune.
Some tear colored silks,
cutting them into strips several fen wide,
each five cun long,
sewing and embroidering them to wear.
Some spin colored threads into strands,
cutting and wrapping them around arms.
These in the long run bring no benefit to fortune or misfortune,
but only waste and destroy silk threads,
confusing and alarming the common people.
Some cut and trim patterned silks and fine gauzes,
stealing an inch of eight colors,
to create patterns of elm leaves, endless knots, and water waves,
piercing and stitching finely,
making into boxes, bags, skirts, jackets, and covers,
wasting hundreds of bolts of silk,
using ten times the effort.
Such kinds of people,
neither assist farmers nor working women,
nor benefit the world,
yet sit and eat fine grain,
consume the bright day,
ruin completed work,
turning the whole into the broken,
the sturdy into the flimsy,
the large into the small,
the easy into the difficult,
all should be prohibited.
The mountains and forests cannot provide fuel for wildfires,
nor can the rivers and seas fill a leaking cup.
Emperor Xiàowén personally wore plain clothing of yíbù,
and sandals made of leather,
using a sword with a leather belt,
and used document bags as curtain drapery in the palace.
In the intense summer heat,
he wanted to build a terrace,
calculating the cost to be a million,
but considered it extravagant and did not proceed.
Now, the wealthy and noble families in the capital,
in clothing, food and drink, carriages, ornamentation, and residences,
all exceed the royal standards,
and have greatly overstepped their bounds.
The servants and concubines all wear fine hemp cloth from Shēngyuè,
use silk from Tóngzhōng,
wear delicate patterned gauze,
ice silk and brocade.
Rhinoceros horns and ivory, pearls and jade,
amber and tortoiseshell,
are used for ornaments on rockery.
Gold and silver make intricate carvings,
deer fur for shoes,
adorned with colored silk,
arrogant and extravagant, overstepping their lords,
boasting and competing.
This is what the wise Gōngzǐ lamented about,
now seen among servants.
For the wealthy, at weddings,
ten carriages accompany each bride,
with servant riders flanking all sides,
forming a procession.
The rich compete to outdo each other,
while the poor feel ashamed if they fall behind.
As a result, the expenses of a single feast,
can ruin a lifetime's toil.
In ancient times, when people were granted enfeoffment,
only then could they wear fine silk and ride in horse carriages.
Today, unable to entirely restore the ancient ways,
commoners can indeed be exempt,
yet they go beyond even Emperor Xiàowén,
insisting on delicate clothing,
shoes made of deer fur,
adornments of beautiful colors,
and decoration of socks with embroidery,
enhancing carriages and horses,
and raising many slaves.
Those who manage to live like this,
neither grow grain,
nor contribute anything but become parasites.
Confucius said:
"In ancient burials,
the deceased were wrapped with twigs,
and buried in the wild,
without mounds or trees,
and no set mourning period;
later sages changed this with inner and outer coffins,"
using paulownia wood for the coffin,
and hemp fabric for the cover,
not reaching the water below,
nor leaking odors above.
In later times, they used Chinese parasol, cypress, locust, fir, and catalpa,
each chosen from local sources,
joined with glue, lacquer,
held together with nails,
smoothly planed,
seamlessly assembled,
ensuring strength and reliability,
making them suitable for use.
However, later noble families in the capital,
insist on timber from Jiangnan,
bringing in camphor, catalpa, and Nan timber;
even distant provinces,
compete to imitate.
The camphor and catalpa,
originate from very remote places,
growing deep in mountains and valleys,
reaching atop mountain peaks,
along cliffs a thousand steps high,
across rivers a hundred zhàng wide,
resting precariously on rugged terrain,
difficult to access,
taking successive days to spot,
and months to fell and process,
requiring groups to move them,
oxen teams to transport,
oil and water routes at sea,
crossing through Huai rivers upstream,
traveling thousands of miles,
to reach Luòyáng.
Artisans sculpt and treat the wood,
taking months and years,
calculating the work for a single coffin,
amounting to countless labor.
Its weight, nearing ten thousand pounds,
requires a large crowd to lift,
large carts to transport.
From east to Lè'làng,
west to Dūnhuáng,
within tens of thousands of miles,
all compete to use them.
Such expense and effort harms agriculture,
and is truly lamentable!
In ancient times, burial mounds were not tall.
When Zhōng Ní's mother passed away,
her grave was four feet high,
crumbling in the rain,
and his disciples offered to repair it.
Confucius wept, saying:
"The rites do not require repairing graves."
"For Lǐ's death,
there was a coffin but no outer coffin."
Emperor Wén was buried at Zhǐyáng,
Emperor Míng at Luònán,
with no treasures secured,
no ancestral temples built,
nor grand mausoleums raised.
Though the burial mounds were humble, their virtue was exalted.
Now, noble families in the capital,
and powerful families in counties,
do not provide lavish care in life,
but engage in grand funerals in death.
Some go as far as carving gold and engraving jade,
choosing fine camphor and catalpa,
dedicating fertile lands for cemeteries,
burying treasures and effigies of people and horses,
building large tombs,
planting extensive pines and cypresses,
with residences and shrines,
indulging in ostentation.
Favored ministers and noble families,
regional and genealogical houses,
whenever a funeral occurs,
their territories send officials,
bringing carriages and tents,
lending items for entertaining guests,
competing for grandeur.
This adds no worth to the final rites,
no increase to filial actions,
but causes upheaval and disturbance,
and harms officials and the people.
Considering the precincts of Hào and Bì,
the tombs of Kings Wén and Wǔ,
the fortifications south of the city,
and the grave of Zēng Xí,
Duke Zhōu was not unfaithful,
nor was Master Zēng unfilial,
believing that honoring rulers and fathers,
does not depend on wealth gathering.
Elevating names and ancestors,
is not determined by carriages.
Confucius said:
"Excessive wealth damages virtue,
and leads to losing ritual respect."
Duke Líng of Jìn taxed heavily for decorative walls,
and The Spring and Autumn Annals considered this unworthy of a ruler.
Huá Yuán and Lè Yǔ buried Duke Wén of Jìn lavishly,
and The Spring and Autumn Annals condemned them as unworthy ministers.
How much more inappropriate is it for ordinary officials and commoners,
to surpass their rulers and exceed heavenly ordinances?
During Emperor Jǐng's reign,
Wǔyuán Marquis Wèi Bùhài was stripped of his title for violating burial laws.
During Emperor Míng's time,
Sāng Mín of Chuāngyáng lost his title for excessive tomb measures.
Today, the trend of extravagance and departure from fundamentals,
excessive luxury beyond superiors,
is exceedingly severe!
All criticisms here,
are not due to people's nature,
but rather the result of chaotic policies and insufficient cultural guidance.
Kings ruling the world,
observing the people to educate them,
can change customs and habits,
bringing about peace and prosperity.
Note:
Mountain heights do not rise without accumulation,
but increase step by step.
Valleys do not deepen without formation,
but gradually sink.
Thus, unceasing accumulation leads to high mountains like Sōng Shān;
continued reduction reaches the profound depths of the Yellow Springs.
This is not only true of mountains and rivers,
but also of human conduct.
If a commoner accumulates good deeds without slacking,
he will surely attain the virtue of Yán Huí and Mǐn Sǔn.
If he accumulates evil without cease,
he will surely earn the infamy of Jié and Zhí.
This is not only true of commoners,
but also of ministers.
If one accumulates righteousness tirelessly,
one will surely develop a will for integrity and duty.
If one accumulates wickedness without end,
one will surely give rise to thoughts of violence and regicide.
This is not only true of ministers,
but also of rulers.
If governance and education accumulate virtue,
they will surely bring the blessing of peace and stability.
If actions and measures repeatedly err,
they will surely bring the calamity of peril and ruin.
Therefore, Confucius said:
"Tāng and Wǔ did not become kings because of a single good deed,
nor did Jié and Zhòu perish because of a single evil act.
The rise and fall of the Three Dynasties
lay in what they accumulated."
For those who accumulate much good,
even if there is one evil deed,
it is called a mistake,
not enough to cause ruin.
For those who accumulate much evil,
even if there is one good deed,
it is called an accidental hit,
not enough to ensure survival.
If rulers hear this,
they should be filled with trepidation.
If commoners hear this,
they should change their demeanor.
Thus, the noble person is "trembling with fear,
growing more cautious each day,"
restraining himself and reflecting thrice daily,
"planning for what is not yet seen."
Confucius said:
"Goodness not accumulated is insufficient to establish a reputation;
evil not accumulated is insufficient to destroy oneself.
"When sages and worthies humbly reform,

Qìng Fēng and Bó Yǒu,
indulged recklessly in wine,
immersed without restraint,
and thus ruined their families.
Jìn Píng neglected governance,
confused and losing his will,
with good ministers failing to correct him,
so disaster befell them all.
Chǔ Zhuāng and Qí Wēi,
initially had indulgent conduct,
suffered weakening defeats,
nearly falling into chaos and ruin.
But midway they were able to awaken and understand,
diligently caring for the people's affairs,
laboring their spirits and pondering bitterly,
striving tirelessly.
One brought forth Chén Yīng,
enfeoffed and appointed Guǎn Sū,
summoned Jímò,
and boiled the magistrate of Ā.
Thus they were able to revive their states,
strengthen and dominate the feudal lords,
honored and eminent in their time,
remembered with longing by later generations,
their fine names passed down,
recorded in books and records.
From this perspective,
there are those who aspire to be rulers;
their conduct is the same.
To know oneself is called clarity;
to conquer oneself is called strength.
If there is something improper, one never fails to know it;
knowing it, one never repeats it.
This is why Yánzǐ was praised as nearly perfect.

making you very firm.
Making you truly abundant,

Sufficient to destroy oneself.

think small evils are harmless and do not eliminate them.

This is why Jué and Jǔ misled the state and never returned,

the hidden accumulates to become
prominent, oh so prominent;

Sages are always cautious of the subtle.
King Wén was cautious and reverent,

pondering and being careful of the minute,
guarding early against what has not yet sprouted.
Thus they achieved great peace and passed it to their descendants.
Moreover, wickedness and righteousness
are like water and fire, not sharing the same source;
they cannot flourish together.
If righteous nature prevails,
one values oneself and cannot bear to compromise,
so Bó Yí starved to death without regret.
If wicked nature prevails,
one becomes accustomed and cannot bear to abandon it,
so Wáng Mǎng usurped the throne without shame.
This is the result of accumulated evil habits.
The accumulation of evil habits is not brief,
nor is reaching death caused by a single act.
Generations grade people accordingly.

This saying is good,

securing his nature and destiny,
making it very firm.
Making you faithful and generous,
why not govern?
And increasing you greatly,
making you very abundant.
Why not follow and practice the five constants,
nurture one's nature and destiny in accordance,

securing his nature and destiny,

why would you not govern well?

making all very plentiful.

How illuminating are these words!

States thrive through worthies,
and decline through flattery;
rulers find security through loyalty,
and peril through jealousy.
This is a constant principle through the ages,
and known to all the world.
Yet declining states and imperiled rulers follow one another without end—
is it really that the world lacks loyal, trustworthy, upright, and righteous men?
Truly, it is that the way of loyalty, trustworthiness, uprightness, and righteousness cannot be practiced.
Within ten paces,
there must be lush grass;
in a hamlet of ten households,
there must be outstanding men.
The birth of worthy talents
follows one after another like sun and moon,
never lacking or ceasing.
Thus, even chaotic Yīn had three humane men,
and small Wèi had many noble men.
With Hàn's vast expanse,
the multitude of scholars and people,
the clarity and brightness of the court,
the cultivated governance of high and low—
yet among officials there are no upright clerks,
in positions there are no good ministers.
This is not because the present age lacks worthies,
but because worthies are suppressed and cannot reach the court of the sage ruler.
Those who aspire to the Way have few friends,
those who chase vulgarity have many companions.
Thus, the whole world abounds in factions and selfishness,
competing in superficial show while pursuing flashiness.
Those who recommend scholars
no longer base it on their substance and backbone,
nor gauge their talent and conduct;
they simply fabricate empty praises,
sweeping generalizations and hollow talk.
Selecting the capable to record them,
among dukes, ministers, provincial inspectors, and their assistants,
there are nearly two hundred as "flourishing talents" and "filial and incorrupt."
Examining their records one by one,
their virtue matching Yānyuān, Bǔ, and Rǎn,
yet examining their actual conduct and ability,
most do not reach the medium level.
If they were truly as described in the documents,
then this would mean gaining two hundred great worthies each year.
If so, then why do disasters and anomalies cause famine?
This shows these are not true reflections of reality.
Praising fine rice and meat
may please the face,
but it is not as edible as coarse grains and wild herbs in the mouth.
Depicting Xīshī and Máoqiáng
may delight the heart,
but they are not as serviceable as an ugly wife or plain concubine before one.
Exaggerating high praise,
forcibly covering flaws,
to deceive and boast,
may gratify the ear,
but it is not as reliable as loyal selection and genuine conduct for official service.
Zhōu Xiǎn was constrained by his times,
hence Sū Qín;
Yān Kuài coveted empty fame,
hence yielded to Zǐzhī—
both abandoned substance for reputation,
the error of being misled by clamor.
The sage is pure,
the worthy is mixed;
Zhōugōng did not seek perfection,
his four friends were not alike in all aspects,
how much more in decadent ages?
Thus, those assisted by Gāozǔ,
the generals and ministers of Guāngwǔ,
were not falsely recommended,
nor were they demanded to excel in all ways;
what Qín discarded,
what Wáng Mǎng rejected,
the two founders employed to punish violence and chaos,
achieving order and stability.
In an age of peace,
to say there are no scholars,
repeatedly opening broad selections,
yet failing to obtain the upright—
this is truly infuriating!
The enlightened ruler's edict is like a sound,
and the loyal minister's response should be like an echo,
whether long or short, large or small,
clear or murky, fast or slow,
they must harmonize with each other.
Therefore, when seeking a horse, ask about horses;
when seeking a donkey, ask about donkeys;
when seeking an eagle, ask about eagles;
when seeking a piebald horse, ask about piebald horses.
Through such teachings and commands,
rewards and punishments will be certain.
Lofty theories that deceive one another
are not as good as loyal discussions that are honest and sincere.
Moreover, jade is polished with stone,
metal is treated with salt,
brocade is washed with fish,
and cloth is cleansed with ash.
Thus, it is inherent that the base can govern the noble,
and the ugly can refine the beautiful.
The wise discard shortcomings and adopt strengths,
thereby achieving merit.
The enlightened ruler employs scholars in the same manner.
Things have their appropriate uses;
their materials are not wasted—
how much more so for people?
Cultivating oneself, acting with caution,
being sincere, upright, and honest,
pure, clean, and unsullied,
tranquil, indifferent, and non-interfering—
these are the foundation of transformation.
Worrying for the ruler, grieving for the people,
perceiving alone the roots of disorder,
loving goodness, hating evil,
strict and clear in rewards and punishments—
these are the talents for governance.
The enlightened ruler embraces both and employs them together.
Vessels for evil conduct
are used like gold, jade, precious governance, or strong iron.
Without these two treasures,
if one merely strives for novelty to seek fame,
feigning tranquility to deceive the masses,
then customs will be corrupted and transformation harmed.
Those in this age who admire emptiness
are called "hard and white."
Such "hard and white" conduct
is detested by enlightened rulers
and not adopted by royal institutions.
Therefore, when selecting the worthy and recommending scholars,
one must examine their purity and simplicity,
speak based on facts,
and if they have minor flaws,
do not forcefully embellish them
to amplify empty reputations.
A person with a single ability
should contribute their own strength;
whether in action or stillness, speech or silence,
do not force them to combine all.
Otherwise, how could discussions of Xiāo Hé, Cáo Shēn, Zhōu Bó, and Hán Xìn
ever be sufficient?
Figures like Wú Chén, Dèng Yǔ, Liáng Tǒng, and Dòu Róng
could achieve tenfold.
Assign each according to their suitability,
measure their talents and appoint them to positions,
then no office will be neglected,
meritorious achievements can be accomplished,
great peace can be attained,
and the qílín can arrive.
Moreover, Yān was small,
its status humble,
yet King Zhāo was able to gather outstanding talents from other states,
launched campaigns to punish violence and chaos,
and achieved governance and strength.
Now, with the vast expanse of Hàn territory,
and the Son of Heaven revered and enlightened,
if there is not a single good minister,
this truly shows no compassion for the worries and sufferings of the millions,
and no urgency for the assistance of the worthy in governance.
Confucius said:
"They have not thought of it;
how could it be far away?"
Loyal and good officials are indeed easy to find;
it is merely that the sage kings do not desire them.
In the earliest times,
when the common people first appeared,
there was no distinction between high and low,
yet order arose naturally.
Heaven had not yet intervened,
and rulers had not yet been established.
Later, gradually, there was deceit and coercion,
some oppressed and bullied others,
encroachment and plunder did not cease,
becoming a great harm to the people.
Then Heaven mandated sages to shepherd them,
so they would not lose their nature.
All within the Four Seas received benefits,
none were not covered by virtue.
All together supported and upheld them,
calling them the Son of Heaven.
Thus, when Heaven establishes a ruler,
it is not out of favoritism for this person
to enslave the people,
but rather to punish violence, eliminate harm, and benefit the common people.
Therefore, through human plans and spiritual consultations,
the capable are placed in position.
The Book of Songs says:
"Great is God!
He looks down with majesty.
He surveys the four quarters,
seeking the people's suffering.
Only these two states,
their governance is unattained.
Only these four states,
who will investigate and consider?
God points to them,
detesting their wicked ways.
Then He turns His gaze westward,
this is where He grants consideration."
This passage means
that the governance of the two states, Xià and Yīn, was lacking,
indulging in extravagance, boastfulness, and excess.
God detested this,
and again sought a sage for the people's suffering,
investigating and considering with the four states of the world to place him there.
Previously, summoning good people,
disliking extravagance, boastfulness, and limitless excess,
they only considered models and examples,
clearly establishing rituals and order,
creating excellent laws and arts,
hanging them for eternity.
Therefore, the Commentary says:
"In establishing rituals,
the highest objects do not exceed twelve—
this is the way of Heaven."
Thus, the former sages had regulations for the ceremonial plowing,
limits for offerings to spirits,
restraint in personal indulgence,
and measures for honoring the worthy.
High and low, great and small,
noble and base, close and distant—
all had their degrees of dignity.
Ranks diminished step by step,
each sufficiently provided according to their爵位,
public and private affairs reaching their respective levels,
rituals practiced, virtue and righteousness upheld.
At this time,
within the Nine Provinces,
covering three thousand li,
there were eight hundred states.
As for the distribution of emoluments,
it was based on the standard of the highest-ranking farmers,
beginning with commoners serving in official positions,
whose emoluments were sufficient to replace farming,
and could support nine people.
The lower-ranking officers of the feudal lords were the same.
Middle-ranking officers received double that of lower-ranking officers,
supporting eighteen people.
Upper-ranking officers received double that of middle-ranking officers,
supporting thirty-six people.
Grandees received double that,
supporting seventy-two people.
The ministers of small states
received twice that of grandees.
The ministers of medium-sized states
received three times that of grandees.
The ministers of large states
received four times that of grandees,
supporting two hundred eighty-eight people.
Each ruler received ten times that of his ministers.
The Three Dukes of the Son of Heaven had fiefs comparable to those of dukes and marquises,
covering about one hundred li square.
Ministers had fiefs comparable to those of earls,
seventy li square.
Grandees had fiefs comparable to those of viscounts and barons,
fifty li square.
Chief officers had fiefs comparable to those of attached states,
thirty li square.
Those who achieved merit were enfeoffed.
Thus, official affairs were devoted to the public good,
with no concern for private households;
children and younger siblings devoted themselves to learning,
without interfering in wealth and profit,
closing their doors and keeping to themselves,
not competing with the common people,
and the path to hunger and cold
was not fallen into;
ministers were well-supported and not constrained,
officials cherished their positions and were not greedy,
the people were tranquil and strong,
and thus the foundation of great peace was established.
Then, careful tribute selection was implemented,
clearly demoting and promoting as necessary,
so that officials were suited to their positions,
and each person fulfilled their duties;
"Reverently following the August Heaven,
respectfully instructing the people in the seasons,"
"Together with my wife and children,
taking food to those in the southern fields";
the rulers emphasized moderation in rituals,
rectifying themselves to set an example for those below,
and those below were pleased with their governance,
each gladly exhausting themselves to serve and support their superiors.
Thus, Heaven and Earth interacted harmoniously,
Yīn and Yáng were balanced and peaceful,
the people had no deceit or hidden evils,
the mechanisms of governance did not falter,
virtuous energy flowed, and songs of praise arose.
Later, suddenly, nurturing the worthy was neglected, and "The Deer Cry" expressed longing;
turning away from clans and families, "Gathering White Southernwood" expressed resentment;
implementing land tax, "The Large Rat" arose;
heavy levies and taxes were reported through translations;
the distribution of emoluments became skewed, and "Qīngfǔ" criticized;
envoys were settled, and "Miánmán" satirized;
thus, decline, disorder, and weakness ensued.
When the Zhōu house declined, the Five Hegemons arose;
the Six States were exhausted, and the violent Qín rose;
they turned away from righteousness and principle, esteeming power and force;
they abandoned rituals and practiced greed and rapacity;
they imposed heavy levies and taxes to enrich themselves,
strengthening their ministers to weaken the branches;
civil virtue did not earn enfeoffment or rank,
and feudal lords did not gain [their due].
Thus, the worthy could not practice rituals to follow the Way,
and ranked ministers could not avoid wrongdoing in pursuit of profit.
Rulers frequently issued pardons, indulging criminals,
and the people, without shame, engaged in much theft.
Why?
Because corrupt energy intensified and influenced those above,
and hardships pressed, driven by hunger and cold.
This is why Zāng Hé could not interrogate the thieves.
The Book of Songs says:
"The great wind has its path,
the greedy man ruins his kind."
"You taught them,
and the people imitate this."
Thus, when the ancient kings were about to issue commands and decrees,
they were earnest,
fearing only that they might miss the mark and lead to evil.
Therefore, they established canons as standards for the people,
shared by high and low alike,
with no private distortions.
The Three Offices established laws,
and it was unheard of to pardon the guilty
or treat prison bribes as treasures.
Thus, an enlightened ruler, facing the multitude,
must follow the correct path,
neither weary of having nor craving more,
but strive for moderation in rituals and generosity to those below,
restoring virtue and promoting transformation,
so that all may flourish in nurturing life and compete in integrity and shame.
Thus, when officials are upright, the people are transformed;
when wicked hearts are dismissed, deceit and hidden evils cease.
Only then can harmonious energy be achieved and great peace attained.
The Book of Changes says:
"The sage nurtures the worthy to benefit the myriad people."
The people are the root,
the ruler takes the ministers as the foundation.
Only then can heights be scaled;
horses must be fat,
only then can distant goals be reached.
If a ruler does not focus on this but wishes to achieve great peace,
it is like building a thin foundation and expecting a high wall,
or having emaciated steeds and demanding a long journey.
That it cannot be achieved is certain.
In treating illness,
one must first know the deficiency or excess of the pulse,
and where the energy is blocked,
then prescribe a remedy.
Thus, the disease can be cured and life prolonged.
In governing a state,
one must first know the sufferings of the people,
and the origins of calamities,
then establish prohibitions accordingly.
Thus, deceit can be stopped, and the state can be secure.
Today, what harms good people the most
is nothing greater than frequent pardons.
When pardons and redemptions are frequent,
the wicked flourish, and the good suffer.
How can this be made clear?
It is said:
In families of filial piety and fraternal duty,
who cultivate themselves and act cautiously,
not violating prohibitions from above,
from birth to death,
they have not an ounce of crime;
yet when pardons and redemptions are frequent,
they never receive favor,
but often suffer harm instead.
Why?
When upright and honest men serve as officials,
they do not avoid the powerful,
nor do they shirk their superiors.
In carrying out supervision and inspection,
they are already discontented,
and the factions of the cunning and crafty
further add slanderous words.
Knowing that pardons will soon come,
they then collectively act unjustly, inflicting wrongs and injustices,
falsely accusing and imposing legal penalties.
Now, if the ruler recklessly applies punishments,
the highest being death or exile,
the lowest being wrongful condemnation,
and the families of the wronged
only then begin to plead for review and report the facts to prove their innocence,
it is already of no benefit to the dead.
As for recluses and wandering scholars,
good and noble men,
who are slandered and falsely accused by flatterers and sharp-tongued individuals,
the lowly and wronged people
who can reach the palace gates
are less than one in ten thousand,
and those who receive an audience
are no more than one in a hundred.
Even after facing the Shàngshū,
many are sent away empty-handed,
again, six or seven out of ten.
Even if they undergo investigation,
the commanderies and prefectures look to each other,
delaying the true matters.
Waiting from spring and summer until autumn and winter,
and from autumn and winter again into spring and summer,
those who encounter pardons in such circumstances
are too numerous to count.
Moreover, the cautious and diligent people,
who follow the ways of Heaven,
share the benefits of the land,
choose not to violate the soil,
are careful in their conduct and frugal in their spending,
accumulating bit by bit,
may still commit minor offenses.
These simple, good people are the foundation of the state.
The frivolous and wicked youths,
the unprincipled and violent people,
who contemplate treacherous and evil deeds,
rise up to become robbers and thieves,
using wealth and lust to kill others’ parents,
slaughter their children,
exterminate their families,
seize their bribes,
and engage in greed, cruelty, and lawlessness.
The corrupt and wicked officials,
who plunder and kill the innocent,
oppress and wrong the common people,
all hope that the sage emperor will punish the wicked and redress grievances,
thereby resolving accumulated resentment.
Instead, he pardons them all in one stroke,
allowing the wicked to gather in celebration and boast,
while old thieves pass by their doors with hidden loot,
filial sons see their enemies but cannot seek revenge,
and rightful owners see their stolen goods but cannot reclaim them.
There is no pain greater than this.
Therefore, before a pardon is issued, there is often a sudden cold spell,
because there are many people filled with grievances, sorrow, and hatred.
Nurturing weeds harms the crops;
showing favor to evildoers harms the good people.
The *Book of Documents* says:
"King Wén established punishments,
and for these there is no pardon."
Thus, when the ancient kings established penal laws,
it was not because they took pleasure in injuring people’s flesh
or cutting short their lifespans,
but to deter treachery, punish wickedness, and eliminate harm to the people.
The world originally could not govern itself,
so a king was established to rule over it.
The king’s duty lies in upholding the heavenly mandate,
jointly administering rewards and punishments.
Thus, the classics state: "Heaven appoints the virtuous,
with five distinctions and five emblems;
Heaven punishes the guilty,
with five penalties and five applications."
The *Book of Songs* criticizes: "They ought to be guilty,
yet you instead release them."
In ancient times, only the founding ruler,
who inherited a state of extreme chaos,
and bore the evils of the previous king,
saw his people turn into enemies,
with none who did not become bandits, thieves, violators of righteousness, evildoers, and plunderers.
Having overthrown the old regime and received the throne,
he became their parent,
and thus was justified in issuing one pardon.
For successors thereafter,
there should be no such pardons.
Why?
The ruler matches Heaven in benevolence,
nurturing the myriad people to achieve great accomplishments.
He cannot consider nurturing evildoers and sparing the guilty as benevolence,
nor regard indulging heaven’s enemies as wisdom.
Now, those with inherently wicked natures,
at home show no filial piety or fraternal duty,
in public show no respect,
are frivolous, arrogant, and contemptuous,
violent and without discernment,
openly act with intimidation, insult, and encroachment for gain,
and consider cruelty and brutality as virtue.
Thus, those who repeatedly violate the king’s laws
are the enemies of the people,
the most foolish and extremely wicked individuals.
Even if they escape shackles
and leave prison,
they never change their remorseful hearts.
They boast of their cunning and arrogance,
and upon release, how often do they not again violate the law?
In Luòyáng, there are even those who arrange murders,
called "contractors of killings."
They accept a hundred thousand in payment,
and give several thousand to their agents.
They also heavily bribe local officials,
who collude with them in wickedness.
Profits run deep,
with networks and accomplices intertwined,
reaching up to noble relatives and favored ministers.
They persuade those above,
and their requests are carried out below.
Thus, even with strict magistrates and governors,
they ultimately cannot break up or eradicate these networks.
Why?
All who dare commit great wickedness
must have talents surpassing the masses,
and be able to ingratiate themselves with those above.
They distribute ill-gotten wealth widely,
offer flattering words,
and manipulate each other.
Without the integrity and uprightness of a Dìwǔ Gōng,
who would not be swayed?
Now, investigating the masterminds of murder in Luòyáng,
their numbers reach as high as several tens,
and as low as four or five.
As long as they live, the killings do not cease,
all due to the repeated pardons granted.
From this perspective,
the nature of great wickedness
can never be transformed.
Even if pardoned yearly,
it only encourages further wickedness.
Some are deluded,
believing that celestial phenomena have signs,
and when the weather indicates a pardon,
the ruler should follow it and bestow grace.
But this is not necessarily so.
The king, being supremely noble,
communicates with Heaven’s essence.
When his heart has thoughts,
and his mind has considerations,
even before he speaks or shows expression,
Heaven responds with changes.
If there are auspicious or ominous signs,
or the moon follows the stars,
this may indeed correspond to events.
Thus, when auspicious or strange phenomena appear,
they may serve as warnings to the ruler.
If he neglects to examine them,
these are consequences of his own actions,
yet he mistakenly attributes them to Heaven’s will,
which is incorrect.
Common people also say:
"In former times, when a pardon was intended,
horses were first sent to patrol the markets and neighborhoods,
listening at street corners,
and all would say a pardon was coming.
Thus, knowing Heaven’s instruction,
the ruler would then bestow grace."
If such words were believed,
it would be a grave error.
Human nature
is inclined to speculate.
Seeing prolonged overcast weather, they predict floods;
seeing prolonged sunny weather, they predict drought;
seeing slight price increases, they speak of famine;
seeing slight price drops, they speak of abundance.
Yet sometimes they are right, sometimes wrong.
From this perspective,
what the people say
does not necessarily reflect the truth of the world.
In earlier times, pardons and commutations were rare,
and the people had no expectations of them.
In recent times,
pardons and commutations have become frequent,
so every spring and summer,
they hope for another pardon.
Families with guilty members,
hoping for lucky reprieves,
thus spread such words
to console themselves.
If a benevolent ruler hears this
and believes it to be Heaven’s instruction, following it hastily,
there is no greater mistake.
Many argue:
"If too long passes without a pardon, wickedness will flourish,
and officials will lose control,
so pardons and commutations are needed to resolve this."
This is the very root of chaos,
the words of those who do not understand the origins of fortune and misfortune.
The reason people lightly turn to banditry,
and officials easily engage in wickedness and concealment,
is because pardons and commutations are frequent, fostering hope for leniency.
If criminals faced lifelong consequences,
and were certain to be punished when caught,
then schemes for wickedness would be thwarted,
and thoughts of evil would cease.
Good commutations may be acceptable,
children can be taught to be gentle,
and average people
can be guided downward.
Thus, the proverb says:
"If pardons are issued yearly,
even slaves and children scoff."
This means that if the king’s punishments are not enforced,
even the most pained and aggrieved will lightly offend,
let alone the cunning?
If pardons are granted out of fear that there are too many bandits and wickedness cannot be overcome,
then this is to repay evildoers on behalf of the state.
Heaven’s way rewards good and punishes excess.
"Heaven’s work, man carries it out."
Thus, all who establish kingship
do so to punish wickedness and nurture upright goodness.
To instead indulge wickedness and rebellion
is the greatest folly.
Furthermore, a country does not have constant order,
nor does it have constant chaos.
If laws and decrees are enforced, the country is orderly;
if laws and decrees are lax, the country is chaotic.
There is no constant enforcement of laws,
nor is there constant laxity of laws.
If a ruler respects the law, the law is enforced;
if a ruler disdains the law, the law is lax.
In the past during the time of Emperor Xiàomíng,
talent was recommended,
and gratitude was expressed by passing the gates.
When the meal was finished,
the emperor asked about any unusual news.
The response was:
"There are nine notorious thieves in Wū,
who often steal from the province according to the governor,
but have never been caught."
The emperor said:
"Are you not the officer from the southern province?"
The reply was:
"Yes."
The emperor was then extremely angry,
and said:
"The thief arises within your jurisdiction and you cannot capture him,
then what talent do you have to be recommended?"
He was beaten several hundred times,
then dismissed from office,
and the state and district governors were severely reprimanded.
Within ten days,
the thieves were apprehended and executed.
From this, it can be seen that
capturing and eliminating bandits
relies on clarifying the law,
not on repeated pardons.
Nowadays, without clearly implementing rewards and punishments to distinguish good and evil,
or strictly supervising the officials to capture the crafty,
but instead repeatedly pardoning to encourage them,
an edict often says:
"Acts of treason and disobedience,
those not eligible for pardon, are all pardoned,
with the intention of making gentlemen reflect and start anew."
Year after year this is proclaimed,
yet never has a villainous person or useless official
been seen to change their mind, repent, and commend the edict.
When officials present matters,
they also consider past minor offenses when granting pardons,
hindering today’s clear actions.
Therefore, revising the past and working on the present,
such a renewing edict
is also not credible.
The Book of Songs criticizes:
"The gentleman often swears,
yet disorder thereby increases."
Therefore, it is better to make promises sparingly,
and surely keep them.
If there cannot be complete abolition of pardons,
then making them rare and only once in a generation,
would certainly reduce rogues by eighteen or nine parts.
In the past, when Dàsīmǎ Wú Hàn was old and ill and about to die,
Emperor Shìzǔ asked him for final advice.
He replied:
"I am foolish and lack wisdom,
sufficient only to know not to grant pardons."
"Things gather according to their kind,
and elements are grouped by category."
"A person's feelings are all revealed in their words,"
therefore those who argue against pardons
are either self-disciplined and cautious in conduct,
or surely concerned, sad, and cautious, detesting wickedness.
Those who favor frequent pardons
either do not understand pardon duties,
or surely harbor internal worries and wish to gain from it.
When a ruler issues decrees,
he must consult with his ministers.
The treacherous among the ministers
will certainly conceal their crimes.
Even upright officials
have public faults.
Unless they were like Yù Quán or Lǐ Lí,
who would sacrifice themselves to rectify the state?
Thus, they all involve private considerations in discussing public governance.
Consulting a fox about a fur coat,
when is that ever appropriate?
The old texts say:
"The people's luck is misfortune for the state."
For one who is guilty to suffer punishment,
for wrongs to be righted and truth to be upheld
is the celestial order
and the king’s law.
Therefore it is said:
"Do not allow cunning evasion
in order to discipline the unreliable."
If wronging the good to favor the wicked,
this is called "gathering resentment as virtue."
The late emperor established the law,
discussing stabbing with intent.
Why?
Because they harbored wicked intentions,
with intent to kill.
The wise ruler has affection for his subjects,
but if there is intent to kill,
therefore punishing it,
how much more for an actual crime?
In the Shàngshū, the Kanggào states:
"The king says:
'Alas!
Fēng,
be careful in meting out punishments.
If one has a small crime, do not save it;
they only aim to continue,
acting out of non-compliance;
caution you,
even for minor offenses,
cannot go unpunished.'"
It is said that even if a person's crime is small,
it is not due to minor mishaps,
but rather they intend to persist in wrongdoing,
thus even if small,
it must not go unpunished.
Why?
Because it is inherently stubborn and evil.
"For large crimes without intent to persist,
they should instead be pardoned as a mistake.
Simply do that,
having reached the limit of their crime,
then it should not be punished."
It means that although someone may commit a serious crime,
if they do not intend to persist in evil,
it is merely an error,
thus should not be punished.
In such cases,
even saying pardon is permissible.
Precious metals were used to redeem crimes,
pardon was used for clemency,
all intended for good and upright people,
who occasionally made mistakes,
and were unfortunately implicated.
The former kings reviewed and judged criminal cases,
considering intentions to
save good people,
not to allow undue leniency for evil and treacherous acts that harm people.
Thus, the Zhōu guān had eight classes of offenses,
this is how the former kings maintained order and led to peaceful times.
The Yì Jīng thus observed people to set teachings,
adapting to changing circumstances.
Today, saving the world,
cannot depart from this intention.
Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn,
made an agreement with his ministers,
saying unless they were from the Liú family, they would not be made kings,
and without martial achievements, no one would be made marquis.
Emperor Xiàowén first enfeoffed his maternal grandfather,
and established it as a rule,
implementing it until today.
Emperor Xiàowǔ ennobled the Chancellor,
to honor virtue,
later this was also continued.
Jiànwǔ eventually ended it.
Historical records indicate,
Jì, Xiè, Bóyí, Gāoyáo, and Bóyì,
were daily enfeoffed lands.
During the time of King Xuān of Zhōu,
the assisting great ministers,
aiding governance with virtue,
also were rewarded with lands.
Thus Yǐn Jífǔ composed two eulogistic poems,
in the Poem it says:
"Shēnbó rises to serve,
the king carries on his matters,
in the city of Shě,
the southern nation follows this model."
It also says:
"The four horses are grand and bold,
the eight bells clang and jingle.
The king orders Zhòngshānpǔ,
to fortify the east."
This describes how Shēnbó and Shānfǔ, through their civil virtues, achieved peace,
and the king awarded them with pleasant lands,
bestowing them with lavish garments.
The hexagram Shìkè (Biting Through),
with movement below and brightness above,
its "Xiàng" (Image) says:
"The ancient kings used it to clarify punishments and rectify laws."
Now, in a custom of accumulated negligence,
if rewards are not generous, goodness is not encouraged;
if punishments are not severe, evil is not deterred.
Therefore, all who wish to transform customs and change practices,
in their implementation of rewards and punishments,
must make them sufficiently startling and awe-inspiring,
so that the people will then change their views.
If a sage ruler truly examines his ministers with discernment,
those who exhaust their energy, fulfill their duties, and achieve merit,
he should not begrudge the expense of gold, silk, or noble titles;
for those who harbor treachery and conceal wickedness, showing no sign of reform,
he should plan for the decisive application of axes and executioners' blades.
Then, worthy ministers like Wáng Chéng, Huáng Bà, Gōng Suì, and Shào Xìnchén
could be obtained in every commandery;
divine auspicious responses
could be achieved within a single year.
The reason a state is a state
is because it has people;
the reason people are people
is because they have grain;
the reason grain flourishes and multiplies
is because there is human labor;
the reason labor can be accomplished
is because of daily effort.
In a well-governed state, the days are relaxed and long,
so its people have leisure and surplus strength;
in a disordered state, the days are hurried and short,
so its people are burdened with toil and lack strength.
When we say the days of a well-governed state are relaxed and long,
it is not because we petitioned Xī Hé to make the sun move slowly,
nor is it because we could increase the divisions of the clepsydra or add to its markings.
Rather, it is because the ruler is discerning and the officials are well-governed,
those below follow the right path and attain their proper places,
so the people are tranquil and have surplus strength,
and therefore perceive the days as long.
When we say the days of a disordered state are hurried and short,
it is not because we petitioned Xī Hé to make the sun gallop fast,
nor is it because we could decrease the divisions of the clepsydra or reduce its markings.
Rather, it is because the ruler is not discerning, so the officials are chaotic and villains arise,
laws and decrees are sold and corvée duties and taxes are numerous,
then the common people are distressed by oppressive governance,
officials are exhausted by regulations and rituals,
the wronged can only obtain justice by going to prison,
the steadfast can only gain protection by forming private connections,
treacherous ministers act recklessly above,
corrupt practices spread below,
gentlemen load their gifts and race in carriages,
commoners clutch their wealth and hurry about,
and therefore perceive the days as short.
The "Shī" (Book of Songs) says:
"The king's affairs are never done,
I have no leisure to care for my father."
This means that in ancient times, with leisure, one could practice filial piety,
but now, pressed and hurried, one cannot provide support.
Confucius said that when the population is numerous, enrich them;
once enriched, then educate them.
Thus, ritual and righteousness arise from sufficiency,
theft and robbery arise from poverty,
wealth and honor arise from ample leisure,
poverty and want arise from having no time.
The sages deeply understood that labor is the foundation of the people and the basis of the state,
therefore they strove to reduce corvée duties and cherish the people's time.
Thus, Yáo commanded Xī Hé,
"Reverently conform to the august heavens,
and respectfully instruct the people in the seasons";
Shào Bó, hearing lawsuits, could not bear to trouble the people,
so he adjudicated beneath the pear tree,
and was able to bring about harmonious times and render punishments unnecessary.
Now it is not so.
Myriad officials harass the people,
magistrates and chiefs show off their own importance,
the common people abandon farming and sericulture to rush to government offices,
yet unless it is morning or evening, they cannot gain access,
unless they have connections, they cannot get an audience,
whether a lawsuit proceeds or not, it drags on for months,
the whole household stops working,
to watch over the matter,
the family of the litigant
then requests neighbors to respond and deliver provisions,
by the time the matter is concluded,
they have ultimately lost a year's labor,
and thus in the world, there are certainly those who suffer hunger because of this;
yet the petty officials and vulgar clerks in charge of the statutes
are utterly unaware of it.
When commanderies and counties have already added injustice,
and the provincial authorities do not rectify it,
the people are forced to ruin their households to survive,
and travel afar to the central government offices.
If the central offices cannot clearly discern truth and falsehood,
they merely wish to dismiss the cases by using the excuse of the long hardship's cost,
so they arbitrarily set a rule,
ordering these cases to be noted for a hundred days,
and only then will they transfer documents;
if it is not a full hundred days,
they repeatedly create new numbers,
greatly violating the principle of Shào Bó adjudicating beneath the pear tree.
This is what is called reciting the three hundred poems,
but when entrusted with governance,
cannot apply them;
what is the use of having many, then?
Confucius said:
"In hearing lawsuits,
I am like anyone else."
From this perspective,
those of average talent and above,
can all deliberate on the distinction between right and wrong,
and understand the principles of punishments and laws;
local officials and village clerks
are sufficient to make judgments,
so that there are no complaints.
Yet the reason they do not
is because there is a cause.
The "Zhuàn" (Commentary) says:
"Those who hate the upright and detest the correct,
truly are many and have followers."
Now, the upright are steadfast and correct and do not bend their will,
they show no favor to clerks.
The opposing party strives to win over those in charge with goods and wealth,
so the local officials and village clerks join with them to oppose the upright family,
later, when the situation reverses, the clerks are implicated,
so together they wrong them in court.
For a weak commoner to litigate against a powerful clerk,
his position is inferior.
Therefore, the county sides with the local office,
later, when there is a reversal,
the senior officials are implicated,
so the whole county opposes him at the commandery.
For one person to litigate against a whole county,
his position is inferior.
Therefore, the commandery sides with the county,
later, when there is a reversal,
the Grand Administrator is implicated,
so the whole commandery opposes him at the province.
For one person to litigate against a whole commandery,
his position is inferior.
Therefore, the province sides with the commandery,
and is unwilling to adjudicate,
so finally he travels afar to the central government offices.
The central offices cannot investigate clearly,
but merely wish to impose monetary fines,
then the poor and weak, with little wealth, will never finish even after ten days or fulfill the required period.
The wealthy and rich, with ample money, can hire agents to go on their behalf,
filling up a thousand days,
not merely a hundred.
If lawsuits are handled like this,
it is effectively assisting the powerful and cunning while suppressing the poor and weak;
what injustice can be rectified?
It is not only local lawsuits.
Military officials adjudicating legal cases
also often begin by being wronged by petty clerks,
and end by being doubly wronged by high ministers.
Grievances thus remain unavenged,
then they encounter amnesty decrees,
and cannot be pursued further,
upright men harbor grievances and knots of injustice but cannot obtain trust,
cunning clerks promote villainy and treachery but are not severely punished.
This is why commanderies and counties easily oppress the common people,
and why there is so much hunger and poverty in the world.
Apart from Heaven being moved and stirred,
sending down disasters that damage the grain,
if we speak only from the perspective of human labor and observable affairs:
now, from the Three Excellencies down,
to the counties, districts, townships, and villages,
and the assistants and supervising couriers,
all the offices in charge,
the people abandon farming and sericulture to attend to them;
lawsuits and accusations,
and responding to clerks on official matters—
for each one person involved,
a hundred thousand people waste a day;
if we calculate further down,
for one person having a matter,
two people are needed to deliver provisions,
this means three hundred thousand people leave their work each day.
Taking the average farmer as standard,
then three million mouths suffer hunger each year.
Then, how can bandits and thieves be eliminated,
how can peace and prosperity be achieved?
Regarding the conduct of women,
it is valued that they remain pure and chaste.
Now, having been married off,
they feel ashamed to return to their natal family’s door.
If the local officials pardon them,
they are thus allowed to remain in the household they have already entered.
This surely fails to illuminate the root cause of disorder,
and does not consider the words born of chastity and purity.
A chaste woman does not change her heart repeatedly;
hence there is the poem “Not a Pebble.”
She does not act wrongly so as to leave behind sorrow;
thus her intention to return to her parents’ home is praised.
Once betrothed, she does not change,
for this is how to uphold chastity and bring peace to her father and brothers.
Those who do not follow this but are fickle in virtue—
these are originally families without shame,
places where chastity and devotion are absent.
For such people,
what shame or regret is there?
They disrespect their fathers and brothers,
and are licentious and depraved women.
They do not consider righteousness and principle;
carelessly neglecting a single virtue,
they borrow capital to make a living,
flee and take refuge elsewhere,
eventually bringing upon themselves the calamity of being disemboweled, beheaded, and having their lineage extinguished—
where does this not occur?
The former kings, based on human emotions of joy and anger that cannot be restrained,
established rituals and institutions to honor virtuous yielding;
for what people can restrain,
they set up laws and prohibitions to clarify rewards and punishments.
Now, in market transactions, do not deceive each other;
in marriages, do not practice fraud—
these are not impossible for human nature.
Therefore, it is better to establish righteousness and follow the law,
cutting off the source [of such evils].
Although initially it may cause shame and regret for one person,
in the end, however,
it brings long-term benefit for ten thousand generations.
“A small punishment serves as a great warning”—
this is how to preserve the small and aid the stubbornly wicked.
The essential principle of establishing laws
must be to encourage good people to cultivate their virtue and delight in governance,
and to make wicked people feel the pain of their calamities and repent of their actions.
For any woman betrothed to several families,
even if she bears ten sons,
and receives a hundred pardons,
do not allow her to return even once to her private household;
then such treachery will cease.
Otherwise, shave the heads of the husband and wife,
and exile them to a harsh county a thousand li away—
only then can their hearts be poisoned and their posterity cut off.
When treachery and disorder cease, then great peace will arise.
Moreover, chaste and pure widows,
some with both sons and daughters,
wealthy and abundant in goods,
wish to uphold the rites of a single marriage,
fulfill the duty of sharing the same grave,
maintain their chastity firmly,
resolutely determined to die,
with no thought of ever being betrothed again.
Yet they encounter unkind uncles,
or unrighteous brothers,
who either covet the betrothal gifts,
or desire their wealth and valuables,
or have private designs on their sons,
and thus forcibly deceive them into remarrying,
oppressing and coercing them to be sent away.
Some hang themselves in their rooms,
drink poison in the carriage,
lose their lives and perish,
leaving their young children orphaned.
This is akin to coercing someone to commit suicide.
Sometimes the later husband brings many retainers,
using force to threaten and carry her off,
guards seize and hold her,
and only after several days does she relent—
no different from forcibly abducting someone to be a wife.
Women are soft and weak,
easily overpowered and coerced by the crowd,
confined and distressed for days.
Afterward, even if they wish to restore their original resolve,
they may hang themselves or swallow poison.
Those who governed the world without strict regulations—
were the Three Sovereigns;
those who drew symbols and transformed the four regions—
were the Five Emperors;
those who clarified laws and prohibitions and harmonized the realm—
were the Three Kings.
Those who implemented rewards and punishments and unified the myriad people—
are well-governed states;
where the ruler establishes laws but they are not carried out below—
is a disordered state;
where ministers create policies and the ruler does not control them—
is a doomed state.
Therefore, the reason the people do not fall into disorder
is that there are officials above;
the reason officials are without treachery
is that there are laws in office;
the reason laws are followed smoothly
is that the state has a ruler;
the reason the ruler’s position is honored
is that he personally embodies righteousness.
Righteousness is the ruler’s governance;
laws are the ruler’s commands.
When the ruler thinks rightly to issue commands,
and none, whether noble or base, wise or foolish, can disobey,
then the ruler is positioned above,
and the common people are governed below.
If the ruler issues commands but the noble ministers and arrogant officials do not comply,
then the ruler is nearly assassinated,
and the people are nearly in revolt.
Now, laws and decrees
are what the ruler uses to govern his state.
If the ruler issues commands but they are not obeyed,
it is as if there were no ruler.
If the sovereign’s commands are not followed, then the ministers’ commands prevail—
the state is in danger.
Laws and decrees
are the reins, bridle, whip, and crop of the ruler;
and the people
are the carriage and horses of the ruler.
If ministers abolish the ruler’s laws and prohibitions and implement their own policies and commands,
then they are seizing the ruler’s reins and crop,
and driving alone themselves.
The foolish and benighted ruler sits idly on the left,
while treacherous ministers and rebellious men hold the reins on the right.
This is why Qí Zōu Mǎ Rú drowned Duke Hú in the Jù River,
and why Sòng Yáng Shū Zāng brought about Huà Yuán’s defeat at the hands of the Zhèng army—
and none could control it.
Thus, Chén Héng seized Duke Jiǎn in Xúzhōu,
and Lǐ Duì harmed Lord Fù in Shāqiū—
all because they used their venom to seize the ruler’s reins and crop.
The “Wén Yán” therefore says:
“When a minister assassinates his ruler,
or a son assassinates his father,
it is not a matter of a single morning or evening.
The causes have accumulated gradually,
due to failure to discern and change early.”
Therefore, officials who recklessly violate the law,
and ministers who recklessly create commands,
must be executed.
Critics will surely argue that punishments and executions should not be used,
and that moral transformation alone can be relied upon.
This is not the argument of those who understand adaptation,
nor the words of those who discuss declining ages.
Even the highest sages did not surpass Yáo and Shùn,
yet they exiled the four villains;
the greatest virtue did not surpass King Wén and King Wǔ,
yet they blazed with anger.
The Book of Songs says:
“If the gentleman is angry,
disorder may quickly cease;
if the gentleman is pleased,
disorder may quickly end.”
Therefore, the gentleman has joy and anger
to stop disorder.
Thus, there is using execution to stop killing,
and using punishment to guard against cruelty.
Moreover, governing the world is like climbing a hill:
one must first tread on the lower parts,
and only then can one step on the heights.
Therefore, first achieve a well-governed state,
and then the governance of the Three Kings can be implemented;
equal the Way of the Three Kings,
and then the transformation of the Five Emperors can be carried out;
equal the Way of the Five Emperors,
and then the Way of the Three Sovereigns can be followed.
Moreover, laws
are the governance of the former kings;
commands
are one’s own orders.
The governance of the former kings is shared with the multitude;
one’s own orders are to control people individually.
If the ruler can truly confer laws and occasionally be lenient,
issue commands and ensure they are carried out,
then none of the officials and clerks will dare not wholeheartedly follow his commands.
If his commands are not disobeyed,
then laws and prohibitions will surely be enforced.
Thus, if government orders are surely carried out,
and statutory prohibitions are surely followed,
then a state that is not well-governed
has never existed.
This is the principle of relaxation and tension,
using the present to practice the ancient,
the method of balancing severity and leniency, honor and humility.
The people of the most ancient times
were pure, sincere, and simple.
The highest sages governed them
with tranquility and non-action,
embodying the Way and practicing virtue,
simplifying punishments and minimizing authority.
Without killing or executing,
the people transformed themselves.
This is the highest form of virtue.
When virtue gradually declined and grew thin,
wicked thoughts began to sprout.
The next sages succeeded them,
observed the people and established teachings,
instituted punishments and rewards,
and used authority to encourage them.
They not only created the five weapons,
but also established laws
to correct and discipline them.
The Book of Songs says:
"Prepare your chariots and horses,
bows, arrows, spears, and weapons,
to guard against emergencies and set an example,
to drive away the barbarians from afar."
Therefore, it is said:
"The establishment of weapons has been long."
Passing through five dynasties
down to the present,
no state has ever flourished without virtue or become strong without weapons.
Now, ingenious weapons and equipment
fill the government arsenals,
and the words of Sūn Wǔ and Wú Qǐ
clamor in the ears of generals.
Yet when the generals employ them,
advancing to battle leads to defeat,
and retreating to defense results in the loss of cities.
Why is this?
It is said:
The situation between both sides
is not heard by the sovereign;
the factors determining victory or defeat
are not clear in the generals' minds.
When soldiers advance, they gain no benefit, and when they retreat, they have no fear.
This is the reason for it.
To bear a heavy load up a slope
and gallop a thousand miles
is a hardship for a horse.
Yet a well-trained horse delights in it
because Wáng Liáng is skilled enough to make it exert its strength.
To be the first to ascend and break through enemy formations,
to face death against formidable foes
is a hardship for the people.
Yet a man of principle delights in it
because an enlightened ruler is worthy of dying for.
The reason why people are willing to rush toward death without shirking
is not that they seek profit,
but because they thereby avoid harm.
This is true for all, whether worthy or base, foolish or wise;
only what they consider beneficial or harmful differs.
If they do not seek fame,
then they seek substantial rewards;
if they do not avoid disgrace,
then they avoid calamity and chaos.
Apart from these four things,
even a sage king cannot secure his ministers,
nor can a loving father be certain of his sons.
An enlightened ruler deeply understands this,
so he elevates benefits and makes harms evident to trade with his subordinates,
causing all—close or distant, noble or humble, worthy or base, foolish or wise—
to comply with his commands before attaining their desires.
Thus, when the army drums thunder
and banners are raised together,
all soldiers become fervent and excited,
competing to die fighting the enemy.
Is it really because they tire of long life
and delight in harmful death?
Rather, it is because the righteous seek to make a name for themselves,
and the greedy seek to obtain rewards.
Now, officials who follow the army and die in public service,
numbering in the hundreds of thousands,
receive no honor of condolences or sighs from above,
nor substantial salaries or rewards from below.
Men of principle have nothing to encourage or admire,
and ordinary men have nothing to covet for gain.
This is why people feel discouraged and slack,
unwilling to die again.
Since the army was raised,
it has been exposed in the field for five years.
Officers in charge of troops
number in the thousands,
and large and small battles
occur a hundred or more times a year,
yet achievements are rare.
Examining their defeats one by one,
there is no other reason
than that the generals do not understand changing circumstances,
and the soldiers are not encouraged to die fighting the enemy.
That the soldiers cannot die
is because the generals cannot set an example.
When rewards are promised, they are not given;
