when punishments are mentioned, they are not carried out.
Soldiers who advance face the calamity of dying alone,
while those who retreat enjoy the fortune of living among the many.
This is why they lose their will to fight in battle
and instead compete to flee northward.
Sūnzǐ said:
"A general must possess wisdom,
benevolence,
respect,
integrity,
courage,
and strictness."
Thus, wisdom is used to outwit the enemy,
benevolence to win over the masses,
respect to attract the worthy,
integrity to ensure rewards are given,
courage to boost morale,
and strictness to unify commands.
Therefore, outwitting the enemy enables adapting to changes;
when the masses are attached and loving, they think of fighting hard;
when the worthy and wise gather, stratagems succeed;
when rewards and punishments are certain, soldiers exert their strength;
when courage is boosted, the army's momentum doubles itself;
when authority and commands are unified, only the general's orders are followed.
Only with these six qualities
can one repel the enemy and capture foes,
assisting the ruler and pacifying the people.
When the Qiāng first rebelled,
the generals and commanders, with their established orders and groups,
relying on abundant reserves,
occupying strategic cities with advantageous positions,
commanding a force of a hundred thousand,
leading brave and outstanding officers,
to suppress a newly rebellious, scattered, and weak foe,
attacking small bandits who came on their own,
could not capture or destroy them
and were instead defeated by them.
Thus, the rebellion spread like rising clouds,
forming alliances horizontally and vertically,
sweeping through Bìngzhōu and Liángzhōu,
invading Sīlì internally,
plundering Zhào and Wèi in the east,
raiding Shǔ and Hàn in the west,
leaving five provinces devastated
and six commanderies erased.
This was not a disaster from Heaven,
but the fault of the senior officials.
Sūnzǐ said:
"The general
is the arbiter of the people's fate
and the master of the state's safety or peril."
Therefore, in all commanderies with bandits,
the grand administrators, magistrates, and chiefs must understand military affairs.
Now, observing the generals,
they lack both the ingenuity to decide and adapt to the enemy
and the integrity to clarify rewards and enforce punishments.
Moreover, their soldiers and people are very poor,
their weapons are not regularly practiced,
and the general's favor is not consistently cultivated.
Suddenly, when an emergency arises,
the officers violently oppress their soldiers,
and the soldiers, with their clumsiness, face the enemy's skill.
This is driving the grievances of officers and soldiers to resist foes
and binding their hands to await the bandits.
If a general cannot encourage his soldiers,
and soldiers cannot wield their weapons effectively,
these two are equivalent to having no army.
Without soldiers or an army,
yet wanting to engage in battle,
their defeat
is a matter of course.
Therefore, it is said:
Their defeat
is not a disaster from Heaven,
but the fault of the general.
Talented men in the world
only worry about lacking models.
Thus, if there is land,
the people can be enriched;
if there are marketplaces,
merchants can come;
if there are soldiers and people,
the state can be strengthened;
if there are laws and orders,
treachery and evil can be prohibited.
A state cannot be governed from the outside,
and an army cannot be commanded from within the court.
The senior officials of commanderies and counties,
fortunately possessing the authority to decide on these several matters,
yet fail to fulfill the enlightened decree and pacify the people—
this is also due to corruption, incompetence,
and having no substance.
For the world to have extraordinary men,
only then can extraordinary affairs be settled;
there must be extraordinary failures in governance,
only then do they become apparent.
Therefore, when selecting officials who command troops,
one should choose those of outstanding talent and substantial virtue,
who surpass others in profound and exceptional abilities,
possessing wisdom and adaptability,
and are fit to serve as generals and commanders.
One must not carelessly follow seniority,
nor favor relatives,
entrusting them with military authority.
This is what is called handing one's own state over to the enemy.
The governance of a sage king
extends universally and embraces all with love,
showing no partiality to those close and intimate,
and no neglect of those distant and remote.
Fortune and misfortune,
he shares with the people;
feelings of sorrow and joy,
he extends to others with empathy.
He regards the people as his own children,
and rescues them from disaster as if pulling a hand from a fire.
Thus, all within the four seas rejoice,
and all are harmoniously employed.
In the past, the Qiāng rebels turned traitor,
starting from Liángzhōu and Bìngzhōu,
extending to Sīlì,
bringing calamity east to Zhào and Wèi,
and plundering west to Shǔ and Hàn.
Five provinces were devastated,
six commanderies obliterated,
across a thousand lǐ in circumference,
the countryside left without a single survivor,
with banditry and calamity
ceasing neither day nor night.
The common people were annihilated,
as if scorched away by the sun and moon.
Yet scholars from the inner commanderies who were not afflicted by the disaster
all claimed that they should be indulged for now,
awaiting the opportune moment from Heaven.
With intentions like these,
how can this be the heart of humanity!
When the Qiāng first rebelled,
the high ministers and senior officials all wished to abandon Liángzhōu,
retreating to safeguard the Three Adjuncts,
but the court would not heed them.
Later, the Qiāng invaded,
and many critics regretted not following that misguided proposal.
I secretly laugh at them;
this is what is called regretting whether you make peace or not,
yet failing to understand the principle of change.
A land has no border?
Without borders, the state perishes.
Therefore, if Liángzhōu is lost,
then the Three Adjuncts become the border;
if the Three Adjuncts are penetrated inward,
then Hóngnóng becomes the border;
if Hóngnóng is penetrated inward,
then Luòyáng becomes the border.
Extending this analogy,
even if you go all the way to the Eastern Sea, there will still be a border.
Now, instead of strengthening the military to exterminate the enemy,
and selecting talent to secure the entire territory,
they say the borders cannot be defended,
wishing to cut off territory themselves first,
showing weakness to the enemy—
is this not deluded!
In the past, Yuè Yì, with the tiny state of Yān,
shattered the powerful Qí,
his might shaking the world—
truly he could be called an excellent general.
Yet the magistrate of Jímò defended a solitary city alone,
holding out for six years without falling,
ultimately preserving his people.
Tián Dān, with his forces exhausted,
led five thousand cavalry,
attacked and drove back the enemy,
recovering over seventy cities of Qí—
he could be called skilled in the use of troops.
Yet he besieged Liáo and Jǔ for years,
and in the end could not capture them.
These were cases of the strongest attacking the weakest,
the wisest scheming against the most foolish,
yet still they could not prevail—why?
The answer is:
in attack, one is often insufficient,
while in defense, one often has surplus.
Previously, the various commanderies
all occupied walled cities and commanded large forces.
The wisdom of the Qiāng rebels
is not equal to that of Yuè Yì or Tián Dān;
the strategic positions of the commanderies and counties
are not as difficult as Liáo, Jǔ, or Jímò.
Yet none were willing to concentrate on steadfast defense;
instead, they forcibly drove and coerced their people,
abandoned granaries and storehouses,
and fled, turning their backs on their cities.
From this, it is evident
that the hardship was not due to lack of provisions in the cities,
but only due to the generals' incompetence.
To repel the enemy and bring peace to the people,
the key lies in appointing the worthy,
not in reducing territory.
When Qí and Wèi retreated and defended,
their states did not thereby gain security.
When Zǐyīng cut territory himself,
Qín did not thereby survive.
Emperor Wǔ repelled the barbarians and expanded the borders,
extending them for several thousand lǐ:
opening Lèlàng in the east,
establishing Dūnhuáng in the west,
crossing Jiāozhǐ in the south,
and building Shuòfāng in the north.
He finally pacified Nányuè,
executed and beheaded the king of Dàyuān.
Wherever the imperial armies marched,
none were not vanquished and destroyed.
Now the enemy arises near the capital region itself,
yet we cannot capture them—
this is our own failure,
not the fault of having borders.
When the lips are gone, the teeth feel cold;
when the body is injured, the heart aches—
these are inevitable matters.
Why still doubt them?
A noble person perceives the signs,
especially when they are already evident.
Recently,
the border calamity shook like thunder,
blazed like the sun and moon,
yet those who discuss it all avoid the subject,
calling it mere banditry and theft.
With shallow, placating words,
they lull the noble-minded into complacency,
wanting the court to regard the enemy as insignificant
and not worry early.
Thus the harm has reached this extent,
and still they do not wish to rescue.
A proverb says:
"When the pain is not on your own body, you speak of enduring it;
when the money does not come from your own household, you speak of giving it."
If the sons and brothers of the high ministers suffered from the Qiāng calamity,
with urgency pressing day and night like the border people,
then they would compete in saying the Qiāng must be exterminated.
Now, simply because they themselves feel no grief or anguish,
they sit upright and follow one another,
and furthermore do not clearly prepare defenses,
but contentedly idle in leisure,
lying back and leaving it to Heaven's will.
The Qiāng come and go freely,
penetrating deep and killing many;
only then do they, in disarray,
go together to the court,
speak polite words and apologize,
then withdraw and talk of the situation.
When they gather sitting in the court hall,
they lack the sincere earnestness of grieving for the state and pitying the people,
but merely look at each other,
none willing to oppose and stop it.
As the day grows late and time passes,
deliberations reach no conclusion,
and they themselves say they must wait for later.
Later, when they obtain a little peace,
they serenely forget and abandon it.
Within ten days or so,
the enemy again causes harm;
military dispatches fly back and forth,
urgent alerts arrive in rapid succession,
and then again they are alarmed and panicked as before.
Proceeding in this manner
for nine years now,
hoping they might reform and do good,
they instead emerge again to do evil.
Wandering and crumbling,
what end will there be!
The Spring and Autumn Annals censured "Zhèng abandoning its army";
how much more abandoning the people!
If one person sighs in sorrow,
the Kingly Way is impaired;
how much more when a million masses
shout, wail, and weep, moving the heart of Heaven!
Moreover, the state is founded upon the people,
and the noble are rooted in the lowly.
Therefore, the sage kings nurtured the people,
loving them as their own children,
worrying for them as for their own families,
bringing security to those in danger,
preserving those facing destruction,
saving them from calamities and hardships,
and eliminating disasters and chaos.
Thus, the expedition against the Guǐfāng [a northern tribe]
was not due to a fondness for warfare,
nor was the repulsion of the Xiǎnyǔn [another northern tribe]
driven by greed for territory.
It was "to invigorate the people and cultivate virtue,"
and to secure the borders and realm.
"In ancient times,
the Son of Heaven guarded [the realm] through the Four Barbarians,"
"and from those Dī and Qiāng tribes,
none failed to come with tribute."
All under Heaven submitted in gratitude,
and even the spreading reeds relied on his virtue.
How much more so when our own people nearby suffer such calamities—
can we not rescue them?
The reason why the people serve their superiors
is because they cherish righteousness and gratitude.
When in pain, they become shameless;
when afflicted by disaster, they become unkind.
Resentment, hostility, and grievance
arise from shamelessness.
Now, the Qiāng rebellion has lasted long!
The harm inflicted is great!
The common people are in dire straits!
Anxieties and disasters run deep!
Superiors and subordinates follow one another
without seeing an end to it.
Not appointing a great general to sweep away the vile foe,
while the provinces gradually initiate corvée labor,
continuously without cease,
is like using a bamboo screen to block the wind
or scooping sand to dam a river—
incapable of providing any defense,
it merely exhausts oneself.
Now, several provinces station over a hundred thousand troops,
all fed from the government granaries,
costing several million hú of grain annually,
plus monthly wages.
Yet this consumption by these men
is impossible to fully supply,
and yet they fear the temporary expense of sending them out—
this is truly poor planning.
Moreover, what is precarious is easily toppled,
and what is doubtful is easily transformed.
Now the foe has newly seized border lands;
they dare not yet feel secure,
and are easily shaken.
The people have newly lost their old attachments;
their longing has not yet faded,
and they can easily be rallied.
It is truly appropriate to take this opportunity to dispatch a great general to punish and subdue them,
to pressure, coerce, disperse, and destroy them.
If we allow them time and leisure,
allowing them to accumulate wealth and status,
and each becomes settled and secure,
then they will be difficult to move.
The *Zhōu Shū* says:
"All those sages must seize the moment."
Therefore, strategies for offense and defense
must be decided early.
Those who understand the reality of fortune and misfortune
cannot be deluded by empty arguments;
those who examine the circumstances of order and chaos
cannot be swayed by ornate rhetoric.
Thus, for matters that are not in doubt,
the sage does not deliberate;
for floating, baseless theories,
the sage does not listen.
Why?
Because plans should not contradict visible reality and then provoke further debate.
Therefore, an enlightened ruler first fully understands human sentiments;
he does not solely rely on excellent generals.
He cultivates his own preparations,
not depending on others,
thus he can attack and surely defeat the enemy,
and in defense, surely preserve himself.
When the Qiāng first rebelled,
their plans were not yet sound,
their factions not yet formed,
their masses not yet united,
their weapons not yet prepared.
Some held bamboo or wooden sticks,
others joined empty-handed,
scattered and foraging for food,
without any commander—
they were very easy to crush.
Yet the commandery governors and county magistrates
were all cowardly, timid, and weak, not daring to attack.
Thus, they allowed the foe to ride their victory and grow stronger,
destroying provinces and commanderies,
their flames growing daily,
devastating the Sānfǔ region,
"even extending to the Guǐfāng."
This has now accumulated for ten years.
The people suffer harm,
and it has not ceased to this day.
Yet foolish and ignorant individuals
still say we should not provide aid,
but wait for Heaven's timing.
With intentions like this,
are they even human?
The benevolent extend from themselves to others;
the wise assess achievements and handle affairs.
Now, the high ministers and nobles internally do not grieve the pain of the soldiers and people being destroyed,
externally do not consider the disaster of prolonged warfare.
Each harbors their own narrow concerns,
seeking only to evade immediate responsibility,
merely saying we should not mobilize troops,
and no longer understand how to apply the guiding principles of emperors and kings,
or trace the ultimate outcome of calamitous changes.
The *Yì* [*Classic of Changes*] discusses controlling invaders,
the *Shī* [*Classic of Poetry*] praises vigorous campaigns;
since ancient times there has been warfare—
it is not only today.
The *Zhuàn* says:
"Heaven produced the Five Materials,
and the people use them all;
to abandon one is impossible—
who can eliminate arms?
Arms are used to awe the unruly and display civil virtue.
They are why the sage rises,
and why the disorderly are cast down."
Duke Huán of Qí, Duke Wén of Jìn, and Duke Xiāng of Sòng—
feudal lords of a declining age—
still felt ashamed that under Heaven there was mutual destruction they could not save,
how much more so the Lord of the Four Seas, mandated by August Heaven?
The great officers of Jìn and Chǔ,
ministers of small states,
still felt ashamed if their own persons were invaded,
how much more so the Son of Heaven's Three Dukes, who bear responsibility for the world?
Gōngliú's benevolent virtue
extended widely to the spreading reeds;
how much more so to blood-endowed humans,
his own kind?
If one person sighs in distress,
the Kingly Way is impaired;
how much more so when a million people are being destroyed?
The *Shū* [*Classic of Documents*] says:
"The Son of Heaven acts as father and mother to the people."
As parents to their children,
how can they sit and watch them being slaughtered and flayed by bandits and rebels,
or stand by and see them being devoured like dogs and pigs?
Setting aside benevolence and kindness,
let us speak in terms of calculated benefit.
The state is founded upon the people,
and the noble are rooted in the lowly.
I wish you to consider: since the beginning of creation,
who has seen the people in danger while the state was secure?
Who has seen those below poor while those above were rich?
Therefore it is said:
"He who rules a state
treats the people as his basis.
If the people are truly emaciated,
how can the ruler become fat?"
That the small people receive Heaven's enduring mandate—
I secretly hope the sage ruler deeply considers the wounds and illnesses of the state's foundation,
and foresightedly ponders whence fortune and misfortune arise.
Moreover, things have their flourishing and decline,
times have their shifts and changes,
affairs have their triggers and convergences,
and people undergo transformations.
For the wise to measure the signs—
is this not appropriate!
Míngmíng made up for deficiencies west of the river;
Fànlǐ collected debts at Gūxū;
thus they established great merit in their own time,
and their fine names have been passed down endlessly.
Now the border regions are in turmoil,
daily unleashing clan disasters;
the people day and night hope the court will save them,
yet the high ministers and nobles consider the expense troublesome and unacceptable.
I can only secretly laugh at them.
How is this different from Yànzǐ who lightly regarded the stores in granaries but regretted a single cup of dregs?
Now they only know to cherish the visible, meager coins and grain,
but do not know that the yet-unseen [danger] awaits the people first;
they know corvée labor is difficult to mobilize,
but do not know that the Central States await border peace.
The Book of Songs laments: "Some know not the cries of distress,
Some toil in misery and hardship."
Now, the high officials and nobles, simply because they themselves are unharmed,
thus compete in ceding the nation's territory to the enemy,
and slaughtering the sovereign's people to feed the Qiāng.
To devise strategies like this
cannot be called wise;
to serve as ministers like this
cannot be called loyal;
their wisdom and talent are insufficient to allow them to deliberate.
Moreover, all within the Four Seas
is what the sage bequeaths to his descendants;
official positions and duties
are what the multitude of ministers rely upon for their livelihood.
What is passed down to descendants
is intended to bring peace for ten thousand generations;
what one relies upon for livelihood
is each to fulfill their own part.
Therefore, if their words are not long-lasting in practice,
their tasks cannot be long endured.
This indeed is what an enlightened ruler must scrutinize carefully,
and what a sage sovereign must decide independently.
Now, to say one does not wish to mobilize the people or cause them trouble is acceptable.
If so,
then one should prepare defenses and fortifications.
According to the necessary plan of today,
make the enemy dare not come,
gaining nothing;
make the people not fear the bandits,
and thus suffer no losses.
But now it is not so;
they merely fear the toil and hardship of the people's labor,
yet lightly allow them to suffer the great calamity of destruction and death.
Such men are not the people's ruler,
not the people's generals,
not the sovereign's assistants,
not masters of victory.
Furthermore, deliberation
is the manifestation of clarity;
speech
is the expression of the heart.
"Because they possess it,
therefore they resemble it."
A proverb says:
"How to subdue stubbornness?
Nothing is better than listening to it."
Now, all those who say the border can be left unguarded and yet remain peaceful
ought indeed to send themselves or their sons and younger brothers to serve as Commandery Governors, County Magistrates, Assistants, or Captains on the border;
only then will the truth of right and wrong be settled,
and saving the border will be without trouble.
If the border is without trouble,
the Central Kingdom can then attain peace and stability.
Those who govern a state
must illuminate and examine the true and false of distant and near affairs,
foresee the origins of fortune and disaster,
then they can fully utilize the strength of their ministers,
and preserve and prosper their state and families.
When the Qiāng first rebelled,
it was newly arisen,
their weapons and equipment were not yet prepared;
some enemies held bronze mirrors to resemble weapons,
some carried wooden boards and tables to resemble shields,
in fearful confusion and disorder,
they could not yet hold their ground.
A single city could easily control them,
yet the commanderies and counties were all in great turmoil.
When the common people suddenly suffered calamity and disaster,
losing their wealth and goods,
people grieved and were stirred to anger,
each wishing to take revenge;
but the generals and commanders were all cowardly, inferior, weak, and soft,
not daring to attack and strike,
merely sitting and drafting documents,
to deceive the imperial court.
In reality, killing a hundred commoners, they reported one;
killing one enemy, they reported a hundred;
sometimes the enemies were many but they called them few,
sometimes they were few but they called them many.
They twisted and turned with clever writings,
seeking convenience and profit for themselves,
and not solely concerned with the great strategy of worrying for the state,
or grieving for the people's deaths.
Moreover, they squandered and dispersed money and grain,
exhausting the government storehouses,
then again borrowed from the people,
forcibly seizing wealth and goods.
Families of thousands and tens of thousands
were stripped bare, left with nothing;
the myriad people were left depleted,
and those who consequently followed with death,
were all starved to death by the officials.
The cruelty and pain they caused
was worse than encountering the enemy.
Bandits and enemy robbers
pass by suddenly,
not necessarily causing death or injury.
But when officials search, plunder, and seize,
trampling people into the mud,
some families and clans are overturned and exterminated,
with no survivors;
some orphaned women,
become slaves and maidservants,
are seen sold far away,
to the point they cannot sustain themselves,
too many to count.
This moves Heaven and brings disasters,
especially violating the principles of Yīn and Yáng.
Moreover, scholars value stability and dislike moving,
cherishing and longing for their ancestral graves,
which is the same for the worthy and unworthy alike.
For the common people, moving
is worse than being executed.
Execution by law only means one person in the family dies.
But losing all wealth and goods,
being driven from their land and moved far away,
unaccustomed to local customs,
不适应水土,
mostly whole families perish,
few are able to return.
The Dài horse gazes north,
the fox dies with its head toward its mound;
border people are simple and honest,
especially disliking being kept inland.
Though they know the disaster is great,
they still wish to guard their inherited livelihoods,
die in their native place,
truly they do not wish to leave it at all.
Commandery Governors and County Magistrates,
fearing and disliking military affairs,
all because they were originally not people of this land,
the pain does not touch their bodies,
disaster does not reach their families,
thus they compete to move the commanderies and counties inward.
They even dispatch officials and soldiers,
to harvest the people's crops,
tear down their houses,
level their walls and fortifications,
destroy their livelihoods,
forcibly seize and drive them,
moving them inward,
abandoning the weak and frail,
leaving them to die there.
At this time,
the myriad people resent and suffer,
weeping blood and crying out,
truly distressing the spirits and moving Heaven's heart.
But the common people are simple and lowly,
unable to reach the imperial court themselves,
dependent on the officials' households,
pressured by their authority and severity,
not daring to have any attachment.
The people, already deprived of land and livelihood,
also suffer from locusts, drought, and famine,
flee eastward along the roads,
scattered and displaced,
in Yōu, Jì, Yǎn, and Yù,
Jīng, Yáng, Shǔ, and Hàn,
starving and dying,
again losing more than half.
The borderlands thus became desolate and barren,
to this day uninhabited.
Tracing the origin of the disaster,
it is all due to the faults of officials.
Now, land
is the foundation of the people,
truly it cannot be left long barren and uncultivated.
Moreover, when Biǎn Què treated illness,
he examined blockages and opened stagnations,
supplementing the deficient,
draining the excess,
thus illnesses were cured and his name became renowned.
When Yī Yǐn assisted Tāng,
he established light and heavy measures to facilitate exchange,
reducing surpluses to supplement deficiencies,
thus the Yīn was well-governed and the ruler respected.
Jiǎ Yì grieved over the illness of hemiplegia and paralysis.
Now the border commanderies span a thousand lǐ,
each district originally had two counties,
households numbered only a few hundred,
yet the Commandery Governor's jurisdiction stretches ten thousand lǐ around,
empty without people,
fine fields abandoned and not opened for cultivation;
the central provinces and inner commanderies,
though they plan land and expand territories,
cannot produce a border,
yet their populations are a million households,
with a complete set of fields,
people are numerous, land is barren,
with nowhere to set foot,
this is also a case of hemiplegia and paralysis.
The Book of Zhou states:
"When the land is vast but the people are few,
its resources cannot be fully utilized;
this is called empty land,
which can be invaded and conquered.
When the land is small but the population is large,
the people do not truly belong to the ruler,
and can be exhausted and lost."
Therefore, land and population must be proportionate.
Now, the border commanderies suffer many hardships and heavy corvée duties,
often leading them into calamity.
If we do not work to promote benefits and eliminate harms,
and provide incentives for them,
then they will never be restored,
and they will harbor thoughts of rebellion.
The Western Qiāng and northern tribes
will inevitably develop covetous desires,
which is truly a great concern.
All artisans produce tools,
and all are used to fortify the borders,
distributed in double quantities—
is this due to private favor?
It is precisely to secure the interior.
The former sages established laws,
also striving to strengthen the borders,
in order to stabilize the Central Kingdom.
It is like a household encountering bandits:
the elderly, young, weak, and frail must be placed in the center,
while the strong, brave, and martial guard the outside.
Those inside provide for their needs,
those outside defend against dangers;
like the qióngqióng and jùxū creatures,
they rely on and support each other,
and thus all survive in safety.
According to imperial edicts and laws:
for a population of two hundred thousand,
or a border commandery of one hundred thousand,
one Filial and Incorrupt candidate is recommended annually;
officials are appointed, and each generation recommends one incorrupt official.
Since the Qiāng rebellion,
the registered population has decreased,
and the commandery governors have changed frequently,
so that for ten years no recommendations have been made.
Officials work diligently but receive no recognition,
the virtuous and talented accumulate but are not fully utilized,
the gentry have no expectations,
the farmers have no profit to seek;
thus, they flee from disasters in farming,
and none are willing to go to the borders.
In ancient times, to benefit the people,
they were enticed with benefits,
not coerced with punishments.
The Book of Changes says:
"The ancient kings inspected the regions, observed the people, and established teachings."
Therefore, in the early years of the Jiànwǔ era,
when border commanderies were obtained,
even if they had only a few hundred households,
they were ordered to recommend Filial and Incorrupt candidates annually,
to attract people to come.
Now it is truly appropriate to temporarily order border commanderies to recommend one Filial candidate,
and each generation to recommend one incorrupt official,
adding one Míngjīng official with a salary of one hundred shí,
so that people from interior commanderies who bring their wives and children to settle,
after five years or more,
are treated equally with the local residents,
and all become eligible for recommendation.
Furthermore, recruit people to transport grain to cultivate the border lands:
from distant commanderies, one thousand hú;
from nearby commanderies, two thousand hú;
and confer the rank of Wǔ Dàfū.
For those who do not desire rank,
allow them to receive double the price for grain compared to interior commanderies.
In this way,
both gentlemen and commoners will each gain benefits,
and even if we wish to stop them from going,
we will be unable to do so.
This is the essential method to equalize hardship and joy, balance corvée duties, populate the border regions, and stabilize the Central Kingdom.
When heaven and earth were separated, there were spirits and people;
people and spirits have different duties, but their vital essence communicates.
Actions have summons,
fate has encounters and followings;
the timing of good and bad fortune,
heaven makes it difficult to trust.
Even sages and worthies, though perceptive, do not act solely on their own authority,
so they established divination to consult the spirits.
Confucius said, "The virtue of the yarrow stalks is round and spiritual,
the virtue of the hexagrams is square and wise."
He also said:
"When a gentleman is about to act,
he asks, and then it speaks;
it receives the command and responds."
Thus, when Yǔ obtained Gāo Yáo,
and King Wén selected Lǚ Shàng,
both were foretold by omens,
divination confirmed their thoughts,
and thus their good fortune was achieved.
When a gentleman hears of good, he is encouraged and advances joyfully;
when he hears of evil, he reflects and corrects his faults,
thus he remains tranquil and receives much fortune.
When a petty person hears of good,
or hears of evil, he becomes fearful and acts recklessly,
thus he is frantic and agitated and meets with much misfortune.
Therefore, all divination
is about inquiring into the circumstances of good and bad fortune,
speaking of the timing of rise and decline,
urging people to cultivate themselves, act cautiously, and welcome good fortune.
Moreover, when sage kings established divination,
they did not consider it auspicious to oppose the people,
nor did they rely solely on it to decide matters.
Thus, in the divination of the "Hóng Fàn,"
great harmony is esteemed.
The Book of Documents also says:
"We consult your great turtle,
but dare not claim to know good fortune."
The Book of Songs says:
"My turtle is already weary,
it no longer tells me the plan."
From this perspective,
the nature of yarrow stalks and turtle shells,
perhaps they change with the times, becoming frugal or easy—
is it not due to sincerity or lack thereof?
Or is it that the world lacks talents like Shǐ Sū,
and few understand the spirits?
As for the divination by the Zhou historian for Jìng Zhòng,
and Zhuāng Shū's divination for Mùzǐ,
they can be said to be capable of "exploring the profound and seeking the hidden,
probing the depths and reaching far."
If Duke Xiàn had heeded Shǐ Sū's words earlier,
and Mùzǐ had long prepared according to Zhuāng Shū's warning,
then the slanders of Lí Jī and Shù Niú
would have had no way to enter,
and there would have been no disaster of kingdom destruction and personal danger.
Sages greatly valued divination,
yet for matters that were not doubtful,
they did not inquire.
They greatly revered sacrifices,
but prayers that were not according to ritual,
they did not perform.
Therefore, it is said:
"Sages do not trouble divination,"
"Respect ghosts and spirits but keep them at a distance."
Ghosts and spirits have different energy and concerns from humans;
unless there is a specific reason,
what have they to do with us?
Thus, Confucius praised King Zhāo of Chǔ for not sacrificing to the River,
and criticized the Jì clan for offering sacrifices to Mount Tài.
Now, common people are misled by divination
and sacrifice to ghosts that are not theirs;
is this not deluded?
There are also those who falsely assign surnames to the five notes,
establishing talismanic ranks for the five dwellings—
this is extremely deceitful!
In ancient times, there were yīn and yáng,
and then the five phases.
The Five Emperors relied on the movement of energy,
to generate the people;
as generations passed,
surnames and given names emerged to distinguish the people.
Names
are meant to distinguish the masses and highlight the individual,
not to record the five notes or determine hardness and softness.
Now, common people cannot trace their ancestral origins,
but instead wish to determine the five phases based on sounds and speech—
nothing could be more erroneous.
Fish live in water to survive,
birds rely on nests to lay eggs.
If one does not trace their origins,
and merely harmonizes sounds,
then calling a bird a fish—
can it be placed in water?
Calling a fish a bird—
can it perch on a tree?
These are impossible things.
Naming a foal a calf,
it will still become a horse.
Thus, the sound of a surname
must follow the progenitor who ruled.
Tàihào, essence of wood,
ruled by succeeding the Year Star;
his descendants should all correspond to the note Jué.
Shénnóng, essence of fire,
ruled by succeeding Mars;
his descendants should all correspond to the note Zhǐ.
Huángdì, essence of earth,
ruled by succeeding Saturn;
his descendants should all correspond to the note Gōng.
Shàohào, essence of metal,
ruled by succeeding Venus;
his descendants should all correspond to the note Shāng.
Zhuānxū, essence of water,
ruled by succeeding Mercury;
his descendants should all correspond to the note Yǔ.
Even if names change a hundred times,
the sound and nature remain unchanged.
Common craftsmen also say:
"For a house of the Shāng note,
it is suitable to have the gate facing west."
This is again false.
The Five Phases should go out riding their conqueror,
and enter dwelling in their sheltered place to be peaceful and auspicious.
For the Shāng note to face east upon entering—
entering east is instead considered metal attacking wood,
then the vital spirits within the household will battle daily.
The same applies to all Five Phases.
They also say:
"Houses have distinctions of Gōng and Shāng notes,
and years of direct correspondence."
If so,
by increasing or decreasing the number of gates on the house,
can one then change its note and bypass its correspondence?
Now, for one house,
people of the same surname conflict,
some auspicious, some inauspicious;
for one palace,
people of the same surname conflict,
some promoted, some dismissed;
for one palace,
when Chéng and Kāng resided there, it flourished,
when Yōu and Lì resided there, it declined.
From this perspective,
it is clear that auspiciousness, inauspiciousness, prosperity, and decline do not lie in the house.
As for various deities like Tàisuì, Fēnglóng, Gōuchén, Tàiyīn, Jiāngjūn, and others,
these are celestial officials,
not to be served by common people.
Heaven has these spirits
to assist in completing yin and yang and benefiting things,
just as human governance has prefects, governors, magistrates, and chiefs.
Why be angry when facing them?
Why resent when turning away?
The way of ruler and people is close,
yet it is not fitting to blame each other;
how much more so for spirits, who are extremely noble,
and whose rituals differ from humans—
how can they be expected?
Moreover, wanting to make people avoid ghosts
is like saying roads cannot be traveled
and houses cannot be lived in.
This refers to worthy gentlemen and noble persons who uphold an upright heart
and possess firm spirits.
As for worldly petty people,
ugly concubines and servant women,
shallow, ignorant, and foolish,
habits already formed,
and repeatedly stirring their spirits to break their courage—
now, not following where their sincere spirits incline,
but forcing them with what they fear
will only increase their ailments.
How to clarify this?
The reason humans are human
is not because of this eight-foot body,
but because they have spirit and vitality.
People who die from terror
are not afflicted by illness,
nor by human wrongdoing.
Yet they end up with irreparable damage
because their sincere spirit has left them.
Mèng Bēn toyed with fierce tigers without fear,
while infants fear ants and insects and cry out.
Now, some learned men wish to force weak and sickly fools
to do what they cannot,
and I fear this is not entirely good.
The foundation of transforming customs
lies in opening their minds and rectifying their spirits.
Now, people live without seeing the correct path,
growing up amid depravity and deception;
their belief in it
is difficult to quickly dispel.
Only a king can change it.
For all humans, auspiciousness and inauspiciousness
depend mainly on conduct,
and are determined by fate.
Conduct is one's own substance;
fate is Heaven's decree.
What lies within oneself
can certainly be done;
what lies with Heaven
cannot be known.
Shamans and diviners offering prayers
can also assist,
but without virtue, it will not work.
Shamans and scribes praying and invoking
are means to commune with spirits and remedy minor issues,
but for great fate,
they can do nothing.
It is like people petitioning officials:
they can resolve minor faults,
but cannot escape serious crimes.
Suppose there is a person here
who day and night disdains and insults the teachings of ruler and father,
violates the prohibitions of ancient kings,
does not restrain his own heart,
nor thinks to reform and do good,
but hastily sends petitions seeking exemption—
he will certainly not succeed.
It is better to cultivate oneself,
be careful, fearful, and cautious,
not violating the necessary commands of superiors.
Thus, Confucius did not heed Zǐlù,
saying, "I have been praying for a long time."
The Classic of Filial Piety says:
"Thus,
in life, parents are at peace with them,
in sacrifice, ghosts enjoy their offerings."
From this perspective,
if virtue and righteousness are not violated,
then ghosts and spirits will enjoy;
ghosts and spirits receiving enjoyment,
then blessings and prosperity will flourish.
Thus, the Book of Songs says:
"Abundant blessings descend,
simple blessings descend,
dignified and solemn in demeanor.
Already drunk, already full,
fortune and prosperity come in return."
This says that when human virtue and righteousness are lush and beautiful,
spirits enjoy offerings to drunkenness and fullness,
and in return repay with blessings.
The Duke of Guó invited spirits and quickly perished,
Zhào Yīng sacrificed to Heaven and swiftly was destroyed;
this is what is called spirits not enjoying their sacrifices,
and people not attending to their affairs.
Thus, the historian of Lǔ wrote:
"When a state is about to flourish,
it listens to the people;
when about to perish,
it listens to spirits."
King Zhāo of Chǔ did not pray away the clouds,
King Jǐng of Sòng did not shift the blame,
Zǐchǎn rejected Pízào,
Duke Wén of Zhū defied the diviner and scribe;
these all examined themselves and understood the Way,
awaiting fate with their own persons.
Yàn Píngzhòng said:
"Prayers can be beneficial,
curses can also be harmful."
Jì Liáng's remonstrance to the Marquis of Suí,
Gōng Zhīqí's persuasion of the Duke of Yú—
they can be said to understand the way of Heaven and humans,
and comprehend the distinction between spirits and people.
Evil cannot overcome virtue,
wickedness cannot vanquish righteousness;
this is the constant principle of Heaven.
Though there may be occasional deviations,
the wise hold fast to the correct path
and do not approach licentious spirits.
What are called licentious spirits
are idle, malevolent essences and beings,
not true deities with official duties.
That ghosts have such beings
is like humans having those who use deceitful words and false flattery to seek gain.
If one lures them,
they will come from afar without cease,
and in the end there will surely be misfortune.
It is the same with ghosts and spirits.
Therefore, Shēn Xū said:
"What people dread,
their own vital energy attracts.
If people create no opening,
evil will not arise of itself."
This means that people should not have excessive fears;
excessive fears and groundless dread
actually bring about omens and portents.
Moreover, just as humans have ranks and positions,
ghosts and spirits have nobility and baseness.
Heaven and Earth, mountains and rivers, the altars of soil and grain, the five sacrifices, and all the lords and ministers who have meritorious service to the people—
these are what the Son of Heaven and the feudal lords command to be sacrificed to.
As for the solitary utterances of shamans and sorcerers,
the objects of awe and fear among petty people,
the seven spirits such as Tǔgōng, Fēishī, Jiùmèi, Běijūn, Xiánjù, Dānglù, and Zhífú,
and the minor taboos observed in folk practices—
these are not what the Heavenly King should fear.
In former times, the capital did not guard against them,
nor did it undertake projects to establish prohibitions
in order to attract auspicious responses and omens;
yet its descendants flourished and multiplied,
not less than before.
Furthermore, if a ruler fears his ministers,
or superiors yield to inferiors,
it will surely show weakness and invite encroachment;
this is hardly the way to attract blessings.
I have observed in historical records
that when rulers cultivate their persons and are clear in rewards and punishments,
the state is well-governed and the people are at peace.
When the people are content and joyful,
Heaven is pleased and increases their allotted span.
Therefore, the *Book of Documents* says:
"The king receives Heaven's enduring mandate through the small people."
Confucius said:
"What Heaven assists is compliance;
what people assist is trustworthiness.
To act with trustworthiness and think of compliance,
and moreover to honor the worthy—
thus from Heaven comes protection,
with good fortune and no不利."
This is the very foundation for repelling calamities and attracting blessings and goodness.
The *Book of Songs* says,
"Heaven produces the multitude of people,
and for every thing there is a norm."
Therefore, the human body, form, and appearance all have their patterns and categories;
bones, physiognomy, features, and flesh each have their divisions,
revealing the term of life's destiny
and manifesting the signs of nobility and baseness.
In a single person's body,
the energies of the Five Phases and Eight Trigrams are all present.
Therefore, Shī Kuàng said, "A ruddy complexion indicates short life,"
for the fire element family names are easily extinguished.
The *Appended Phrases* of the *Book of Changes* states:
"The Xùn trigram represents people with many white eyes."
Those with prominent whites on all four sides die by weapons—
this is like metal overcoming wood.
The *Classic* says:
"Taking from near, it draws from the body;
taking from afar, it draws from things."
"The sage, seeing the utmost intricacies of the world,
models them through forms and appearances,
representing things according to their appropriateness."
This is also what the worthy observe,
recording the past to know the future,
and establishing them as rules and models.
The methods of judging a person's physiognomy
lie sometimes in the face,
sometimes in the hands and feet,
sometimes in the gait,
sometimes in the voice.
The face should be broad, even, moist, and lustrous;
the hands and feet should be deep-lined, fine, clear, and straight;
the gait should be steady, calm, and well-supported;
the voice should be warm, harmonious, and centered.
Head, face, hands, and feet,
body shape and bone joints
should all be proportionate and well-matched.
This is a general outline.
Bone structure indicates the signs of emolument;
complexion and aura indicate the portents of good and ill fortune;
facial areas indicate the timing of years;
moral conduct attracts these three;
Heaven bestows destiny and nature decisively.
Signs may be clear or subtle;
colors may be deep or light;
conduct may be shallow or profound;
destiny may depart or arrive.
Therefore, the timing of good and ill fortune,
the success or failure of rank and position,
are not always certain.
If not for intelligence and wisdom,
and careful, precise attention,
who can hit the mark?
In the past, Nèishǐ Shū Fú passed through Lǔ,
and Gōngfū Áo, hearing of his ability to judge people by physiognomy,
presented his two sons to him.
Shū Fú said:
"Gǔ will nourish you,
Nán will bury you.
Gǔ has a full lower face;
he will surely have descendants in Lǔ."
When Mù Bó grew old,
Wén Bó supported him in life;
when he died,
Huì Shū presided over the mourning.
Lǔ eventually established Xiànzǐ
to continue the line of the Mèng clan.
And Wángsūn Yuè judged Qiáo Rú,
Zǐshàng nearly [judged] Shāng Chén,
Zǐwén worried about Yuè Jiāo,
Shū Jī detested Shí Wǒ,
Dān Xiānggōng observed Jìn Lì,
Zǐgòng observed Zhū and Lǔ,
Zāng Wén listened to Yù Yuè,
Chén Xián saw Zhāng ◇—
worthy men and enlightened scholars,
observing with good intent,
never missed the mark.
And Táng Jǔ's judgments of Lǐ Duì and Cài Zé,
Xǔ Fù's judgments of Dèng Tōng and Tiáohóu—
even the Director of Fate allotting emoluments,
reviewing their deeds,
could not surpass them.
Nevertheless,
that humans have bone structure
is like the myriad things having species and kinds,
or timber having constant suitability.
The skilled craftsman, according to the pattern,
assigns each its use:
the curved is fit for wheels,
the straight for carriage bodies;
sandalwood is fit for spokes,
elm for hubs.
This is the correct method and general principle.
If there is the material,
but the craftsman does not utilize it,
what can be done?
Therefore, all physiognomists
can predict the ultimate potential,
but cannot make it necessarily come to pass.
Land of ten varieties,
though the fertile soil is rich,
will not yield without plowing;
a horse of a thousand lǐ,
though its bone structure is complete,
will not reach [its destination] without the whip.
A vessel blank uncarved
does not become a utensil;
a scholar unserving in office
does not attain position.
In such cases,
Heaven and Earth cannot determine nobility or baseness,
nor can ghosts and spirits determine poverty or wealth.
Some, sons of kings and dukes,
serve in office to old age
without attaining emolument.
Some, commoners and lowly servants,
unexpectedly rise up
to the highest ranks and positions.
This is receiving Heaven's mandate and nature,
which is inevitably so.
The *Book of Songs* says, "Heaven is difficult to rely upon";
the substance of nature and destiny,
the attraction of moral conduct,
are bestowed and received in complex interweaving—this is unchanging.
However, its main principles are:
bone structure is primary,
complexion serves as an indicator.
The appearance of the five colors
flourishes and fades in due season.
The wise, upon seeing auspicious signs,
cultivate goodness to welcome them;
if they show signs of worry,
they examine their conduct and correct faults.
Fools act contrary and perverse,
failing to reflect and consider;
even if auspicious signs appear,
their fortune turns to disaster.
Ah, gentlemen,
should you not be reverent?
As for dreams:
some are direct,
some symbolic,
some spiritual,
some from thought,
some personal,
some from external influence,
some seasonal,
some opposite,
some from illness,
some from nature.
In ancient times, King Wǔ of Zhōu,
while Yì Jiāng was pregnant with Tàishū,
dreamed that the Lord-on-High said to her:
"I command that your son be named Yú,
and I give him Táng."
When he was born,
the palm of his hand bore the character "Yú,"
and thus he was named accordingly.
King Chéng destroyed Táng,
and subsequently enfeoffed him there.
This is called a directly corresponding dream.
The Book of Songs says:
"Bears and brown bears
are auspicious signs for sons;
adders and snakes
are auspicious signs for daughters."
"Many fish signify
a truly bountiful year;
banners and pennons signify
a household flourishing and numerous."
This is called a symbolic dream.
Confucius was born in a time of disorder;
by day he pondered the virtue of the Duke of Zhōu,
and by night he dreamed of him.
This is called a dream of concentrated thought.
When a person thinks of something,
he dreams of its arrival;
when he has worries, he dreams of the matter.
This is called a dream of memory and thought.
In present affairs,
if a noble dreams of something, it is auspicious;
if a commoner dreams of it, it is ominous;
if a gentleman dreams of it, it is glorious;
if a petty person dreams of it, it is shameful.
This is called a dream of personal status.
Duke Wén of Jìn, during the battle of Chéngpú,
dreamed that the King of Chǔ was upon him, sucking his brains—
a most dreadful omen.
Yet when the battle came,
he achieved a great victory.
This is called an extremely opposite dream.
Dreams during overcast rain
make people weary and confused;
dreams during severe drought
make people chaotic and scattered;
dreams during extreme cold
make people resentful and sorrowful;
dreams during strong winds
make people feel tossed and blown.
This is called a dream influenced by climate.
Spring dreams are of growth and birth,
summer dreams are of height and brightness,
autumn and winter dreams are of ripening and storing.
This is called a seasonally responsive dream.
Yīn illnesses bring dreams of cold,
yáng illnesses bring dreams of heat,
internal illnesses bring dreams of chaos,
external illnesses bring dreams of eruption,
the dreams of all illnesses
may be scattered or gathered.
This is called a dream of bodily energy.
People's emotions and minds
differ in likes and dislikes;
some consider this auspicious,
some consider this inauspicious.
Each should examine himself,
constantly interpreting according to his own circumstances.
This is called a dream of innate nature.
Therefore, those that first show discrepancies
are called spiritual;
what one thinks of by day,
he dreams of by night—
suddenly auspicious, suddenly inauspicious,
good and evil unreliable—
are called from thought;
noble and base, wise and foolish,
male and female, old and young—
are called personal;
wind, rain, cold, and heat are called from influence;
the waxing and waning of the five phases are called seasonal;
when yīn reaches its extreme, it becomes auspicious;
when yáng reaches its extreme, it becomes inauspicious—
these are called opposite;
observing one's ailments,
examining one's dreams—
these are called from illness;
the mind's essence, likes and dislikes,
verified in affairs—
these are called from nature.
All these ten types
are the general outline of dream interpretation.
Yet the determination of auspicious and inauspicious often tends to be opposite;
what is the reason for this?
Is it because human wakefulness is yáng,
human sleep is yīn,
and the workings of yīn and yáng are opposite?
This also refers to cases that are not very clear.
Suppose one dreams of an auspicious event and feels great joy in one's mind,
emanating from the essence of the heart—
then it is truly auspicious.
If one dreams of an inauspicious event and feels great fear, worry, and sorrow,
emanating from the essence of the heart—
then it is truly ominous.
As for the so-called dreams of death and injury in autumn and winter,
the auspicious ones accord with the season.
Nevertheless,
wealth can be a great harm;
it would be better not to dream of it at all.
In general, the main principles for examining dreams are:
clean, fresh, and beautiful,
appearance firm and robust,
bamboo and trees lush and fine,
palaces, rooms, tools, and vessels newly made,
upright and open,
bright, warm, and gentle,
images of rising, ascending, and flourishing are all auspicious and joyful,
plans followed and affairs accomplished.
All foul, filthy, rotten,
withered, desolate, and foggy,
leaning, crooked, and deviant,
mutilated, unstable,
blocked, dark, and obscure,
disintegrating, falling, descending, and declining images are all
plans not followed,
undertakings not accomplished.
Monstrous, strange, and abnormal,
hateful and detestable things all signify worry.
Painted embryos,
carved and engraved unrealities,
earthenware empty and hollow—
all signify being deceived.
Actors, performers, dancers,
images of jesters and children at play—
all signify laughter and joy.
This is the greater part of it.
Sometimes dreams are very clear yet have no interpretation,
sometimes very subtle yet have a response;
why is this?
The answer:
What is fundamentally called a dream
is a term for what is obscure and not fully discernible,
a confused and muddled designation.
Therefore, one should not rely solely on them to decide matters.
When people discuss plans and affairs,
rise and act upon them,
there are still cases of non-compliance;
how much more so with forgotten, random dreams—
can they be certain?
Only when there is a genuine, sincere influence,
a message from spirits and deities,
is there interpretation.
Thus, when a gentleman has an unusual dream,
it is not without reason;
there must be some cause for it.
When a petty person has an unusual dream,
it is not merely riding on chance;
sometimes there is an omen.
Therefore, Wǔ Dīng dreamed of obtaining a sage and found Fù Yuè,
while the Second Emperor dreamed of a white tiger and lost his domain.
Extraordinary dreams
mostly have causes and rarely occur without reason.
Now, in the dreams of a single sleep,
there may be frequent transformations,
with various things arriving in succession,
yet the dreamer cannot thoroughly understand their meaning,
so diviners sometimes fail to interpret them accurately.
This is not the fault of divination,
but rather the error of the dreamer.
Sometimes the dream is clear,
but the interpreter fails to connect and observe it in context,
so the auspicious or inauspicious signs do not manifest.
This is not the deceitfulness of the texts,
but rather the error of the interpreter.
Thus, the difficulty of dream divination
lies in reading its texts.
In dream divination, one must carefully examine its changes,
scrutinize its signs,
internally assess the emotions and intentions,
and externally evaluate the interactions of the Five Phases,
so that the symbols of fortune and misfortune,
the manifestations of good and evil,
may become visible.
Moreover, when people see auspicious signs and cultivate virtue,
fortune is certain to be achieved;
when they see auspicious signs but indulge in excess,
fortune turns into calamity.
When they see ominous signs and respond with arrogance and contempt,
calamity is certain to occur;
when they see ominous signs and respond with caution and fear,
calamity turns into fortune.
Thus, when Tàisì had an auspicious dream,
King Wén did not dare to rest in its good fortune,
but first sacrificed to the multitude of spirits,
then consulted the diviners in the Bright Hall,
and together paid homage to the auspicious dream.
He cultivated self-reflection and caution,
hearing good news as if it were a cause for concern,
and thus was able to achieve good fortune and possess the world.
When Duke Guó dreamed that Rùshōu bestowed upon him fields and lands,
he believed himself to have received good fortune,
imprisoned the historian Yín,
and ordered the state to celebrate the dream.
He heard of a cause for concern as if it were good news,
and thus brought about calamity, leading to the destruction of his domain.
The Yì Jīng says:
"It causes one to know fear,
and also to understand calamities and their causes."
Whenever one has an unusual dream that stirs the heart,
or encounters signs of others' fortune or misfortune,
or observes the complexion and aura,
regardless of whether they are good or evil,
one should always be fearful, cultivate self-reflection,
and meet them with virtue.
Only then can one encounter good fortune,
and "the blessings of heaven endure forever."
Gēngzǐ asked Qiánfū:
"The virtues of Yáo and Shùn
cannot both be praised as supreme;
is this truly like Hánzǐ's analogy of the spear and shield?"
Qiánfū said:
"This is to fail to understand difficulty and to fail to understand categories.
Now, a shield is for defense,
its nature is beneficial;
a spear is for offense,
its nature is harmful.
Thus, the spear is an instrument of harm,
the shield an instrument of protection;
they cannot both be supreme at once,
which is inherent in their functions.
The relationship between Yáo and Shùn
is that of human beings,
not like spear and shield.
Their Way is one of shared benevolence,
and they do not harm each other.
How could Shùn and a shield not both be strong?
How could Yáo and a shield not both be worthy?
Moreover, the virtue of Yáo and Shùn
is like two candles illuminating a dark room:
the first candle already fully illuminates it,
and when the second candle is added, it becomes even brighter.
This is not because the first candle is dim and the second bright,
but because the two complement each other to create great light.
The two sages complemented each other's virtue to achieve the merit of great peace.
Thus, the movement of the great roc
is not due to the lightness of a single feather;
the speed of the qíjì
is not due to the strength of a single leg.
Many excellent things complement each other,
and their accumulated effects are boundless.
Yáo and Shùn being both praised as supreme
is precisely in accordance with this principle."
Bóshū said:
"You are mistaken.
When Hán Fēi used the spear and shield as an analogy,
he intended to borrow their incompatibility
to question the impossibility of Yáo and Shùn coexisting as supreme.
But to discuss their inherent nature as benevolent or harmful
is to miss the meaning of this analogy, is it not?"
Qiánfū said:
"Analogies
arise when direct explanation is unclear,
so we borrow the characteristics of things to clarify.
Things have their characteristics
not because of their names,
but because of their true nature.
Now you cite the nature of their names as an analogy
and expect me to disregard their names,
which confuses me.
Moreover, I have heard that answering yīn with yáng
is called forced argument;
discussing the west to question the east
is called forced objection.
If you wish to be certain, you should reflect on yesterday's points,
and then seek understanding,
rather than forcing the issue arbitrarily."
Gēngzǐ said:
"Zhōu Gōng knew of the wickedness of Guǎn and Cài,
yet appointed them to assist Wǔ Gēng,
allowing them to unleash their poison,
and then executed them.
Was this not unkind?
If he did not know,
was he not unwise?
One of these two faults
must apply."
Qiánfū said:
"The texts say the two sons supported Wǔ Gēng, their father, in rebellion,
but is this truly of the same category?
Or is it entirely opposite?
Moreover, Heaven knew of Jié's wickedness yet made him emperor of Xià,
and knew of Zhòu's wickedness yet made him king of Yīn,
allowing them to oppress the two states,
harm the people,
unleash their poison extensively,
and bring about their own destruction.
Could this also be called unkind or unwise?"
Gēngzǐ said:
"Not so.
As for Jié and Zhòu,
they were not kin to Heaven,
so Heaven entrusted them without concern
and punished them without grief.
Now, Guǎn and Cài, in relation to Zhōu Gōng,
had the kinship of brothers,
the affection of flesh and blood.
He appointed them without assessing their ability,
entrusted them with tasks they could not bear,
so it is said to differ from the relationship between Jié, Zhòu, and Heaven."
Qiánfū said:
"The August Heaven has no kin;
the sovereign who inherits the throne
serves Heaven as a father.
The king is a son,
thus he serves Heaven as a father.
All people within the realm
'are none not the king's subjects.'
If they commit crimes, they must be punished;
the king's law is impartial.
Without bias or partiality,
kinship and distance are treated alike.
'Great righteousness overrides kinship,'
this is the principle of honoring the king.
The impartiality of Heaven is the foundation of Zhōu Gōng's virtue.
Beyond this,
I know nothing further."
Qínzǐ asked Qiánfū:
"Plowing and sowing are the foundation of life,
while study and inquiry are the branches of endeavor.
Lǎo Dān has said:
'The great man dwells in the substance,
not in the ornamentation.'
Yet Confucius said:
'In plowing,
hunger may be found;
in study,
emolument may be found.'
May I ask, if all people in the world
were to abandon their plows and hoes to compete in pursuing study together,
what would happen?"
The Recluse said:
"An excellent question!
The gentleman labors with his mind,
the petty man labors with his strength.
Therefore, what Confucius praised
refers to the gentleman.
Now, based on what the eyes see,
farming is the foundation of eating.
Based on the mind's inquiry into the Way,
learning is also the foundation of farming.
The *Book of Changes* says:
'What establishes the Way of Heaven is called yīn and yáng;
what establishes the Way of Earth is called softness and hardness;
what establishes the Way of Man is called benevolence and righteousness.'
Those who turn against virtue bring disaster."
The Recluse said:
"Alas!
Have you not yet understood this?
Let me tell you.
As for the gentleman,
his worthiness is fit to rule a state and his virtue is fit to nurture the people.
Those fit for this position
are only men of benevolence and righteousness.
Therefore, those who possess benevolence and righteousness
are called gentlemen.
Formerly, Xúnzǐ said:
'Benevolence means loving others;
loving others,
therefore one cannot bear to endanger them.
Righteousness means gathering people;
gathering people,
therefore one cannot bear to bring chaos upon them.'
Thus, the gentleman admonishes and corrects day and night,
diligent and tireless,
worried about the ruler's peril and downfall,
grieving over the people's chaos and dispersal.
Therefore, the worthy man and gentleman,
extending their benevolent and righteous hearts,
love their ruler as parents,
and love the people of the world as younger brothers and sons.
If parents are about to face the calamity of a fall,
or younger brothers and sons are about to suffer the disaster of drowning,
how could they remain silent!
Thus, 'the benevolent are sure to be brave,'
and the virtuous are sure to be righteous.
"Moreover, if an entire state falls into chaos,
there is no safe place for oneself.
The *Book of Songs* says:
'None are willing to think of the chaos;
who has no parents?'
This means all will be harmed,
but those with parents will grieve more deeply.
Therefore, the worthy man and gentleman,
while concerned for the people,
also act for themselves.
When the roof tiles are full above,
and moisture soaks below,
if the ridgepole breaks and rafters collapse,
one fears being crushed.
Thus, when a great house begins to tilt,
those below do not wait for orders;
each vies to prop it up with pillars.
The benevolent, in protecting others' households,
are also acting for themselves.
The *Book of Changes* says:
'If the king is enlightened,
all receive his blessings.'
Therefore, Cìshì leaned against a pillar and sighed,
and the Chǔ woman raised a banner to rouse the king.
Can the grace of benevolence and kindness,
the feelings of loyalty and love,
ever truly cease?"
It is said:
"For people, value the old;
for vessels, value the new.
Brothers grow distant over generations,
friends grow close over generations."
This is the principle of social intercourse,
the nature of human feelings.
Now it is not so;
many think of the distant and forget the near,
abandon the old and turn to the new.
Some grow more distant over the years,
some cast each other aside midway.
They forget the ancient sages' canonical warnings,
and betray long-standing solemn oaths.
Why is this?
Step back and examine it,
and it can be understood.
Circumstances have a constant tendency,
principles have an inherent logic.
When one is wealthy and noble, people compete to attach themselves—
this is the constant tendency of circumstance.
When one is poor and lowly, people compete to leave—
this is the inherent logic of principle.
Associating with the wealthy and noble
brings, from above, the utility of praise and reputation,
and from below, the benefit of goods and wealth.
Associating with the poor and lowly
entails, at best, the expense of relief and loans,
and at least, the loss of lending and borrowing.
Now, even if an official possessed the wickedness of both Jié and Zhí,
if he arrived in a carriage drawn by four horses to visit a scholar,
the scholar would still consider it an honor and welcome him—
how much more if there were real benefits?
Even if a commoner possessed the worthiness of both Yán and Mǐn,
if he came to the door clad in coarse cloth,
people would still consider it a disgrace and fear his return—
how much more if there were real losses?
Therefore, it is easy for the wealthy and noble to be fitting,
hard for the poor and lowly to be appropriate.
Fine clothes are called extravagant and presumptuous;
poor clothes are called destitute and distressed.
Walking slowly is called starving and famished;
walking quickly is called fleeing debt.
Not waiting upon others is called arrogant and rude;
visiting frequently is called begging for food.
An empty-handed visit is considered without sincere intent;
bringing gifts is considered wanting a loan.
Respect and humility are considered incompetence;
assertiveness and pride are considered dissatisfaction.
These are the fetters and hardships,
the bitter cruelty of poverty and lowliness.
Occupying a humble, lowly position,
bearing the deep sorrow of the 'Northern Gate,'
one is reproached at home by wife and children,
and mocked abroad by gentlemen.
At fine gatherings, one cannot follow ritual;
at farewell feasts, one cannot match the crowd.
Goods and wealth are insufficient to foster goodwill;
strength and influence are insufficient to support in urgency.
Long-standing joyful friendships,
affections and bonds, become distant and unconnected.
Then people, without cause, naturally grow estranged and distant.
As estrangement grows, the lowly become increasingly self-conscious and withdraw daily,
while the noble increasingly focus on their faction and forget them.
For the increasingly estranged lowly,
submerged in the lower depths,
to hope the daily-forgetting noble will remember them—
this is why the 'Valley Wind' laments inner devastation,
and why Jiè Tuī fled to the deep mountains.
Where association brings benefit, there is mutual closeness;
where association brings harm, there is mutual estrangement.
Therefore, long-standing oaths that are abandoned
are surely of no use.
Associations that gradually grow close
are surely beneficial.
When vulgar people associate,
benefit gives rise to closeness;
accumulated closeness gives rise to affection;
accumulated affection gives rise to approval;
accumulated approval gives rise to esteem.
If feeling esteems someone,
then unconsciously the heart feels close to them,
and the mouth praises them.
Without benefit, estrangement arises;
accumulated estrangement gives rise to hatred;
accumulated hatred gives rise to disapproval;
accumulated disapproval gives rise to aversion.
If feeling feels aversion toward someone,
then unconsciously the heart excludes them,
and the mouth slanders them.
Therefore, the wealthy and noble, though new acquaintances,
grow closer daily in influence;
the poor and lowly, though old acquaintances,
grow more distant daily in influence.
This is why the commoner cannot compete with the official.
Worldly rulers do not examine how friendships arise,
but blindly believe the words of esteemed ministers.
This is why the pure scholar remains hidden and obscured alone,
while the treacherous and ambitious form factions and soar aloft."
In the past, the guests of Wèi Qí
drifted away to Wǔ'ān;
the officials of Chángpíng
shifted to Guànjūn;
Lián Pō and Zhái Gōng
saw their numbers wax and wane.
Now, with the virtue of these four lords,
relying on the longstanding grace of old nobility,
their guests were still like this;
how much more so for those born in poverty and lowliness?
Only those with the manner of ancient martyrs,
men of purpose and righteousness,
are not thus.
Where grace has been bound,
it is never untied for life;
where the heart feels commitment,
lowly status only deepens it.
The *Book of Songs* says:
"The good man, the gentleman,
his demeanor is constant,
his heart is as if knotted."
Thus, only after the year turns cold do we know the pine and cypress are the last to wither;
only in hardship do we know a man's commitment is firm.
Hóu Yíng and Yù Ràng
gave their lives to repay grace;
Zhuān Zhū and Jīng Kē
exerted their lives to be of service.
Thus, death can be chosen,
but abiding by it is difficult.
Páng Xūn and Bó Diāo,
once received,
also immediately acted righteously in return;
how much more so for those long favored?
Thus Zōu Yáng said of them:
"A tyrant's dog can be made to bark at Yáo;
a robber's guest can be made to assassinate Yóu."
Are these empty words?
Vulgar men are shallow and shortsighted,
eager for immediate gain.
Seeing benefit in attending, they are the first to arrive;
considering something useless, they lag behind.
Therefore, those who seek haste
compete to push upward, with no time to receive those below;
they strive to chase ahead, with no leisure to care for those behind.
Thus Hán Ānguó could give Tián Fén five hundred pieces of gold,
but could not relieve a single poor man;
Zhái Fāngjìn praised Chúnyú Cháng,
but could not recommend a single scholar.
Now, Ānguó and Fāngjìn
were loyal and good men of former generations,
and yet they were still like this;
how much more so for petty officials at the end of the road?
This is why treacherous heroes form cliques to advance,
and why reclusive gentlemen become increasingly obscured.
If not for a wise and sagely ruler,
who could illuminate and discern this?
Moreover, the birth of resentment and hatred
is like the meeting of two men.
If they face each other,
with mutual affection,
pushing their intentions to the extreme,
their sincere hearts shoot toward each other,
piercing heart and marrow.
The height of love and joy
makes them lightly die for each other;
thus Hóu Shēng and Yùzǐ slit their throats without regret.
If they turn their backs,
their hearts and feelings are at odds.
Pushing their intentions to the extreme,
they part and run in opposite directions,
one to the farthest east, the other to the farthest west.
Their hearts are not yet decided,
thus Chén Yú and Zhāng Ěr, in old age, destroyed each other completely without feeling pain.
From this we observe
the principle of social intercourse:
its emotional aspect is great indeed.
It is not only friendship that is thus;
the relations between ruler and minister, husband and wife are also like this.
When there is joy,
not even father and son can come between them;
when there is discord,
not even sworn enemies can surpass it.
Therefore, the sage is always cautious in small matters to ensure a firm end.
Wealth and honor are not necessarily to be valued;
poverty and lowliness are not necessarily to be despised.
Human hearts differ in their preferences;
their measures differ by tens of thousands.
Xǔ Yóu declined the imperial throne;
a vulgar man will fight for a county office.
Mèng Kē refused a salary of ten thousand *zhōng*;
a petty man covets a peck of grain.
Thus it is said:
"Quails and wrens flock together,
active all day without rest,
hopping and gathering in disorder,
never leaving the mugwort and reeds.
Swans and wild geese fly high,
pairs parting and separating,
reaching thousands and tens of thousands,
their aim set on ponds and marshes.
The phoenix soars above the yellow calendar,
hovering within the great clarity,
drifting with the auspicious wind,
now restrained, now lofty, with ease.
Yet its will is still unsatisfied;
it chirps and cries at length,
stamps, calls, and shakes its wings,
ascends the crimson clouds,
approaches the Dipper and Pole Star,
inhales the dew of yang,
goes ten days without eating,
and its mind is still discontented."
These three kinds differ in their pursuits,
each content with what they do.
Thus Bóyí gathered ferns without regret;
Cháofǔ dwelled in trees by his own will.
From this we observe
that the will and measure of a scholar
are truly difficult to fathom.
All you gentlemen,
should not presume on wealth and honor to despise the poor and lowly,
thinking that the poor and lowly must submit to you.
The *Book of Songs* says:
"Virtue is light as a hair,
but few among the people can lift it."
There are four great difficulties in the world,
which people are unable to practice:
the first is forbearance,
the second is fairness,
the third is reverence,
the fourth is steadfastness.
Forbearance is the root of benevolence;
fairness is the root of righteousness;
reverence is the root of propriety;
steadfastness is the root of trustworthiness.
When these four roots stand together,
the four practices are complete;
when the four practices are fully present,
this is called true worthiness.
If the four roots are not established,
the four practices do not form;
if not one of the four practices exists,
this is called a petty man.
What is called forbearance:
the gentlemanly man
considers how others would forbear with me,
and acts with friendly tones.
Thus, if the ruler does not open his sincere heart to show worthies and loyal men,
the worthies and loyal men also have no way to reach him.
The *Book of Changes* says:
"When the king is enlightened,
all receive his blessing."
Therefore, loyal ministers must await an enlightened ruler to manifest their integrity;
good officials must obtain an observant lord to accomplish their merit.
If the ruler is not enlightened,
then high ministers conceal matters below and suppress loyalty,
and all offices abandon the law to flatter the noble.
Loyal speech is that by which security is achieved;
if not offered, there will surely be danger.
Laws and prohibitions are that by which order is achieved;
if not upheld, there will surely be chaos.
Whether loyal speech is offered or not,
whether laws are upheld or not,
the handle of this lies with the ruler,
not something subjects can accomplish.
Therefore, the sage seeks it within himself,
and does not demand it of those below.
All those in superior positions,
if their methods are clear and rewards and punishments certain,
though they speak not a word, order will naturally prevail.
Merchants double their profits
to surpass each other.
If one can become wealthy and noble,
even if he accumulates cunning and evil,
people will compete to praise him,
and he will never be seen as wrong.
If one dwells in poverty and lowliness,
even if respectful and cautious, he is deemed unworthy,
and never seen as right.
This is why customs and transformation gradually decay,
and why ritual and righteousness fade and decline.
There are three things in the world that are truly distressing.
What are these three?
They are:
when affection is actually shallow yet words profess depth,
when concern is truly neglected yet the language feigns worry,
when one harbors no intention of coming yet outwardly sets a date.
If you do not trust them, you fear losing the worthy;
if you trust them, you are misled by others.
These are the most detestable things in the vulgar world.
Therefore, Confucius deplored words exceeding deeds,
and the *Book of Songs* laments: "Grand, empty words,
issue from the mouth.
Artful speech is like a reed-organ's sound,
the face is thick indeed."
Now, in the friendships of the common world,
without mutual understanding and scrutiny, they seek deep and firm bonds.
They bare their hearts and clasp wrists,
beat their breasts and swear oaths,
merely wishing to shield and defend each other in discussions.
But on the day they part ways,
after gaining what they wanted,
they then abandon and forget each other.
Some, having received another's kindness and virtue,
first help and support them,
but if unable to lift them up,
then proceed to slander them,
creating flaws and rifts,
openly saying, 'I spared no effort,
but alas, it simply could not be done.'
The *Book of Songs* says:
"Had I known it would be like this,
better had I never been born."
First harmony, then discord;
a beginning but no end—
it is not as good as having no intention from the start,
rather than forcing a solemn vow.
"When gentlemen make frequent covenants,
disorder is thereby increased."
The way of the great man
is to be comprehensive and not partial;
subtle words convey mutual understanding,
as if matching tallies in secret—
what need is there for covenants?
Confucius was respectful and cautious,
seeming as if he could not speak,
yet it is also said, "In solemn speech,
he was simply careful."
A scholar values having words,
but also detests a garrulous mouth.
Therefore it is said:
"When substance and refinement are balanced,
then one becomes a gentleman."
Better than being untrustworthy,
to be firm, resolute, simple, and slow of speech
is still closer to benevolence.
Alas, how lamentable!
All people nowadays
speak squarely but act roundly,
their mouths are upright but their hearts are wicked;
their actions contradict their words,
their hearts oppose their mouths.
Discussing antiquity, they knowingly praise Bóyí, Shūqí, Yuán Xiàn, and Yán Huí;
speaking of the present, they necessarily mention official rank, title, and position.
In empty talk, they know to consider virtue and righteousness as worthy;
in actual recommendations, they must put family prestige and service record first.
Even if a man living in obscurity personally practices the conduct of Yán Huí and Mǐn Sǔn,
possesses the quality of diligent humility,
holds the talent of Yī Yǐn and Lǚ Shàng,
and cherishes the way of saving the people,
his lack of support in this age
is already clear!
A saying goes:
"For people, the old are best;
for vessels, the new are best.
Brothers grow distant over generations,
friends grow closer over generations."
This is the principle of social intercourse,
the natural feeling among people.
But now it is not so;
they often think of the distant and forget the near,
turn their backs on the old and turn toward the new.
Some, over the years, grow increasingly distant;
