others, midway along the road, cast each other aside.
They forget the classical warnings of the former sages,
and betray long-standing solemn oaths.
Why is this so?
Step back and examine it,
and one can also understand.
Circumstances have a constant tendency,
principle has its inherent nature.
When one is wealthy and noble, people strive to attach themselves—
this is the constant tendency of circumstance.
When one is poor and lowly, people strive to leave—
this is the inherent nature of principle.
Those who associate with the wealthy and noble
gain, from above, the benefit of praise and recommendation;
from below, the advantage of goods and wealth.
Those who associate with the poor and lowly
incur, on a large scale, the expense of relief and loans;
on a small scale, the loss of lending and borrowing.
Now, even if an official possesses the wickedness of both Jié and Zhí,
if he arrives in a carriage drawn by four horses to visit a scholar,
the scholar will still consider it an honor and welcome him—
how much more if he actually brings benefit?
Even if a man living in obscurity possesses the worthiness of both Yán Huí and Mǐn Sǔn,
if he comes to the door dressed in coarse cloth,
people will still consider it a disgrace and fear his coming again—
how much more if he actually causes loss?
Therefore, it is easy for the wealthy and noble to find fitting company,
but difficult for the poor and lowly to find suitable companionship.
Fine clothes are called extravagant and presumptuous;
poor garments are called destitute and wretched.
Walking slowly is called famished and starving;
walking quickly is called fleeing debt.
Not waiting upon others is called arrogant and rude;
visiting frequently is called begging for food.
An empty-handed visit is considered without sincere intent;
presenting gifts is thought to desire a loan.
Respect and humility are considered unworthy;
holding one's head high is considered lacking virtue.
These are the constraints and slights suffered by the man in obscurity,
the bitter harshness of poverty and lowliness.
Occupying a humble, low position,
bearing the deep sorrow of the "Běimén" ode,
internally reproached by wife and children,
externally ridiculed by gentlemen and officers.
At fine gatherings, he cannot follow proper ritual;
at farewell feasts, his provisions do not reach the multitude.
His goods and wealth are insufficient to foster good relations;
his strength and influence are insufficient to support in urgent need.
The joy of long friendship,
the bond of affection, becomes distant and unconnected—
then people, without cause, naturally grow distant and estranged.
As estrangement gradually increases, the lowly become ever more self-conscious and withdraw daily,
while the noble become ever more focused on their own factions and forget them.
For one who is increasingly estranged and lowly,
submerged in the lower reaches,
to hope that the noble who forget him daily
—this is why the "Gǔ Fēng" ode speaks of inner devastation,
and why Jiè Zhītuī went deep into the mountains.
Where association brings benefit, there is mutual closeness;
where association brings harm, there is mutual estrangement.
Therefore, long-standing oaths that are abandoned
are certainly of no use.
Friendship that gradually grows close
is certainly beneficial.
Common people in their mutual relations:
benefit gives rise to closeness,
accumulated closeness gives rise to affection,
accumulated affection gives rise to approval,
accumulated approval gives rise to regarding as worthy.
If feeling regards someone as worthy,
then unconsciously the heart grows close to them,
and the mouth praises them.
Without benefit, estrangement arises;
accumulated estrangement gives rise to hatred,
accumulated hatred gives rise to disapproval,
accumulated disapproval gives rise to regarding as wicked.
If feeling regards someone as wicked,
then unconsciously the heart excludes them,
and the mouth slanders them.
Therefore, the wealthy and noble, even if new acquaintances,
their influence leads to daily closeness;
the poor and lowly, even if old acquaintances,
their influence leads to daily estrangement.
This is why the man in obscurity cannot compete with the official.
Worldly rulers do not examine how friendships arise,
but blindly trust the words of esteemed ministers.
This is why the pure scholar remains alone in obscurity,
and why the treacherous and ambitious form factions and soar aloft.
In the past, the guests of Wèi Qí
drifted away to Wǔ'ān;
the officials of Chángpíng
transferred to Guànjūn;
Lián Pō and Zhái Gōng
saw their numbers wax and wane.
Now, with the virtue of these four lords,
relying on the long-standing favor of old nobility,
their guests were still like this—
how much more so for those born in poverty and lowliness?
Only those with the spirit of ancient heroes,
men of purpose and righteousness,
are not thus.
Where kindness has been bound,
it is never undone for life;
where the heart feels commitment,
lowly status only deepens it.
The Book of Songs says:
"The good man, the gentleman,
his demeanor is constant,
his heart is knotted firm."
Thus only when the year grows cold do we know the pine and cypress are the last to wither;
only when the age is narrow do we know a man's steadfastness.
Hóu Yíng and Yù Ràng
gave their lives to repay kindness;
Zhuān Zhū and Jīng Kē
strove with their lives to be of service.
Thus death can be chosen,
but abiding by principle is hard.
Páng Xūn and Bó Diāo,
once received,
also immediately acted with righteousness to repay,
how much more those long favored?
Thus Zōu Yáng said of them:
"A dog of Jié can be made to bark at Yáo;
a guest of Zhí can be made to assassinate Yóu."
Are these empty words?
Vulgar men are shallow and shortsighted,
eager for immediate gain;
seeing advantage in attending, they are first to arrive;
seeing no use, they later turn their backs.
Therefore those who crave haste
vie to push upward, with no time to receive those below;
strive to rush ahead, with no leisure to care for those behind.
Thus Hán Ānguó could give Tián Fěn five hundred pieces of gold,
but could not relieve a single poor man;
Zhái Fāngjìn praised Chún Yú Cháng,
but could not recommend a single scholar.
Now Ānguó and Fāngjìn
were loyal and good men of former ages,
and yet they were like this—
how much more those lesser aides at the end of the road?
This is why cunning heroes flock to advancing cliques,
and why reclusive scholars become ever more obscured.
If not for a wise and sagely ruler,
who could illuminate and discern?
Moreover, the birth of resentment and hatred
is like the pairing of two men.
If they face each other,
kindness and feeling are mutual;
pushing their intent to the extreme,
sincere devotion shoots forth,
piercing the heart, reaching the marrow;
the height of love and joy
makes them lightly die for each other—
thus Hóu Shēng and Yùzǐ cut their throats without regret.
If they turn their backs,
hearts and feelings are at odds;
pushing their intent to the extreme,
they part and flee,
to the farthest east, the utmost west,
yet their hearts are still not at ease—
thus Chén Yú and Zhāng Ěr in old age utterly destroyed each other without pity or pain.
From this we see
the principle of social intercourse
is greatly significant.
Not only is it so among friends,
but also between ruler and minister, husband and wife.
When there is joy,
even father and son cannot come between;
when there is discord,
even sworn enemies cannot surpass it.
Therefore the sage is ever cautious in small things to ensure a firm end.
Wealth and honor may not be worthy of esteem;
poverty and lowliness may not be worthy of contempt.
Human hearts differ in their likings;
their measures are separated by myriads.
Xǔ Yóu declined the imperial throne;
common men fight for a county post.
Mèng Kē refused a salary of ten thousand zhōng;
petty men covet a peck of grain.
Thus it is said:
"Quail and wrens flock together,
ceaseless all day long,
scrambling and gathering, perched in disorder,
never leaving the mugwort and reeds.
Swans and wild geese fly high,
pairs parting, going separate ways,
reaching thousands, attaining tens of thousands,
their aim set on lakes and ponds.
Phoenixes soar above the yellow calendar,
hovering in the great purity,
drifting with the auspicious wind,
now rising, now falling, with ease and grace,
yet still unsatisfied in intent,
they cry out mournfully and long,
stamp, call, and shake their wings,
ascend the crimson clouds,
approach the Dipper and Pole Star,
inhale the dew of yang,
go ten days without eating,
and still their intent remains unfulfilled."
These three kinds differ in their pursuits,
each content with their own way.
Thus Bó Yí gathered ferns without regret;
Cháo Fǔ dwelled in trees by his own will.
From this we observe
that the will and measure of a scholar
are truly hard to fathom.
All you gentlemen,
should not presume to be arrogant toward the poor and lowly because of your wealth and honor,
thinking the poor and lowly must yield to you.
The Book of Songs says:
"Virtue is light as a hair,
yet few can lift it."
In the world there are four great difficulties,
which people are unable to practice:
first, forbearance;
second, fairness;
third, reverence;
fourth, constancy.
Now forbearance is the root of benevolence;
fairness is the root of righteousness;
reverence is the root of propriety;
constancy is the root of trustworthiness.
When these four are established together,
the four practices are complete;
when the four practices are fully present,
this is called true worthiness.
If the four roots are not established,
the four practices do not form;
if not one of the four practices exists,
this is called a petty man.
What is called forbearance:
the gentleman,
in judging others, applies forbearance to himself,
and in action and stillness reflects in his heart;
what he himself lacks,
he does not demand from those below;
what he himself possesses,
he does not ridicule in others;
moved by his own fondness for respect,
he receives scholars with courtesy;
moved by his own fondness for affection,
he treats people with kindness;
wishing to establish himself, he establishes others;
wishing to succeed himself, he helps others succeed;
appreciating that others worry for him,
he first labors for others;
disliking that others forget him,
he often remembers others.
The common sort are not so:
in judging others, they do not apply forbearance to themselves;
in action, they do not reflect in their hearts;
lacking it themselves, they demand it of others;
possessing it themselves, they ridicule others for it;
having no courtesy themselves, they demand respect from others;
having no kindness themselves, they demand love from others;
in poverty and lowliness, they complain that others did not worry for them from the start;
in wealth and honor, they claim it is they who do not worry for others.
To conduct oneself thus
is hardly worthy of being called benevolent.
What is called fairness means:
within, harboring the kindness of the cuckoo bird;
without, holding the heart of a whetstone and arrow;
in evaluating scholars, one must base it on their aspirations and conduct;
in praise or blame, one must verify with actual results;
one does not follow vulgar customs and echo others;
nor chase after popular opinions to form judgments;
if there is goodness,
one does not ridicule poverty and lowliness;
if there is evil,
one does not fear wealth and nobility;
one does not flatter superiors and slight inferiors;
nor despise the old and revere the new.
Common people are not like this:
within, they are biased toward their wives and children;
without, they are misled by close friends;
if pleased, they praise them;
if resentful, they slander them;
their fair judgments have no standard;
their criticism and praise lack verification;
they arbitrarily fawn upon the noble to form cliques;
arbitrarily mimic voices to bark in packs;
they serve the wealthy and noble like slaves;
regard the poor and lowly as hired servants;
they visit the gates of the powerful a hundred times,
but not once go to households without influence.
Holding such a heart,
it is hard to be called righteous.
What is called reverence means:
within, one dares not be arrogant toward family;
without, one dares not slight scholar-officials;
seeing the lowly as if noble,
regarding the young as elders;
their courtesy enters first,
their words come after;
kindness and goodwill are always reciprocated,
courtesy and respect are always repaid;
when seeing the worthy, they do not place themselves above,
but yield to others;
in tasks, they take on the toil,
in dwelling, they follow the humble,
in position, they accept the lowly,
in sustenance, they are content with meager fare.
Common people are not like this:
within, they are rude and disrespectful to wives and children;
without, they belittle and insult close friends;
their intelligence does not distinguish true from false,
their mind does not separate good from ugly;
foolish, they delight in arrogantly looking down on the worthy;
young, they like to bully their elders;
kindness and goodwill are not reciprocated,
courtesy and respect are not repaid;
seeing the worthy, they do not yield;
in gatherings, they cannot defer;
in action, they desire to choose ease;
in dwelling, they desire comfort;
in sustenance, they desire to monopolize abundance;
in position, they contend for honor;
seeing others humble and yielding,
they thus mock them;
seeing others reverent and respectful,
they thus act arrogantly;
being like this, they call themselves worthy, capable, wise, and intelligent.
Behaving like this,
it is hard to be called loyal.
What is called integrity means:
it is the heart.
A person of principle
has sincere and focused emotions,
a mind with unique insight;
not driven by dangerous and vulgar customs,
not confused by the mouths of the multitude;
their intelligence is exceptionally clear,
their heart is steadfast and profound;
standing alone, they are fearless;
withdrawing from the world, they are not distressed;
their heart is firm as metal and stone,
their will lightens the four seas;
thus they guard their heart and establish their trustworthiness.
Common vessels are not like this:
within, they have no steadfastness;
without, they have no standard or measure;
they are unstable, dangerous, and deceitful,
seeking conformity with the world;
their mouths have no fixed judgment,
they do not constantly uphold virtue,
their actions are inconsistent.
Holding such conduct,
it is hard to be called trustworthy.
Now these four kinds of conduct:
their lightness is like a hair,
their weight is like a mountain;
the noble person considers them easy,
the petty person considers them difficult.
Confucius said:
"Is benevolence far away?
I desire benevolence,
and benevolence arrives."
He also said, "Those who understand virtue are few."
The partiality and factionalism of vulgar customs
have been so since ancient times,
not only today.
All gentlemen
compete in arrogance and presumption,
greedy for pleasure, disrespectful and proud,
like merchants doubling profits
to surpass each other.
If one can become wealthy and noble,
even if accumulating cunning and evil,
they vie to praise them,
and in the end see no fault;
if one is poor and lowly,
even if reverent and cautious,
they are only considered unworthy,
and in the end see no right.
This is why customs and transformation gradually decay,
and ritual and righteousness diminish and decline.
There are three things in the world to worry about.
What are the three?
It is said:
emotions are actually thin but words claim thickness;
thoughts are actually neglectful but expressions pretend concern;
intentions are not sincere but outwardly set deadlines.
If you do not trust them, you fear losing the worthy;
if you trust them, you mislead people.
This is what is most detestable about vulgar scholars.
Therefore, Confucius hated words exceeding actions;
the *Book of Songs* laments, "Grand, grand are the big words,
issuing from the mouth.
Artful words like a reed organ,
thick is the face."
Now in the friendships of vulgar customs,
without mutual understanding and examination, they seek deep bonds;
probing hearts and grasping wrists,
patting chests and swearing oaths,
they merely wish to protect and discuss each other;
on the day they part ways,
after obtaining what they want,
they then abandon and forget.
Some, having received others' kindness and virtue,
first use it to aid themselves;
if unable to promote them,
they then slander them,
creating flaws and conflicts,
openly saying, 'I did not spare effort,
but unfortunately it just couldn't be done.'
The *Book of Songs* says:
"Knowing I am like this,
better I had not been born."
First harmonious then discordant,
having a beginning but no end—
it is better not to have had the intention from the start,
than to force oneself to swear oaths.
Gentlemen frequently swear covenants,
thus disorder grows.
The way of the great person
is comprehensive without factionalism;
subtle words mutually resonate,
as if matching tallies;
what need is there for covenants?
Confucius was respectful and cautious,
seeming as if he could not speak;
it is also said, "Solemn speech
is only cautious."
Scholars value having words,
but also detest excessive talk.
Therefore it is said:
"When refinement and substance are balanced,
then one is a gentleman."
Rather than being insincere,
being firm, resolute, simple, and reticent
is closer to benevolence.
Alas, sorrowful indeed!
All people today:
their words are square but actions round;
their mouths are upright but hearts wicked;
actions contradict words,
hearts oppose mouths;
discussing antiquity, they know to praise Bóyí, Shūqí, Yuán Xiàn, and Yán Huí;
speaking of the present, they necessarily mention official ranks and positions;
in empty talk, they know to consider virtue and righteousness as worthy;
in recommendations, they must put family status first.
Even if a scholar personally practices the conduct of Yán Huí and Mǐn Sǔn,
possesses the quality of diligence and humility,
holds the talent of Yī Yǐn and Lǚ Shàng,
and cherishes the way of saving the people,
his lack of support in this age
is already clear!
For a ruler,
there is no greater title than "enlightened";
for a minister,
there is no finer praise than "loyal."
These two virtues
are what rulers and ministers throughout history have jointly desired.
Yet, enlightenment rarely persists,
and loyalty is not found in one out of ten thousand—
not necessarily because they are foolish, dim-witted, and thus earn a bad reputation,
but because they seek it through the wrong means.
Now, enlightenment arises from understanding those below,
and loyalty is achieved through reliance on those above.
"When two people are of one mind,
their sharpness can cut through metal."
Those who can achieve this
possess both praises.
The key lies in clearly wielding methods and techniques,
and personally holding authority and power.
What is called "technique"
prevents those below from deceiving;
what is called "authority"
prevents the situation from falling into chaos.
If techniques are truly enlightened,
then even from ten thousand miles away,
or within the deepest obscurity,
they will inevitably seek to prove their effectiveness;
if authority is truly employed,
then whether near or far, close or distant,
noble or humble, wise or foolish,
all will turn their hearts to it.
By the end of the Zhōu dynasty, it was not so.
They abandoned their techniques and relinquished their authority,
neglecting themselves and relying on others.
Thus, the dukes and ministers gave no thought to loyalty,
and the hundred officials did not exert their full efforts.
The ruler was isolated and obscured above,
while the masses suffered injustice and chaos below.
Hence, the dynasty declined, was encroached upon, and never recovered.
Now, for an emperor,
the benefits are immense,
and the authority is great.
Merely suspending great benefits
is enough to encourage goodness;
merely establishing stern authority
can punish wickedness.
If one displays great benefits to lure the people
and wields great authority to drive them,
then all people in the world
can be made to brave sharp blades without resentment,
and plunge into boiling water and fire without difficulty.
How can it be said that merely leading them to share in governance is not appropriate?
Take hawks and wild birds, for example:
yet hunters control them,
making them strive and strike all day without daring to slacken.
How can there be ministers who cannot be made to exert their full efforts?
The *Book of Songs* says:
"In hewing an axe handle, in hewing an axe handle,
the pattern is not far off."
The art of divine insight
lies within the ruler himself,
yet the ruler neglects it.
Thus, he causes his ministers to clamp their mouths and tie their tongues, not daring to speak.
This is why his ears and eyes become blocked,
and his intelligence and clarity are not attained.
The authority to control those below
is displayed daily before the ruler,
yet the ruler releases it.
Thus, he causes his ministers to slacken and turn their backs on the court.
This is why his majesty and virtue do not shine forth,
and his achievements and fame are not established.
The *Book of Songs* says:
"Though our duties differ,
we are colleagues together.
I come to you with counsel;
listen to me, do not be haughty."
Now, compassion is something all people possess.
Therefore, when the ear hears the sound of crying and wailing,
none fail to feel sorrow, grief, and heartache;
when the eye sees peril and distress,
none fail to feel burning anxiety and rush to rescue.
The bond between ruler and minister is weighty with duty,
while the courtesy among passersby is light.
Even those who merely hear and see in passing,
with no kindness or virtue bestowed,
neither poor nor noble,
still act thus.
How much more, then, should those who face north as ministers and receive favor?
Therefore, advancing loyalty and supporting the imperiled
is what both the worthy and the unworthy jointly desire.
That they truly desire it yet act contrary
is often because they suffer from the path being unprofitable and harmful,
and their words not being trusted, leading to personal ruin.
Looking throughout history at ministers who loved their ruler, worried for their lord, and dared to speak out,
once a well-ordered situation is formed,
the ruler himself cannot disrupt it,
much less his ministers.
When methods and techniques are unclear, and rewards and punishments are not certain,
even if commands are issued daily,
the situation will naturally fall into chaos.
Once a chaotic situation is formed,
the ruler himself cannot govern it,
much less his ministers.
Therefore, in a well-ordered situation,
even if left unattended, it will not fall into chaos;
in a chaotic situation,
even if diligently managed, it will not be well-governed.
Yáo and Shùn were reverent and acted without exertion, yet had abundance—
this was a well-ordered situation.
Húhài and Wáng Mǎng raced about yet had insufficiency—
this was a chaotic situation.
Thus it is said:
"The skilled seek it in the situation,
not blaming others."
Therefore, an enlightened king examines laws and regulations and promulgates teachings and commands,
not acting out of personal interest to deceive the law,
nor defiling teachings to disgrace his mandate.
Thus, his ministers respect his words and uphold his prohibitions,
exhausting their hearts and fulfilling their duties.
This arises from clear methods and techniques and the employment of authority and power.
Now, technique as a way
is subtle and spiritual;
words are insufficient to describe it,

Having surplus,

Authority as a force

Being weighty,

Therefore, an enlightened ruler never displays his techniques to others nor lends his authority to those below.
Confucius said:

Thus, the sage "manifests it in benevolence,

"Spiritual and transforming it,

Only then does he achieve governance and accomplish his merits.
When achievements and works prove effective among the people,
and fine praises spread throughout the world,
then the ruler may be called enlightened,
and the minister may be called loyal.
This is what is meant by "enlightenment arises from understanding those below,
loyalty is achieved through reliance on those above,
when two people are of one mind,
their sharpness can cut through metal."
For a ruler,
there is no greater title than "enlightened";
for a minister,
there is no finer praise than "loyal."
These two virtues
are what rulers and ministers throughout history have jointly desired.
Yet, enlightenment rarely persists,
and loyalty is not found in one out of ten thousand—
not necessarily because they are foolish, dim-witted, and thus earn a bad reputation,
but because they seek it through the wrong means.
Now, enlightenment arises from understanding those below,
and loyalty is achieved through reliance on those above.
When two people are of one mind,
their sharpness can cut through metal.
Those who understand this
possess both praises.
The key lies in clearly wielding methods and techniques,

What is called "technique"

noble or humble, wise or foolish,
all will turn their hearts to it.

They abandoned their techniques and relinquished their authority,
neglecting themselves and relying on others.
Thus, the dukes and ministers gave no thought to loyalty,
and the hundred officials did not exert their full efforts.
The ruler was isolated and obscured above,
while the masses suffered injustice and chaos below.
Hence, the dynasty declined, was encroached upon, and never recovered.

their emotions,
their transformed customs,
their practices.

the branches.
Branches arise from the root,

If the essence of the heart is truly upright,
then treachery and deceit have nowhere to arise,
and wicked intentions have nothing to rely upon.

they mostly become pure, smooth, beautiful, strong, and long-lived;

then the people will mostly suffer eye ailments;
if there is something,
it is the agent of the Way.

then its vital force can arise;
there must be an agent,
then transformation and change can be accomplished.

spirits, ghosts, and the people,

mountains' weight is moved by it,
water's flow is cut off by it,
the sun and moon, though divine, are eclipsed by it,
stars and constellations, though ethereal, fall by it.

at night there is,
great winds overturning carriages and uprooting trees,
fierce lightning turning to ice,
hot springs boiling like soup,
unicorns, dragons, phoenixes,
locusts, caterpillars, and pests—

From this perspective,
the movement and influence of vital force
is indeed vast.
In its transformative workings,
what thing cannot it affect?
Therefore, the highest sages do not focus on governing the people's affairs but on governing the people's hearts.
Hence it is said:
"In hearing litigation,
I am like anyone else.
What is necessary is to cause there to be no litigation!"
"Guide them by virtue,
regulate them by ritual."
Strive to enrich their emotions and clarify principles, emphasizing righteousness.
When the people cherish and love one another, they harbor no intent to harm or injure;
when their actions consider righteousness, they have no treacherous or wicked hearts.

it is not due to the compulsion of laws,
nor the coercion of威严 punishments;
this is the result of transformation through teaching.

then the people will mostly suffer ear ailments;
if it has policies that injure the worthy,

The *Shī* says:
"Thick grow those roadside reeds;
let not sheep or cattle tread them.
Now budding, now forming stalks,
their leaves are lush and dense."
It also says:
"The kite soars to the heavens,
the fish leaps in the deep.
O joyous and affable nobleman,
why not cultivate men?"
Gōng Liú, with his profound virtue,
extended kindness even to plants and trees;
sheep, cattle, and the six domestic animals
were still moved by his virtue.
Reflecting within one's heart:
what one lacks oneself,
one does not demand of subordinates;
what one possesses oneself,
one does not ridicule in others.
Moved by one's own fondness for respect,
one therefore receives scholars with ritual;
moved by one's own fondness for affection,
one therefore treats people with kindness.
"Wishing to establish oneself, one establishes others;
wishing to succeed oneself, one helps others succeed."
Appreciating that others worry about me,
I therefore labor for them first;
disliking that others forget me,
I therefore constantly remember them.
Ordinary people are not like this:
judging others without being lenient toward oneself,
acting without considering one's own heart;
lacking something oneself yet demanding it of others,
possessing something oneself yet ridiculing others for it;
having no ritual oneself yet demanding respect from others,
having no kindness oneself yet demanding love from others;
in poverty and lowliness, blaming others for not worrying about me,
in wealth and honor, considering it right that I do not worry about others.
Conducting oneself thus,
it is difficult to be called benevolent.
What is called impartiality is:
internally harboring the kindness of the cuckoo,
externally holding a heart as straight as a whetstone or arrow;
judging scholars必定 based on their will and conduct,
praise and blame必定 verified by actual results;
not following vulgar customs and echoing mindlessly,
not chasing reputations and forming opinions based on hearsay;
if goodness is present,
not ridiculing poverty and lowliness;
if evil is present,
not sparing wealth and honor;
not flattering superiors while slighting inferiors,
not despising the old while revering the new.
Ordinary people are not like this:
internally biased toward wife and children,
externally misled and confused by close friends;
if pleased, they praise them;
if resentful, they slander them;
their fair judgments have no standard,
their criticism and praise have no verification;
recklessly currying favor with the noble to form cliques,
recklessly echoing voices to join in the pack's barking;
serving the wealthy and noble like slaves,
viewing the poor and lowly like hired laborers;
visiting the gates of the powerful a hundred times,
but not once the homes of the powerless.
Holding a heart like this,
it is difficult to be called righteous.
Therefore, whether the world is good or bad,
whether customs are shallow or deep,
all depend on the ruler.
The supreme sages harmonize virtuous energy to transform the people's hearts,
correct their outward demeanor to lead the masses,
thus enabling every household to be worthy of commendation—
Yáo and Shùn were such rulers.
The next level of rulers personally embody the Way and virtue, promote kindness and compassion,
beautify teachings and instructions, and uphold ritual and deference,

King Wén and King Wǔ were such rulers.
The next level of rulers clarify likes and dislikes and make laws and prohibitions evident,
balance rewards and punishments without favoritism or partiality,
thus enabling the people to avoid wickedness and pursue fairness and justice,
governing weakness and disorder to achieve strength and order—
the mid-dynasty restorations were such.

if one dwells in filth and indulges in passions,
neglects the people's affairs and hastens to wine and pleasure,
draws near to foolish youths and distances oneself from worthy talents,
favors flatterers and alienates the upright and honest,
heavily taxes to reward the undeserving,
capriciously expresses joy and anger to harm the innocent,

damage oneself and lose the state—
