The people of the world called them the Eight Paragons.
His descendant Jiāngyuán
stepped in a giant's footprint and gave birth to Jī Qì.
His physiognomy had a broad chin.
He became Yáo's Minister of Education,
and also oversaw sowing,
farming and planting excellent grains.
When Yáo encountered flood disasters,
he saved the myriad people.
Thus, Shùn appointed him as Hòujì.
Initially,
when the Lièshān clan possessed the world,
his son was named Zhù,
able to plant all grains,
so he was established as the Millet God,
and was sacrificed to from the Xià dynasty onward.
When Zhōu arose,
they replaced him with Qì,
and sacrifice to him to this day.
Tàirèn dreamed of a tall man moving her,
and gave birth to King Wén.
His physiognomy had four nipples.
He became the Earl of the West,
and rose at Qí.
He decided the dispute between Yú and Ruì and began to receive the Mandate.
King Wǔ had double teeth,
defeated Yīn and stopped the slaughter,
and completed the Way of Zhōu.
The Jī clan's other enfeoffments were numerous:
Guǎn, Cài, Chéng, Huò, Lǔ, Wèi, Máo, Dān, Gào, Yōng, Cáo, Téng, Bì, Yuán, Fēng, Xún,
were King Wén's descendants.
Yú, Jìn, Yīng, Hán,
were King Wǔ's descendants.
Fán, Jiǎng, Xíng, Máo, Zuò, Zhài,
were the Duke of Zhōu's descendants.
Zhōu, Shào, Guó, Wú, Suí, Bīn, Fāng, Áng, Xī, Pān, Yǎng, Huá, Hào, Gōng, Mì, Róng, Dān, Guō, Yáng, Páng, Guǎn, Táng, Hán, Yáng, Gū,
Luán, Gān, Línyú, Wáng shì,
all were of the Jī surname.
There was a divine dragon whose head emerged from Chángyáng,
impregnated Rèn Sì,
giving birth to the Red Emperor Kuíkuí.
His personal title was Yándì,
his era title was Shénnóng,
who succeeded the Fúxī clan.
His virtue was associated with the fire element,
thus he was the fire master and bore fire-related names.
Therefore, he carved wood to make plows,
and bent wood to create plowshares and hoes.
He established markets at midday,
attracting the people from all under heaven,
gathering the goods from all under heaven,
exchanging and then departing,
each obtaining what they needed.
His descendant Qìngdū,
united in marriage with a dragon,
gave birth to Yī Yáo.
He succeeded the Gāoxīn clan.
His eyebrows had eight colors.
His era was called Táng.
He created the music "Dà Zhāng".
He was the first to abdicate the throne.
King Wǔ conquered Yīn,
and enfeoffed his descendant at Zhù.
Hánshǐ swallowed a red pearl,
and it was foretold, "The jade flower gives birth to Hàn."
A dragon impregnated Nǚ'ǎo,
and Liú Jì arose.
A great lightning encircled the pivot, illuminating the wilderness,
impregnating Fúbǎo,
giving birth to the Yellow Emperor Xuānyuán.
He succeeded the Yándì clan.
His countenance was dragon-like,
his virtue was associated with the earth element.
He used clouds for reckoning,
thus he was the cloud master and bore cloud-related names.
He created the music "Xiánchí".
He was the first to institute clothing.
His descendant Wòdēng,
saw a great rainbow,
and through mental conception gave birth to Chónghuá Yú Shùn.
His eyes had double pupils.
He served Yáo,
and Yáo then abdicated the throne to him, saying:
"Approach, Shùn!
The celestial mandate rests upon your person.
Sincerely hold fast to the Mean.
If all within the four seas are reduced to poverty,
Heaven's favor will be forever ended."
Thus he received the mandate in the temple of the cultured ancestor.
His era was called Yǒuyú.
He created the music "Jiǔ Sháo".
He abdicated the throne to Yǔ.
King Wǔ conquered Yīn,
and enfeoffed Húgōng Guī Mǎn at Chén,
marrying him to the eldest daughter Dà Jī.
A great star like a rainbow,
descended and flowed to Huázhǔ,
Nǚjié dreamt of union,
giving birth to the White Emperor Zhì Qīngyáng.
His era title was Shàohào.
He succeeded the Xuānyuán clan,
and established his capital at Qūfù.
His virtue was associated with the metal element.
At his establishment,
a phoenix happened to arrive,
thus he used birds for reckoning.
The Fèngniǎo clan were the calendar rectifiers;
the Xuánniǎo clan were the regulators of the equinoxes;
the Bózhào clan were the regulators of the solstices;
the Qīngniǎo clan were the regulators of the beginnings;
the Dànniǎo clan were the regulators of the closings.
The Zhùjiū clan were the Ministers of the Masses;
the Jūjiū clan were the Ministers of War;
the Shījiū clan were the Ministers of Works;
the Shuǎngjiū clan were the Ministers of Crime;
the Gǔjiū clan were the Ministers of Affairs.
The five Jiū clans were those who gathered the people.
The five Zhì clans were the five directors of crafts,
improving tools and implements,
and equalizing the people.
Therefore, he created writing and tallies,
"so that the hundred officials could govern,
and the myriad people could be examined."
He had four talented sons,
named Zhòng,
named Gāi,
named Xiū,
named Xī,
who were truly capable in metal, wood, and water,
thus Zhòng became Gōumáng,
Gāi became Rùshōu,
Xiū and Xī became Xuánmíng.
They reverently attended to their duties,
never failing in their offices for generations,
and thus brought aid to Qióngsāng.
His descendant Xiūjì,
saw a shooting star,
and through mental conception gave birth to the White Emperor Wénmìng Róng Yǔ.
His ears had three perforations.
He served as Yáo's Minister of Works,
overseeing the leveling of water and land,
naming the mountains and rivers,
delineating the nine provinces,
and instituting the nine tributes.
When his work was completed,
he was bestowed a dark jade scepter,
to report his merit to Heaven.
Shùn then abdicated the throne,
commanding as Yáo's edict had,
and Yǔ then ascended the throne.
He created the music "Dà Xià".
His era was called Xiàhòu.
He passed the throne to his son Qǐ.
Qǐ's sons Tàikāng and Zhòngkāng succeeded in turn.
Five brothers,
all possessed of benighted virtue,
unfit for imperial affairs,
descended to the bend of the Luò River,
these were called the Five Guān.
His grandson Xiàng succeeded to the throne,
and the Way of Xià gradually declined.
Thereupon, Hòu Yì moved from Chú to Qióngshí,
and relying on the people of Xià, he supplanted the Xià government,
exterminating Xiàng.
His consort Hòu Mín was just pregnant,
escaped through a hole,
fled to Yǒuréng,
and gave birth to Shàokāng there.
He became the herdsman supervisor of Réng.
Yì, relying on his own archery skill,
did not attend to the people's affairs,
but indulged in hunting wild beasts;
he dismissed Wǔluó, Bóyīn, Xióngkūn, and Pángyǔ,
and employed Hánzhuó.
Zhuó was a slanderous son of the Báimíng clan.
The Báimíng clan detested him and cast him out.
Yí Yì took him in,
trusted him, and employed him,
making him his own minister.
Zhuó practiced flattery within,
and distributed bribes without,
deceiving the people,
and deluding Yì with hunting,
planting deceit and treachery,
to seize his state and family,
and all within and without submitted.
Yì still did not repent,
and as he was returning from the hunt,
his household retainers killed him and cooked him,
fed him to his son,
but his son could not bear to eat him,
and died at the Qióng Gate.
Mí fled to the Yǒugé clan.
Zhuó, using Yì's household, begot Ào and Yì,
relying on their slander, wickedness, deceit, and falsity,
and showing no virtue towards the people,
he sent Ào with an army,
to exterminate the Zhēnguàn and Zhēnxún clans,
settled Ào at Guō,
settled Yì at Gé,
and sent Jiāo to seek Shàokāng.
He fled to Yǒuyú,
and became their kitchen supervisor.
Yú Sī gave him two consorts in marriage,
and enfeoffed him at Lún,
where he had one square *chéng* of land,
and a company of five hundred men.
He was able to spread his virtue,
and begin his plans,
to gather the Xià multitude,
and comfort its officials.
Mí, from Yǒugé, gathered the remnants of the two states,
exterminated Zhuó,
and established Shàokāng.
He then sent Nǚ'ài to spy on Ào,
sent Hòu Zhù to lure Yì,
and thus exterminated Guō and Gé,
restored Yǔ's achievements,
sacrificed to Xià and matched Heaven,
not losing the old heritage.
After seventeen generations, Jié lost all under heaven.
King Wǔ conquered Yīn,
and enfeoffed his descendant at Qǐ,
or at Zēng.
He also enfeoffed the descendant of Shàohào at Qí.
Ào's talent and strength surpassed the masses,
but he relied on his courage and martial prowess and ultimately perished.
Therefore, Nángōng Kuò said:
"Yì excelled at archery,
Ào overturned boats,
yet neither met a natural death."
The Sì surname divided into clans:
Xiàhòu, Yǒuhù, Yǒunán, Zhēnxún, Gǔrǔ, Xīn, Bāo, Fèi, Gē, Míng, Zēng,
all were descendants of Yǔ.
The Yaoguang star was like the moon, pure white,
it moved Nǚshū in the secluded palace of Yōufáng,
and she gave birth to the Black Emperor Zhuānxū.
His physiognomy featured a fused spine.
His personal name was Gāoyáng,
his lineage name was Gònggōng.
He succeeded the Shàohào lineage.
His virtue corresponded to the Water phase,
he used water to mark things,
therefore he had a water-based administration and used water-related names.
Inheriting a period of Shàohào's decline,
the Jiǔlí tribes disrupted virtue,
so he ordered Zhòng and Lí to campaign, instruct, and subdue them.
He observed and calculated the motions of the sun and moon,
and the directions east, west, south, north.
He created the music "Wǔ Yīng".
He had eight talented sons:
Cāngshū, Tuíkǎi, Dǎoyǎn, Dàlín, Méngjiàng, Tíngjiān, Zhòngróng, Shūdá,
who were sagely, profound, broad, and deep,
enlightened, trustworthy, sincere, and honest,
the people of the world called them the Eight Kǎi.
The Gònggōng lineage had a son named Gōulóng,
who could level the nine regions of earth,
therefore he was called Hòutǔ (Lord of the Earth),
after death he became the Earth Spirit (Shè),
and the world sacrificed to him.
Jiǎndí swallowed a swallow's egg and gave birth to Qì,
who became Yáo's Minister of Education (Sītú),
his duty was to be close to the hundred surnames,
and harmonize the five relationships.
Fúdū saw white vapor piercing the moon,
his physiognomy featured two elbows.
His personal name was Tāng,
his lineage name was Yīn.
He brought about great peace.
Later it declined,
and then Wǔdīng was born.
Upon ascending the throne,
he remained silent, not speaking,
contemplating the Way for three years,
and dreamed of obtaining a worthy man to serve as his teacher.
He then sent people to seek, based on the dream image, in remote places throughout the four directions,
and found Fù Yuè,
who was at that time a convict laborer building at Fùyán.
He elevated him to Grand Duke,
and had him offer admonitions morning and evening.
Fearing he might be apprehensive or negligent,
he instructed him, saying:
"If I am metal,
I use you as my whetstone;
if I am crossing a great river,
I use you as my boat and oar;
if in times of great drought,
I use you as the soaking rain.
Open your heart,
and irrigate my mind.
If medicine does not cause dizziness,
the illness will not be cured;
if walking barefoot without looking at the ground,
the feet will be injured.
You must repeatedly cultivate me,
do not abandon me!"
Therefore he was able to achieve a restoration,
and was given the temple name Gāozōng.
By the time of Emperor Xīn, it perished,
and the world called him Zhòu.
King Wǔ enfeoffed Wēizǐ in Sòng,
and enfeoffed Jīzǐ in Cháoxiǎn.
The Zǐ surname divided into clans:
Yīn, Shí, Lái, Sòng, Lè, Xiāo, Kōngtóng, Běiduàn,
all were descendants of Tāng.
In ancient times, the sage kings observed the images in Qián and Kūn,
examined measures through spiritual understanding,
explored the coming and going of fate and calendrics,
scrutinized the virtue and achievements of the various lords,
and then bestowed surnames and designated clans,
thereby making virtue and merit manifest.
Tradition says that when the people's offices reached one hundred,
the sons and younger brothers of kings and dukes, for a thousand generations able to attend to their offices,
were then materially bestowed surnames,
this is called the hundred surnames.
Surnames have a full range of ten grades,
for the king this is called the thousand grades.
In ancient times, Yáo bestowed upon Qì the surname Zǐ,
bestowed upon Qì the surname Jī;
bestowed upon Yǔ the surname Sì,
the clan was called Yǒuxià;
Bóyí was Jiāng,
the clan was called Yǒulǚ.
Down to the Three Dynasties,
if an office had hereditary merit,
then there were official clans,
and it was the same for fiefs.
Later generations became insignificant,
and accordingly took these as surnames,
which then could not be changed.
Therefore, some transmitted the original surname,
some took clan names, fief names, or posthumous names,
some took names from states,
some took names from ranks,
some took names from offices,
some took names from courtesy names,
some took names from events,
some took names from dwellings,
some took names from aspirations.
As for the eras of the Five Emperors and Three Kings,
these are what are called appellations;
Wén, Wǔ, Zhāo, Jǐng, Chéng, Xuān, Dài, Huán,
these are what are called posthumous names;
Qí, Lǔ, Wú, Chǔ, Qín, Jìn, Yān, Zhào,
these are what are called states;
Wángshì, Hóushì, Wángsūn, Gōngsūn,
these are what are called ranks;
Sīmǎ, Sītú, Zhōngháng, Xiàjūn,
these are what are called offices;
Bóyǒu, Mèngsūn, Zǐfú, Shūzǐ,
these are what are called courtesy names;
Wūshì, Jiàngshì, Táoshì,
these are what are called occupations;
Dōngmén, Xīmén, Nángōng, Dōngguō, Běiguō,
these are what are called dwellings;
Sānwū, Wǔlù, Qīngniú, Báimǎ,
these are what are called aspirations;
All these surnames and clans,
emerge from affiliations and cannot be fully recorded.
The Marquis of Wèi destroyed Xíng,
Duke Zhāo married someone of the same surname,
it is said they were all of the same ancestor.
In recent antiquity,
this is not necessarily so.
The bestowal of surnames in ancient times,
in general can be followed,
but the rest is difficult.
The Zhōu house declined and weakened,
Wú and Chǔ usurped titles,
down through the Seven Warring States,
all called themselves kings.
Therefore, the surnames Wángshì, Wángsūnshì, Gōngsūnshì, and those from posthumous names and offices,
each state had its own,
with eighteen hundred states,
posthumous names and offices numbering in the tens of thousands,
so it was impossible for them to be the same.
As for the Sūn surname,
some are of the Wángsūn class,
some are of the various Sūn class,
therefore there are those with the same ancestor but different surnames,
and those with the same surname but different ancestors.
There are also mixtures and complexities,
changes and interminglings,
some follow the mother's surname,
some avoid enmity and grudges.
Determining surnames by pitch-pipes,
only sages could do it.
Now the people have been dispersed for a long time,
few can comprehend musical tones.
Heaven's Lord honors and rectifies their ancestors.
Therefore, I shall briefly record the prominent ones,
awaiting gentlemen to compare and adjust them.
Fúxī's surname was Fēng,
his descendants were enfeoffed in the four states of Rén, Sù, Xūqú, Zhuānyú,
they actually oversaw the sacrifices to Tàihào and Yǒujì,
and were also lords of Dōngméng.
Duke Xī of Lǔ's mother Chéngfēng,
was likely a daughter of Xūqú.
The Jì family wanted to attack Zhuānyú,
and Confucius criticized them.
Emperor Yán's descendants,
Sìyuè Bóyí,
served as Yáo's master of rites,
"settling the people through punishments,"
and was enfeoffed at Shēn and Lǚ.
His descendant gave birth to Shàng,
who served as King Wén's teacher,
conquered Yīn and was enfeoffed in Qí,
some were enfeoffed at Xǔ, Xiàng,
some at Jì,
some at Shēn.
The city of Shēn lies south of Nányáng, north of Wǎn, below Xù Mountain,
hence the Odes say:
"Diligent was the Earl of Shēn,
the king charged him with tasks,
at his city, at Xù,
a model for the southern states."
Thirty li west of Wǎn is Lǚ Wàng.
Xǔ is in Yǐngchuān,
present-day Xǔ County.
The Jiāng Róng dwelled between the Yī and Luò rivers,
Duke Huì of Jìn moved and settled them at Lùhún.
Zhōu, Bó, Gān, Xì, Lù, Yí,
and the Qí clans of Guó, Gāo, Xiāng, Xí, Shìqiáng, Dōngguō, Yōngmén, Zǐyǎ, Zǐwěi, Zǐxiāng, Zǐyuān, Zǐqián, Gōngqí, Hàngōng, Hè, Lú,
all bear the surname Jiāng.
The Yellow Emperor had twenty-five sons,
divided into twelve:
Jī, Yǒu, Qí, Jǐ, Téng, Diǎn, Rén, Jū, Lí, Jí, and Huányī.
During the Spring and Autumn period,
Jìn had Qí Xī,
who recommended his son and nominated his enemy,
renowned for loyalty and integrity.
The ruler of Jǔ bore the surname Jǐ.
At the rise of the Xià,
there was Rén Xī who served as Xià's chariot master,
enfeoffed at Xuē,
later moved to Pī,
his descendant Zhònghuī dwelled at Xuē,
serving as Tāng's left minister.
King Jì's consort Dàrén,
and Xiè, Zhāng, Chāng, Cǎi, Zhù, Jié, Quán, Bēi, Yù, Kuáng Dà,
all bore the surname Rén.
A woman of the Jí clan became Hòujì's principal consort,
nurturing the Zhou ancestors.
The Jí clan was enfeoffed at Yān,
and Duke Wén of Zhèng had a lowly concubine Yān Jí,
who dreamt a deity gave her an orchid, saying:
"I am Bótiáo,
your ancestor.
Hence this orchid, a fragrance of the state,
people wear and adore."
When Duke Wén saw Jí,
he gave her the orchid and favored her.
Jí recounted her dream,
and said:
"Your handmaid is untalented,
fortunate to bear a child;
if you doubt,
dare I present the orchid as proof?"
The duke said:
"Agreed."
Thus she bore Duke Mù.
Branches of the Jí clan
include Kàn, Yǐn, Cài, Guāng, Lǔ, Yōng, Duàn, and Mìxū.
By the Hàn dynasty,
Hédōng had Zhì Dū,
Rǔnán had Zhì Jūnzhāng,
whose surname pronunciation matched ancient Jí,
but written characters differed;
both were renowned in their time.
In the age of Shǎohào's decline,
the Jiǔlí disrupted virtue,
Zhuānxū inherited,
then ordered Nánzhèng Zhòng to oversee heaven and connect with spirits,
ordered Huǒzhèng Lí to oversee earth and connect with the people,
restoring the old norms,
preventing mutual encroachment and profanation,
this is called severing earth from heaven.
Now Lí was Zhuānxū's descendant Wú Huí.
He served as Huǒzhèng under Gāoxīn,
illuminating heaven's brilliance and earth's virtue,
shining across the four seas,
hence named Zhùróng.
Later, the Sānmiáo resumed the Jiǔlí's ways,
Yáo, succeeding Zhòng and Lí, not forgetting the old,
had Xībó restore order.
Thus the Zhònglí clan for generations ordered heaven and earth,
distinguishing their divisions,
through three dynasties,
and were enfeoffed at Chéng.
In the Zhou era,
they served as King Xuān's Grand Marshal,
the Odes praise "the king said to Yǐnshì,
commanded Earl Chéng Xiūfù."
Later they lost their office,
went to Jìn as Marshal,
Simǎ Qiān claimed descent from them.
Zhùróng's grandsons
divided into eight surnames:
Jǐ, Tū, Péng, Jiāng, Yún, Cáo, Sī, Mǐ.
Jǐ surname's descendant Liù Shū'ān,
his descendant named Dǒng Fù,
truly loved dragons,
could seek their desires to feed them,
many dragons returned to him.
He learned to tame dragons,
serving Emperor Shùn.
Granted surname Dǒng,
clan name Huànlóng,
enfeoffed at Zōngchuān.
Zōngyí, Péng surname's Shǐwéi,
both could tame dragons.
Huànlóng Páng, through loyal remonstrance,
was killed by Jié.
All descendants of Zhùróng's sons,
Jǐ surname's branches,
Kūnwú, Jí, Hù, Wēn, Dǒng.
Tū surname's Zōngyí, Huànlóng,
were extinguished by Xià.
Péng surname's Péngzǔ, Shǐwéi, Zhūjī,
were extinguished by Shāng.
Jiāng surname's Huìrén,
were extinguished by Zhōu.
Yún surname's descendants enfeoffed at Yān, Huì, Lù, Bīyáng.
Yān took Zhòngrén as wife,
greedy, covetous, and stingy,
despised worthies and neglected ability,
thus the state perished.
Huì lay between the Hé and Yī rivers,
its ruler arrogant, greedy, miserly,
reducing ranks and cutting stipends,
ministers humble and yielding,
high and low not interacting.
The poet grieved,
thus composed "Lamb Fur," lamenting its pain and sorrow,
"Not the Wind," hoping the ruler would first teach.
Huì Zhòng did not awaken,
the Zhòng clan attacked,
high and low could not command each other,
prohibitions and punishments unenforced,
thus met destruction,
Lù's ruler Yīng'ér,
married Duke Chéng of Jìn's elder sister as wife,
Fēng Shū governed and oppressed her.
Bó Zōng of Jìn angered,
thus attacked and extinguished Lù.
Xún Yīng Wǔzǐ attacked and extinguished Bīyáng.
Cáo surname enfeoffed at Zhū;
Zhū Yánzǐ's branch,
separated as Xiǎozhū,
both extinguished by Chǔ.
Mǐ surname's descendant Xióng Yán,
King Chéng enfeoffed him in Chǔ,
called Yù Xióng,
also named Yùzǐ.
He bore four sons,
Bó Shuāng, Zhòng Xuě, Shū Xióng, Jì Xún.
Xún succeeded as Xíngzǐ,
some enfeoffed at Kuí,
some at Yuè.
The ruler of Kuí did not sacrifice to Zhùróng and Yù Xióng,
Chǔ attacked and extinguished.

The royal clan includes Chǔjì, Lièzōng, Dòuqiáng, Liángchén, Qí, Mén, Hóu, Jìróng, Zhòngxióng, Zǐjì, Yáng, Wúgōu, Wěi, Shàn, Yáng, Zhāo, Jǐng, Yán, Yīngqí, Lái, Láixiān, Jí, Shēn, Diào, Shěn, Hè, Jiǎn, Jíbái, Wǔ, Shěnjiān, Yútuī, Gōngjiàn, Zǐnán, Zǐgēng, Zǐwǔ, Zǐxī, Wángsūn, Tiángōng, Shūjiān, Lǔyáng, Hēigōng,
all bear surname Mǐ.
Chǔjì was Prince Áo's great-grandson.
Fén Mào bore Wěi Zhāng,
Prince Wúgōu.
Prime Minister Sūnshū Áo was Wěi Zhāng's son.
Left Marshal Wù was King Zhuāng's great-grandson.
Lord of Yè Zhūliáng was Wù's third younger brother.
Chǔ senior official Shēn Wúwèi,
also bore surname Wén.
Initially,
Zhòu had the Yǒusū clan with Dájǐ, leading to Yīn's fall.
During King Wǔ of Zhōu,
Yǒusū Fènshēng served as Minister of Justice and was enfeoffed at Wēn.
Later, Luòyì had Sū Qín.
In Gāoyáng's time, there were eight talented sons,
Cāngshū, Tuíkǎi, Dǎoyǎn, Dàlín, Méngjiàng, Tíngjiān, Zhòngróng, Shūdá,
the world called them the Eight Kǎi.
Their descendant Gāoyáo
served Shùn.
Shùn said:
"Gāoyáo!
The barbarians disrupt Xià,
bandits and traitors abound,
you shall be Minister of Justice."
His son Bóyì,
could harmonize the hundred clans to assist Shùn and Yǔ,
taming birds and beasts,
Shùn granted him the surname Yíng.
Later there was Zhòng Yǎn,
who had a bird's body and human speech,
and served as charioteer for the Great Emperor Wù of Xià.
His descendant was Fèi Zhòng,
who begot È Lái and Jì Shèng.
When King Wǔ attacked Zhòu,
he also killed È Lái.
The descendant of Jì Shèng was Zào Fǔ,
who served King Mù of Zhōu as an excellent charioteer.
King Mù traveled to the Western Sea and forgot to return,
whereupon Xú Yǎn rebelled,
and Zào Fǔ drove the chariot,
covering a thousand li in a single day,
to subdue him.
The king enfeoffed Zào Fǔ at Zhàochéng,
and he took this as his clan name.
Later, they lost their position,
until Zhào Sù,
who served as a high minister of Jìn,
and after eleven generations they became ranked as marquises,
after five generations they became King Wǔlíng,
and after five more generations Zhào perished.
The clans of Gōngshū, Hándān, Zīrǔ, Yīngqí, Lóujì, Lú, and Yuán,
were all of the Zhào Yíng surname.
The descendant of È Lái was Fēi Zǐ,
who was skilled at animal husbandry,
and King Xiào of Zhōu enfeoffed him at Qín,
generations governing the land as Commandant of the Western Frontier,
which was the Qín settlement at Qiān.
Later they ranked among the feudal lords,
after five generations they claimed the title of king,
and after six generations the First Emperor was born in Hándān,
hence he was called Zhào Zhèng.
As for Liáng, Gě, Jiāng, Huáng, Xú, Jǔ, Liǎo, Lù, and Yīng,
they were all descendants of Gāo Yáo.
Zhōnglí, Yùnyǎn, Tùqiú, Xúnliáng, Xiūyú,
Báizhí, Fēilián, Mìrú, Dōngguàn, Liáng, Shí, Bái, Bā, Gōngbāgōngbā, Tán, Fù, and Pú,
were all of the Yíng surname.
The descendant of Emperor Yáo was the Táotáng clan.
Later there was Liú Lěi,
who could rear dragons,
and Kǒng Jiǎ bestowed upon him the surname Yùlóng,
to replace the descendants of Shǐwéi.
By the Zhōu dynasty they were the Tángdù clan.
When Zhōu declined,
there was Xí Shūzǐ who fled the troubles of Zhōu to the state of Jìn,
and begot Zǐyú,
who served as Chief Judge,
and rectified the court,
so that the court had no idle officials;
he served as Minister of Works,
and rectified the state,
so that the state suffered no defeats;
thus his clan was called Minister of Works;
he received the fief of Suí,
so his clan was called the Suí clan.
The grandson of Shì Wěi was Huì,
who assisted Dukes Wén and Xiāng,
and was without fault among the feudal lords;
he served as a minister,
and assisted Dukes Chéng and Jǐng,
so that the army had no failed campaigns;
he served as Commander of Chéng,
resided at Fù,
rectified penal laws,
compiled instructional codes,
so that the state had no treacherous people,
and the robbers of Jìn fled to Qín.
Thereupon the Marquis of Jìn requested ceremonial robes and headgear from the king,
and the king commanded Suí Huì to be a minister,
thus he received Fàn,
and was posthumously titled Wǔzǐ.
Wǔzǐ's son Wén,
concluded a covenant between Jìn and Jīng,
subdued the fraternal states,
so that there were no rifts,
thus he received Xún and Lì.
From this, the descendants of Emperor Yáo

included the clans of Táotáng, Liú, Yùlóng, Tángdù, Xí, Shì, Jì, Sīkōng, Suí, Fàn, Xún, Lì, Zhì, Jì, Gǔ, Qiáng, Rǎo, Lí, and Fù. The Chǔ Prime Minister Jiàn once asked Wénzǐ about the virtue of Fàn Wǔzǐ,
and Wénzǐ replied:
"The affairs of the master's household are well-ordered,
his words in Jìn,
are exhaustive and without selfishness,
his invocators and scribes present sincerity without shame,
his household affairs are without suspicion,
and his invocators and scribes do not pray for favors."
Jiàn returned,
and reported this,
and King Kāng said:
"Spirits and men bear no resentment,
it is fitting that the master assisted five rulers as their right-hand man,
and became the leader of the feudal lords."
Thus the Liú clan from Táng down to Hàn,
their virtue was illustrious in the world,
and none matched the flourishing of Fàn Huì.
This too is the achievement of cultivating oneself to bring peace to others.
When King Wǔ conquered Yīn,
he enfeoffed the descendant of Emperor Yáo at Zhù.
Emperor Shùn's surname was Yú,
and also Yáo,
and he dwelled at Guī.
When King Wǔ conquered Yīn,
he enfeoffed Guī Mǎn at Chén,
who was Duke Hú.
The clans of Chén Yuán, Yǎo, Xián, Qìng, Xià, Zōng, Lái, Yí, Sītú, and Sīchéng,
were all of the Guī surname.
Duke Lì's younger son Wán fled to Qí,
and Duke Huán was pleased with him,
appointing him as Minister of Works.
His descendants greatly won the people's hearts,
and eventually seized the rulership and established themselves,
who was King Wēi,
and after five generations they perished.
The people of Qí called Chén Tián.
Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn relocated the various Tián clans to Guānzhōng,
and there were the clans from First to Eighth.
Chancellor Tián Qiānqiū, Sīzhí Tián Rén,
and Dùyáng Tián Xiān, Dàng Tián Xiān,
were all descendants of Chén.
Emperor Wǔ bestowed upon Qiānqiū the privilege of riding a small carriage into the palace,
so the world called him Chancellor Chē.
And Wáng Mǎng claimed to be a descendant of Tián Ān,
and because of the Wáng family he changed his surname accordingly.
Wáng Mǎng's practice of deceit,
was indeed in the manner of Tián Cháng.
The branches of Jìng Zhòng
included the clans of Pí, Zhàn, Jǔ, Yǔ, Xiàn, Zǐ, Yāng, Wú, Fāng, Gāo, Máng, and Qín.
The eldest son of Dì Yǐ was Wēizǐ Kāi,
the elder half-brother of Zhòu.
King Wǔ enfeoffed him at Sòng,
which is present-day Suīyáng.

The Sòng clans of Kǒng, Zhùqí, Hánxiàn, Jìlǎonán, Jùchén, Jīng, Shìfù, Huángfǔ, Huá, Yú, and Dǒng, Ài, Suì, Jiūyí, Zhōngyě, Yuèjiāo, Wán, Huái, Bùdì, Jì, Niú, Sīchéng, Gǎng, Jìn, Zhǐ, Cháo, Bó, Yòuguī, Sānyú, Wángfū, Yí, Zhēng, Zhèng, Mùyí, Lín, Zāng, Huǐ, Shā, Hēi, Wéiguī, Jì, Jù, Zhuān, Jǐ, Chéng, Biān, Róng, Mǎi, Wěi, Huán, Dài, Xiàng, and Sīmǎ,
were all of the Zǐ surname.
Duke Mǐn's son Fúfù Hé begot Sòngfù,
Sòngfù begot Shìzǐ,
Shìzǐ begot Zhèng Kǎofù,
Zhèng Kǎofù begot Kǒngfù Jiā;
Kǒngfù Jiā begot Zǐ Mù Jīnfù;
Mù Jīnfù was demoted to a scholar-official,
so it is said he was extinguished in Sòng.
Jīnfù begot Qífù,
Qífù begot Fáng Shū;
Fáng Shū was pressured by the Huá clan,
and fled to Lǔ,
becoming the magistrate of Fáng,
so he was called Fáng Shū.
Fáng Shū begot Bó Xià,
Bó Xià begot Shūliáng Hé,
who was the magistrate of Zōu,
so he was called Zōu Shū Hé,
and he begot Confucius.
The crown prince Jìn of King Líng of Zhōu,
from a young age possessed accomplished virtue,
was intelligent and broadly knowledgeable,
gentle, respectful, sincere, and quick-witted.
The Gǔ and Luò rivers clashed,
threatening to destroy the royal palace,
and the king wished to dam them.
Crown Prince Jìn remonstrated,
believing it would not accord with the will of Heaven,
and that it would be better to improve governance.
Duke Píng of Jìn sent Shū Yù on a diplomatic mission to Zhōu,
where he met the crown prince.
Engaging him in conversation,
after five exchanges he was at a loss three times,
and withdrew hesitantly.
Returning, he reported to Duke Píng:
"Crown Prince Jìn is only fifteen years of age,
yet I, Yù, am unable to converse with him.
I beg you, my lord, to serve him."
Duke Píng dispatched Shī Kuàng to see Crown Prince Jìn.
The crown prince spoke with him,
and Shī Kuàng was won over by his virtue,
forming a deep bond.
The prince then asked Kuàng:
"I have heard the Grand Master can know the length of a person's years."
Shī Kuàng replied:
"Your complexion is red and white,
your voice clear and strained,
the fire complexion does not signify longevity."
Jìn said:
"Indeed.
Three years from now I will ascend as a guest of the Emperor.
Be careful not to speak of this,
or calamity will befall you."
Three years later, the crown prince died.
Confucius, hearing of it, said:
"Alas!
He killed our lord."
People of the time, because he foreknew the time of his departure,
spread tales calling him Prince Qiáo the Immortal.
After his ascension to immortality,
his descendants fled the troubles of Zhōu to Jìn,
settling in Píngyáng,
and consequently took the surname Wáng.
Their descendants in later generations all delighted in the arts of nurturing life and immortality.
Among the ducal clans of Lǔ,

were the Jiǎo, Hòu, Zhòng, Zāng, Shī, Mèng, Zhòngsūn, Fú, Gōngshān, Nángōng, Shūsūn, Shūzhòng, Zǐwǒ, Zǐshì, Jì, Gōngchú, Gōngwū, Gōngzhī, Zǐgān, Huá, Zǐyán, Zǐqū, Zǐyǎ, Zǐyáng, Dōngmén, Gōngxī, Gōngshí, Shū, Zǐjiā, Róng, Zhǎn, and Yǐ clans,
all of whom were Jī surname from Lǔ.
Among the ducal clans of Wèi,
the Shí, Shìshū, Sūn, Nìng, Zǐqí, Sītú, Gōngwén, Xīguī, Gōngshū, Gōngnán, Gōngshàng, Gōngmèng, and Jiāngzhě clans,
also often held power and favor,
serving as high ministers.
As for Liúhóu Zhāng Liáng,
he was of the Hán ducal clan, Jī surname.
When Qín Shǐhuáng destroyed Hán,
Liáng's younger brother died and was not buried.
Liáng dispersed his family wealth of ten million,
to seek vengeance for Hán,
attacking Shǐhuáng at Bólàngshā,
but mistakenly struck the auxiliary carriage.
Qín's search for the culprit was urgent,
so Liáng changed his surname to Zhāng,
and hid in Xiàpī.
There he encountered the divine man Huángshí Gōng,
who bestowed upon him military texts.
When Péigōng rose in rebellion,
Liáng went and joined him.
Péigōng sent him with Hán Xìn to conquer and pacify the Hán territory,
establishing Héngyángjūn Chéng as King of Hán,
and appointed Liáng as Hán Xìndū.
Xìndū means Sītú.
Common pronunciation being inaccurate,
it was called Xìndū,
or sometimes Shēntú,
or Shèngtú,
but its origin is the single term Sītú.
Later compilers of records did not know the reason for "Xìndū",
and forced a mistaken interpretation,
thinking it meant acting as king's proxy in Xìndū.
All descendants of Huán Shū,
included the Hán, Yán, Yīng, Huòyú, Gōngzú, and Zhāng clans,
all these are later Jī surname descendants of Hán.
Formerly, King Xuān of Zhōu also had a Marquis of Hán,
whose state was near Yān.
Thus the *Shī* says:
"Vast is that Hán city,
completed by the Yān army."
Later, Hán Xī also had the surname Hán.
He was attacked by Wèi Mǎn,
and moved to dwell within the sea.
Bì Gōnggāo shared the same surname as the Zhōu,
and was enfeoffed at Bì,
taking it as his clan name.
When the Duke of Zhōu passed away,
Gāo succeeded to his position.
Later, his descendants lost their position,
becoming commoners.
When Bì Wàn assisted Duke Xiàn of Jìn,
in the sixteenth year, he had Zhào Sù drive the war chariot,
with Bì Wàn as the right-hand man,
and they destroyed Gěng and Wèi, enfeoffing Wàn,
which is present-day Héběi county.
Wèi Kē also took the clan name Línghú.
From Wàn, after nine generations came Wèi Wénhóu.
Wénhóu's grandson Yīng became King Huì of Wèi,
and after five generations it perished.
Bì Yáng's grandson Yù Ràng
served Zhì Bó.
Zhì Bó treated him as a man of exceptional talent from the state,
and Yù Ràng also repaid Zhì Bó with gratitude for being recognized,
the world recorded his righteousness.
The Wèi, Línghú, Bùyǔ, Yèdàfū, Bóxià, and Wèiqiáng clans,
and the Yù clan, all were originally the Bì clan,
fundamentally of Jī surname.
King Lì of Zhōu's son Yǒu was enfeoffed at Zhèng.
The descendants of Zhèng Gōngshū
became the Gōngwén clan.
The Xuān, Jūn, Zǐqiáng, Qiángliáng, Juǎn, Huì, Yǎ, Kǒng, Zhàoyáng, Tiánzhāng, Gū, Wángsūn, Shǐguī, Qiāng, Qiāngxiàn, and Suì clans,
all were Jī surname from Wèi.
Among the ducal clans of Jìn, the Xì clan
also branched to become the Lǚ,
Xì Ruì also took his fief's name to become the Jì clan.
Later there was Lǚ Qí,
styled Jū Bó.
Xì Chōu's estate was at Kǔ,
styled Kǔchéng Shū;
Xì Zhì's estate was at Wēn,
styled Wēn Jì,
each taking these as their clan names.
Among the branches of the Xì clan,
were the Zhōu and Qí clans.
Bó Zōng was killed for his forthrightness,
his son Zhōu Lí fled to Chǔ.
Also, because Xì Wǎn was upright yet harmonious,
he was envied by Zǐ Cháng,
and was executed.
His son Pǐ fled to Wú and became Grand Steward.
Having learned from the conduct of his ancestors and father, who still met disaster despite being upright,
he became flattering and sycophantic, leading to Wú's demise.
All branches of the Xì clan
included the Jì, Lǚ, Kǔchéng, Wēn, and Bó clans;
Jìnghóu's grandson Luán Bīn,
and the Fù, Yóu, Jiǎ, Hú, Yángshé, Jìsù, and Jí clans,
and Duke Xiāng's grandson Sūn Yǎn,
all were Jī surname from Jìn.
Duke Mù of Jìn begot Huán Shū.
Huán Shū begot Hán Wàn,
who served as a senior official of Jìn.
After ten generations came Hán Wǔhóu.
After five generations came King Huì of Hán,
and after five more generations the state perished.
A collateral descendant of King Xiāng, Xìn,
was commonly called Hán Xìndū.
Emperor Gāozǔ considered Xìn a descendant of the Hán kings,
and made him King of Hán.
Later he was moved to be King of Dài,
was attacked by the Xiōngnú,
and surrendered himself.
Hàn sent General Chái to attack him,
and Xìn was beheaded at Cānhé.
Xìn's wife and children fled into Xiōngnú territory.
By the time of Emperor Jǐng,
Xìn's son Tuídāng and grandson Chì came and surrendered.
Hàn enfeoffed Tuídāng as Marquis of Gōnggāo,
and Chì as Marquis of Xiāngchéng.
As for Hán Yān,
during Emperor Wǔ's time he served as Palace Attendant,
enjoying unparalleled honor and favor.
Àndàohóu Hán Yuè,
and former General Hán Zēng,
all were prominent in Hàn.
Their descendants each followed the reigning emperors and were settled in Yánglíng, Màolíng, and Dùlíng.
And those of the Hán clan in Hànyáng, Jīnchéng, and other places,
are all their descendants.
Xìn's descendants who remained in Xiōngnú territory.
The Sì, Fēng, Yóu, Guó, Rán, Kǒng, Yǔ, Liáng, and Dàjì clans.
The ancestors of these ten clans
were sons of Duke Mù,
each taking their courtesy names as surnames.
And the Bóyǒu, Mǎshī, and Chǔshī clans,
all were Jī surname from Zhèng.
Tàibó ruled Wú,
dressed in proper robes with hanging garments,
governing with Zhōu rituals.
Zhòngyōng succeeded him,
cut his hair and tattooed his body,
using nakedness as adornment.
King Wǔ conquered Yīn,
and enfeoffed their descendants in Wú,
granting great gifts to Northern Wú.
Jì Zhá dwelled in Yánzhōulái,
hence his clan name was Yánlíng Jìzǐ.
Hélǘ's brother Fūgài Wáng fled to Chǔ's Tángxī,
and took it as his clan name.
All these were of Jī surname.
In the state of Zhèng, among the senior officials there was Féng Jiǎnzǐ.
Later, in the state of Hán, there was Féng Tíng,
who served as the governor of Shàngdǎng.
He shifted disaster onto Zhào,
leading to the Chángpíng catastrophe.
In Qín, there was the general Féng Jié,
who was executed along with Lǐ Sī.
When Hàn rose,
there was Féng Táng,
who discussed generals and commanders with Emperor Wén.
Later there was Féng Fèngshì,
a man of Shàngdǎng,
who reached the position of general.
His daughter became a Zhāoyí of Emperor Yuán,
and consequently the family settled in the capital.
His grandson, Yǎn,
styled Jìngtōng,
was devoted to learning and valued righteousness.
The various Confucian scholars praised him as "Féng Jìngtōng, of harmonious virtue."
He authored several tens of essays,
and Emperor Zhāng of Hàn cherished and esteemed his writings.
The Jìn senior official Xún Xī served Duke Xiàn.
Later generations commanded the central army,
hence the clan name Zhōngháng.
They were enfeoffed at Zhì.
Zhì Guǒ advised Earl Zhì but was not heeded,
so he separately registered his lineage with the Grand Scribe as the Fǔ clan.
The Jìn senior official Sūn Bó Yǎn was in charge of the archives and records,
hence the surname Jí.
Xīn Yǒu had two sons who supervised them,
hence the clan name Dǒng.
The *Book of Songs* praises King Xuān,
first mentioning "Zhāng Zhòng, filial and fraternal."
By the Spring and Autumn period,
Sòng had Zhāng Báimiè.
Only the Jìn figures Zhāng Hóu and Zhāng Lǎo
were truly from a great family.
Zhāng Mèngtán served as chancellor to Zhào Xiāngzǐ to destroy Earl Zhì,
then fled from rewards for his merit,
farming at Huàn Mountain.
Later, Wèi had Zhāng Yí and Zhāng Chǒu.
By Hàn times,
the Zhāng surname proliferated.
The King of Chángshān, Zhāng Ěr,
was from Liáng.
Chancellor Zhāng Cāng
was from Yángwǔ.
The Marquis of Dōngyáng, Zhāng Xiàngrú.
The Imperial Secretary Zhāng Tāng
augmented and established laws and ordinances,
to guard against wickedness and evil,
benefiting the people.
He also liked recommending worthy and eminent scholars,
thus receiving blessings and protection.
His son Ānshì became General of Chariots and Cavalry,
enfeoffed as Marquis of Fùpíng.
He was sincere, benevolent, frugal, and restrained,
cautious in wielding power and fond of secret virtue.
Therefore, his descendants flourished,
generations having worthy heirs.
He was further enfeoffed as Marquis of Wǔshǐ.
Though encountering the Wáng Mǎng turmoil,
their enjoyment of the state did not cease.
The family altogether produced four dukes,
generations renowned for loyalty, filial piety, righteous conduct, and principle.
Earlier there was Chancellor Zhāng Yǔ,
Imperial Secretary Zhāng Zhōng;
later there was Grand Commandant Zhāng Pú,
a man of Rǔnán,
and Grand Tutor Zhāng Yǔ,
a man of the state of Zhào.
In the capital districts, villages, and neighborhoods,
there was none without Zhāngs.
In Xièyi of Hédōng, there was a Zhāngchéng,
and there was a Western Zhāngchéng.
Could these be the origins of the Jìn Zhāng ancestors?
The Yǎn surname includes Shūyōng, Shūjiū, Shūlóng, Shūgòng, Zhǐlóng, Lí, Yín, Shēn, Huì, Liù, Yuàn, Fěi, and Gāoguó.
The Qìng surname includes Fán, Yǐn, and Luò.
The Màn surname includes Dèng and Yōu.
The Guī surname includes Hú, Yǒu, and Hé.
The Zhēn surname includes Huá and Qí.
The Jǐ surname includes Qī and Shū.
The Yù surname includes Shǔ, Fān, and Tāng.
The Wéi surname includes Ráo, Rǎng, and Chà.
The Wěi surname includes the Chìdí; the Gèng surname includes the Báidí.
These are all highly auspicious surnames.
In Qí there was Bào Shū,
generations being high ministers and senior officials.
In Jìn there was Bào Guǐ.
In Hàn there was Bào Xuān,
generations loyal and upright,
a famous Hàn minister.
In Hàn, Lì Shēng served as an envoy,
his younger brother Shāng as a general.
Now the various Lìs of Gāoyáng are a prominent surname.
In antiquity, Zhòngshānfǔ also had the surname Fán,
posthumously titled Mùzhòng,
enfeoffed in Nányáng.
Nányáng is in present-day Hénèi.
Later there was Fán Qīngzǐ.
The Màn surname was enfeoffed at Dèng,
later taking it as their clan name.
North of Dèng County in Nányáng and north of Shàngcài there is an ancient Dèng city.
North of Xīncài there is an ancient Dèng city.
During the Spring and Autumn period,
King Wén of Chǔ destroyed Dèng.
By Hàn times, there were Dèng Tōng and Dèng Guǎng.
In Later Hàn, Dèng Yǔ of Xīnyě,
for his paramount merit in assisting the founding, was enfeoffed as Marquis of Gāomì.
The Grand Empress Dowager, his granddaughter, was by nature compassionate, benevolent, stern, and clear-sighted.
She restrained the various families from grasping power.
The capital was pure and tranquil,
as if there were no powerful relatives;
she diligently pondered and worried for the people,
day and night without respite.
Therefore, though encountering Qiāng rebellions,
great floods, famine, and scarcity,
she was able to restore things,
bringing order, peace, and abundant harvests.
After the Grand Empress Dowager passed away,
a host of villains conspired together,
competing to add slander and defamation,
destroying the Dèng clan,
to the grief of all under heaven.
The maternal family of Duke Zhāo of Lǔ had the surname Guī.
In Hàn there was Wěi Xiāo Jìmèng.
Duǎn is the same as the Quǎnróng clan.
Their ancestors originally descended from the Yellow Emperor.
As for the Xú, Xiāo, Suǒ, Chángsháo, Táo, Pó, Qí, Jī, Fán, and Tú clans,
these are all old surnames from the Yīn dynasty.
When Hàn rose,
Chancellor of State Xiāo Hé was enfeoffed as Marquis of Cuó.
He was originally from Pèi;
the Xiāos of present-day Chánglíng are his descendants.
Former General Xiāo Wàngzhī;
the Xiāos of Dōnghǎi and Dùlíng are his descendants.
The Imperial Secretary included Fán Yánshòu,
a man of Xiāngyáng in Nánjùn.
The Fáns of Dùlíng and Xīnfēng are his descendants.
The Zhōu, Shào, Bì, Róng, Shàn, Yǐn, Liú, Fù, Gǒng, and Cháng clans,
these were all ducal and ministerial families of the Zhōu royal house for generations.
Zhōu and Shào:
these were the secondary sons of the Duke of Zhōu and the Duke of Shào,
who received the fiefs of the two dukes,
serving as chief officials.
Thus, generations of Dukes of Zhōu and Dukes of Shào continued without end.
Yǐn was originally an official title,
like Sòng having a Grand Preceptor,
and Chǔ having a Lìngyǐn and Zuǒyǐn.
Yǐn Jìfǔ assisted King Xuān with great achievements.
The *Book of Songs* says:
"The Grand Preceptor of the Yǐn clan,
is the foundation of Zhōu."
Duke Mù of Shàn, Duke Xiāng, Duke Qǐng, Duke Jìng—
generations possessed illustrious virtue,
talent next to that of sages.
Therefore, Shū Xiàng praised them, saying they would surely flourish abundantly in the future.
Kǔchéng is a city name,
northeast of the salt ponds.
Later people writing it sometimes wrote it as "Kū."
People of Qí hearing its pronunciation,
then wrote it as "Kùchéng."
People of Dūnhúang seeing the character,
called it "Chēchéng."
Those in Hànyáng,
disliking the characters "Kū" and "Kǔ,"
then changed the writing to "Gǔchéngshì."
Tángxī is the name of a valley,
in Xīpíng of Rǔnán.
Yǔ, with the courtesy name Zǐqǐ—
Qǐ is the character for 'to open.'
Earlier people mistakenly wrote Tángxī as "Qǐ,"
later people altered it,
and then again wrote it as "Kāi."
The ancient figures Qīdiāo Kāi and Gōngyě Cháng—
earlier people wrote "diāo" with the component Yì,
abbreviated it to "Zhōu,"
and writing "yě" further mistakenly as "gǔ,"
later people again transmitted it as "Gǔ,"
or further divided it into the Gǔ, Chéng, Táng, Kāi, Gōng, Yě, Qī, and Zhōu clans.
These several clans
all share the same origin but differ in the end.
Generally, the separation, combination, change, and division of surnames
certainly have many such examples.
One can infer from this case,
but it is difficult to record them all exhaustively.
The Book of Changes says:
"The nobleman distinguishes things by grouping them into categories,"
"accumulates virtue by learning extensively from the words and deeds of the past,"
"studies to accumulate knowledge,
and inquires to distinguish clearly."
Therefore, I have briefly examined historical records,
selected from the classics,
based on the states and territories,
and with clear evidence,
to praise the descendants of sages and worthies,
to arrange the ancestors of various clans,
to explain the origins of surnames,
and to compose these two chapters with this intention,
to present to later worthies for their consideration today.
To be born in the present age,
it is noble to achieve great accomplishments;
the highest is to establish virtue,
the next is to establish words.
If one is mediocre and lacking in talent,
yet first assumes an official position based on superficial ability,
without ever having served in such duties,
there is no way to demonstrate merit.
In my heart, I am often moved,
so I take up the brush to record a few passages,
using words to express my humble feelings,
merely to ensure they are not forgotten.
Though grass and firewood gatherers are lowly,
even the ancient sages consulted them.
I have drafted an account of former worthies,
in thirty-six chapters,
to continue the teachings of the past,
following Zuǒ Qiūmíng's Five Classics.
The legacy of the ancient sages
offers no greater instruction.
Be broad in learning and extensive in knowledge;
when in doubt, think and inquire.
Wisdom is achieved through clarity,
virtue and righteousness are established through effort.
The Master loved learning,
"and never tired of teaching others."
Therefore, I present "In Praise of Learning" as the first chapter.
In all scholarly pursuits,
it is noble to focus on the root and disregard the trivial.
Great men do not seek superficiality;
gentlemen devote themselves to substance.
Though rituals serve as introductions,
they must be accompanied by sincerity.
The customs of the time chase after trivialities,
fearing the destruction of true principles.
Therefore, I present "Devotion to the Root" as the second chapter.
All people know virtue,
yet are often blinded by profit.
They act corruptly while seeking honor,
like covering one's head with a basin and hoping to see the sky.
"The benevolent do not amass wealth;
the wealthy are not benevolent."
To cultivate virtue and conduct,
one must be cautious of its source.
Therefore, I present "Restraining Profit" as the third chapter.
The world does not understand proper judgment,
treating common soldiers as transformed,
without inquiring into their aspirations and conduct,
only recording official ranks and titles.
Wealth and honor gained unrighteously
are what Confucius despised.
Grieving over the decline of customs,
I have thus followed the teachings of the sages from afar.
Therefore, I present "On Honor" as the fourth chapter.
What the worthy suffer,
and what the envious worry about,
is all jealousy toward those superior to themselves,
regarding it as deep resentment.
Sometimes due to minor faults,
sometimes fabricating accusations out of thin air.
It pains me that rulers do not discern this,
but believe slanderous words.
Therefore, I present "The Difficulties of the Worthy" as the fifth chapter.
To trace the origins of clarity,
and describe the birth of darkness,
the failures caused by rejecting advice,
and the formation of calamity and chaos.
Those in power
all desire to monopolize the ruler,
blocking worthy scholars,
to seize sovereign authority.
Therefore, I present "Clarity and Darkness" as the sixth chapter.
Looking up to the former kings,
how they achieved great peace,
examining achievements to promote or demote,
as recorded in the Five Classics.
Rewards and punishments in substance,
not based on empty reputation.
To clarify virtuous words in advance,
how can one not inquire in the court?
Therefore, I present "Examining Achievements" as the seventh chapter.
When rulers select scholars,
they all seek the worthy and capable.
Yet various offices recommend,
competing to advance inferior talents.
"If they hate those who exploit,"
what official can govern well?
Buying medicine but getting a wild goose,
it is hard to act as a physician.
Therefore, I present "Longing for the Worthy" as the eighth chapter.
To trace the origins of heaven and humanity,
interconnected and mutually dependent,
the mechanism to achieve peace and harmony,
lies in the ruler's actions,
upholding laws and selecting the worthy,
the state depends on oneself.
If treacherous individuals steal positions,
who will supervise and inspect?
Therefore, I present "The Foundation of Governance" as the ninth chapter.
Observing past and present,
and extending to written records,
rulers all desire order,
yet ministers often delight in chaos.
Loyalty and deceit intermingled,
each advancing by category,
often suffering from lack of clarity,
and believing treacherous arguments.
Therefore, I present "Hidden Sighs" as the tenth chapter.
Position arises from virtue,
virtue is valued when loyalty is established,
what the state relies upon,
is tied to safety and danger.
Without candid honesty, steadfast integrity,
benevolence, kindness, and harmony,
serving the ruler as heaven,
treating the people as one's children,
then none can preserve their rank,
and maintain a good reputation.
Therefore, I present "Loyalty and Nobility" as the eleventh chapter.
The ancient kings managed wealth,
"forbidding the people from wrongdoing."
The "Hóng Fàn" worries about the people,
the Book of Songs criticizes excessive pursuit of profit.
If the frivolous and deceitful are many,
the foundation of agriculture must decline.
To regulate with measures and rules,
how can one not discuss this?
Therefore, I present "Frivolity and Extravagance" as the twelfth chapter.
Accumulating minor faults harms conduct,
indulging in comfort ruins reputation,
the wise do not indulge desires,
without a repentant expression.
Enough to stubbornly reject advice,
hearing good words but not following them.
Minor comfort summons disgrace,
in the end, there will surely be misfortune.
Therefore, I present "Caution in Minor Matters" as the thirteenth chapter.
An enlightened ruler thinks of the good,
laboring his spirit for the worthy and wise.
If all officials form factions,
not verifying truth and falsehood,
merely pursuing empty praise,
deceiving and dazzling each other,
then holding office and undertaking duties
yields no actual achievement.
Therefore, I present "Substantial Recommendations" as the fourteenth chapter.
The sage nurtures the worthy,
to benefit all the people.
The system of the ancient kings
ensured all were sufficient to replace farming.
Increasing ranks but reducing salaries
must lead to decline.
First increase officials' salaries,
then peace can be achieved.
Therefore, I present "Regulating Salaries" as the fifteenth chapter.
The ruler worries, the ministers labor,
a universal principle past and present.
The ruler thinks of achieving peace,
the subjects should exhaust their benevolence.
Upright and trustworthy gentlemen
all grieve over frequent amnesties.
Crime and disorder flourish,
precisely because of amnesties.
Thus I present "On Amnesty" as the sixteenth chapter.
The former kings governed the world,
wielding both authority and virtue,
rewards included establishing marquises,
punishments involved severe penalties.
With generous rewards and strict prohibitions,
ministers then respected their duties.
To cultivate great peace,
one must follow this method.
Hence, I compose "Three Models" as the seventeenth.
The people are the foundation of the state,
grain is the life of the people.
If there is no leisure time for labor,
how can grain flourish?
Dukes, ministers, and officials
"exhaust and toil the common people,"
lightly seizing the people's time—
truly something to be indignant about and remonstrated against!
Hence, I compose "Cherishing Time" as the eighteenth.
Observing what officials govern,
disputes and lawsuits are most numerous.
Tracing the origin of calamities,
they arise from deceit and fraud.
To cut off their ends,
one must block their source.
If the people have no deception,
the world will then be peaceful and secure.
Hence, I compose "Settling Lawsuits" as the nineteenth.
The Five Emperors and Three Kings,
their superiority and inferiority have reasons.
Though one may wish to surpass the sovereigns,
one must first achieve peace.
"It takes a generation for benevolence to prevail,"
is the teaching of Zhòngní.
Encountering decline and treacherous shepherds,
how can one avoid using punishments?
Hence, I compose "Declining Systems" as the twentieth.
The sage kings, concerned and encouraging,
selected and trained generals and commanders,
bestowing upon them axes of authority,
and granting them power and rank.
Truly, many are obscured and ignorant,
unaware of changing circumstances,
with rewards and punishments unclear—
how can they avoid defeat?
Hence, I compose "Encouraging Generals" as the twenty-first.
Barbarians troubling Xià,
a worry of both ancient and modern times.
Yáo and Shùn worried for the people,
Gāoyáo defended against rebellion;
King Xuān revived the realm,
Nánzhòng campaigned at the borders.
Now the people die daily,
how can they not diminish?
Hence, I compose "Rescuing the Borders" as the twenty-second.
In general, the sentiments of the people
differ from those of the ruler,
unable to consider long-term plans,
supervisors enforce a single system,
if they harbor private opinions,
and take them as state policy.
One should examine their words,
to interrogate their so-called reasons.
Hence, I compose "Border Deliberations" as the twenty-third.
The borders being distant gates,
the grand administrators wield power arbitrarily.
The court offices do not investigate,
believing their treacherous words,
causing commanderies and counties to decay,
driving the people to migrate inward.
Now again there are mounds and wastelands,
I fear rebellious thoughts will surely arise.
Hence, I compose "Substantive Borders" as the twenty-fourth.
Heaven produces divine things,
"the sages take them as models."
Yarrow stalks and tortoise shells for divination,
to resolve doubts and suspicions.
Common practitioners grasp shallow sources,
unable to exhaust their potential.
Since the great are not worthy,
how can they be worth trusting?
Hence, I compose "Divination Categories" as the twenty-fifth.
The "Yì" has scribes and shamans,
the "Shī" has skilled invocators.
The sames first accomplish,
the people later exert effort.
When the myriad people are encouraged and joyful,
the spirits then bestow blessings.
Confucius did not pray,
to illuminate that virtue lies within.
Hence, I compose "Shaman Categories" as the twenty-sixth.
The Five Phases and Eight Trigrams,
are born from yīn and yáng,
endowed with qi, thick or thin,
manifesting their forms.
Heaven inscribes its images,
humans truly receive and complete them.
If one does not cultivate one's conduct,
fortune and prosperity will not arrive.
Hence, I compose "Physiognomy Categories" as the twenty-seventh.
The "Shī" speaks of auspicious dreams,
the transmitted texts also mention many,
observing actions and events,
the verification of omens is not false.
Fortune comes from goodness,
calamity arises from flawed virtue,
the responses of good and ill fortune,
correspond to one's conduct.
Hence, I compose "Dream Categories" as the twenty-eighth.
Debates and difficulties erupt uncontrollably,
causing the Way to be blocked.
Later learners become confused,
not knowing what to follow.
Since the past Gēngzǐ year,
there have been criticisms.
"Do I love debate?"
It is to illuminate the truth.
Hence, I compose "Resolving Difficulties" as the twenty-ninth.
In friendships,
righteousness lies in the six bonds,
"restrained by dignified manners,"
discussing and practicing the kingly Way,
cherishing enduring commitments,
unchanged by high or low status.
Now people have long drifted away,
unable to uphold this.
Hence, I compose "Social Intercourse" as the thirtieth.
The ruler has fine praise,
the minister has a good name,
when the two are of one mind,
their wishes are then fulfilled.
Treasure authority and divine methods,
do not reveal conditions below,
once the governing situation is settled,
none can ultimately overturn it.
Hence, I compose "Clarifying Loyalty" as the thirty-first.
Human and heavenly feelings connect,
qi resonates and harmonizes,
good and evil influence each other,
different aspects transform and change.
The sages operate this,
as if steering boats and chariots,
arousing the people's spirit,
none can contain the excellence.
Hence, I compose "Fundamental Instructions" as the thirty-second.
Enlightened kings govern,
nothing greater than transforming through personal example,
with the Dào and virtue as the foundation,
and benevolence and righteousness as aids.
Thoughts align with governance,
urging the people to broad endeavors,
the four seas are then ordered,
what rise and fall can there be?
Hence, I compose "Transformation Through Virtue" as the thirty-third.
Looking up to the great antiquity,
the movements of the Five Phases,
consulting the "Shī" and "Shū,"
examining previous instructions.
When qi ends and measures are exhausted,
later generations again advance.
Though not necessarily correct,
one may rely on transmitted accounts.
Hence, I compose "Records of the Five Virtues" as the thirty-fourth.
The noble person has broad knowledge,
"of former words and past deeds."
"Classifying clans and distinguishing things,"
in ancient times there were these surnames.
Broadly observing similarities...
Hence, I compose "Records of Clans and Surnames" as the thirty-fifth.
